title: Ravens host 3 OL for workouts, including former Lions C Graham Glasgow
summary: The Baltimore Ravens hosted a trio of offensive linemen for workouts on Tuesday following injuries to centers Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic. Headlining the group was Graham Glasgow, a 10-year veteran with 136 starts for the Lions and Broncos under his belt, including a few dozen at center. He was joined by Kingsley Eguakun, his […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 04: Graham Glasgow #60 of the Detroit Lions runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at Ford Field on December 4, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens hosted a trio of offensive linemen for workouts on Tuesday following injuries to centers Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic. Headlining the group was Graham Glasgow, a 10-year veteran with 136 starts for the Lions and Broncos under his belt, including a few dozen at center. He was joined by Kingsley Eguakun, his backup in Detroit last year, and Kyle Hergel, who finished the 2025 season in Chicago working with then-Bears, now-Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. Glasgow will immediately be an appealing name to Ravens fans for his experience at center and contributions to the Lions’ strong offenses over the past few years. His release in March due to a failed physical designation will require a thorough medical evaluation of his knee, but he could be Baltimore’s best, most obvious solution to their current crisis. With over 3,500 career snaps at both center and right guard, he could move Ioane back to his natural position and use his decade of experience – including two years under Ben Johnson, Doyle’s mentor – to help Lamar Jackson at the line of scrimmage. Eguakun and Hergel profile more as depth options. The former started two games in place of Glasgow in Detroit last year and only plays center; the latter has not played in the regular season since 2024 and can line up at all three interior spots.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens open as massive favorites in Week 4 vs. winless Titans
summary: The Baltimore Ravens’ Week 2 matchup against the New Orleans Saints seemed like a potential trap game with an early 8.5-point line. A perfect storm of injuries, penalties, coaching miscues, and some poor officiating brought about a Ravens loss by seven points, representing a 15.5-point swing from the original line. Week 4 seems significantly less […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 27: Head coach Robert Saleh of the Tennessee Titans looks on during the first quarter against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on September 27, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens’ Week 2 matchup against the New Orleans Saints seemed like a potential trap game with an early 8.5-point line. A perfect storm of injuries, penalties, coaching miscues, and some poor officiating brought about a Ravens loss by seven points, representing a 15.5-point swing from the original line. Week 4 seems significantly less likely to bring such surprises. The Ravens are 11.5-point favorites for their upcoming face-off with the winless Tennessee Titans ( via FanDuel Sportsbook ). Robert Saleh’s defense ranks 10th in points and yards allowed, but the Titans offense has mustered just 37 points and 748 yards through three games, both bottom-three marks in the NFL. Saleh has been in this position before. The last time he faced the Ravens, his 2022 Jets defense held Lamar Jackson to just 230 total yards and the rest of Baltimore’s backfield to just 46 rushing yards. New York’s offense, though, produced only two field goals, went two-for-14 on third down, and turned the ball over three times, leading to a 24-6 Ravens victory. This week’s contest could go in a similar direction. The Ravens are scrambling for answers along their offensive line after “long-term” injuries to Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic , the only centers on the 53-man roster or practice squad. First-round rookie Vega Ioane is likely the team’s immediate answer, but that will bring Andrew Vorhees into the starting lineup at right guard. Not only will Ioane have to pick up the center position after just a handful of snaps there during his 2024 junior season at Penn State, Vorhees will also have to bounce back after a rough 2025 campaign as the Ravens’ starting left guard. Head coach Jesse Minter was optimistic about left tackle Ronnie Stanley’s status during his Monday press conference, but his ability to return from a toe injury also remains to be seen. 2025 fifth-round pick Carson Vinson held up in his first regular-season start and the Titans’ edge rushers have not been especially productive so far, so that may be less of a concern than the interior shuffle. With Zay Flowers trending in a positive direction, the Ravens offense should still be able to put up points, but it may not be able to mount long drives and dominate every second of possession time. Baltimore’s defense, though, will have a chance for a confidence-builder against their easiest opponent of the season. Tennessee is dealing with similar injury issues at right guard after placing starter Fernando Carmona and backup Jackson Slater on IR. Their running game has been solid, but quarterback Cam Ward is averaging just 168 passing yards per game and 5.7 yards per attempt. If the Ravens can built any sort of a lead and force Ward to start dropping back, their defensive line and secondary could feast.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Buffalo Bills were tipping point in Drake Maye’s deterioration
summary: Did the Buffalo Bills break Drake Maye last season? Of course I’m referencing after halftime in the second meeting between the Bills and Patriots in 2025, when Buffalo erased a 24-7 deficit to win 35-31 in Foxboro. Maye has been almost an entirely different quarterback after emerging from the locker room in that contest. In […]
full_text: Did the Buffalo Bills break Drake Maye last season? Of course I’m referencing after halftime in the second meeting between the Bills and Patriots in 2025, when Buffalo erased a 24-7 deficit to win 35-31 in Foxboro. Maye has been almost an entirely different quarterback after emerging from the locker room in that contest. In his 13 games before hosting the Bills in Week 15 last season and including the first half of that game against Buffalo these were his statistics (13.5 contests): Completion rate: 71.8% Yards per attempt: 8.87 Pass TD: 23 INTs: 6 Passer rating: 111.9 Sacks taken per game: 2.52 In the first half against Buffalo in that game, Maye was 9-of-11 for 108 yards (9.8 yards per attempt) without a touchdown or interception. And here are Maye’s numbers starting with the second half of that Bills game onward, entering Week 4 this season (9.5 contests): Completion rate: 64.4% Yards per attempt: 7.75 Pass TD: 15 INTs: 12 Passer rating: 88.1 Sacks taken per game: 3.89 In the second half against Buffalo in that game, Maye was 5-of-12 for 47 yards (3.9 yards per attempt) without a touchdown and one interception. Because I can’t split EPA per play by half, if Maye’s EPA per play is calculated in the 13 games before he faced the Bills at home in Week 15 last year, it was a seismic +0.286. For reference, Josh Allen’s EPA per play (not counting plays with a penalty) in his MVP season of 2024 was +0.260. Then, counting the Week 15 Bills game and afterward until now (10 contests), Maye’s EPA per play has sunk to +0.068 . For perspective here, that figure is in the range of rookie-year Bo Nix and 2024 Geno Smith, his last campaign with the Seahawks, using nflverse data to calculate EPA. Now, of course, in the playoffs, Maye did deal with a challenging stretch of defenses; Chargers (No. 5 regular-season EPA per play allowed), then the Texans (No. 2), then the Broncos in the AFC title game (No. 7), before facing the Seahawks in the Super Bowl (No. 1). But in the final three games of the regular season in 2025 post-Week 15 loss to the Bills, Maye faced the No. 19-ranked Ravens defense, the No. 31-ranked Jets, and No. 23-ranked Dolphins. And thus far in 2026, the Jaguars are No. 2, Seahawks are No. 3, and Steelers are No. 12 in EPA per play allowed defensively. So Maye hasn’t had it particularly easy since Week 15 of last year, but the performance-dip has been seismic. Per the Patriots own website , the Bills played with a single-high safety on 42.9% of his drop backs in the first half of that fateful Week 15 game before switching to a two-high look on 86.7% in the second half. And Maye struggles vs. two-high looks continued in the rest of the regular season and throughout the playoffs, as his passer rating was only 89.2 against them vs. 110.9 against single high. Thus far in 2026, per Fantasy Points Data , Maye does have a robust 9.48 yards-per-attempt average vs. two-high safety alignments but four of his six interceptions have came against them. We’ll see if Maye’s downward trend continues this Sunday in the new Highmark Stadium. If it does, now you know the tipping point came during halftime of last season’s loss to the Bills.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: NFL power rankings: Bills are No. 1, but nobody knows what to make of the Patriots
summary: Three weeks into the 2026 NFL season, there seems to be a growing consensus about the Buffalo Bills. The New England Patriots? Not so much. With Week 3 officially in the books, I compared the latest NFL power rankings from ESPN, NFL. com, CBS Sports, USA Today and Sports Illustrated. The results couldn’t paint much […]
full_text: Three weeks into the 2026 NFL season, there seems to be a growing consensus about the Buffalo Bills. The New England Patriots? Not so much. With Week 3 officially in the books, I compared the latest NFL power rankings from ESPN, NFL. com, CBS Sports, USA Today and Sports Illustrated. The results couldn’t paint much more different pictures of the two AFC East rivals preparing to meet this weekend in Buffalo. The Bills are 3-0 and sits atop four of five national power rankings, while this week’s opponent is apparently anyone’s guess. The Patriots are 1-2 and somehow managed to land everywhere from the middle of the league to nearly dead last. So, how good are the Patriots? Or, perhaps more appropriately after Sunday, how bad are they? Apparently nobody knows. Buffalo has a firm grip on No. 1 Here is where the five outlets ranked the Bills entering Week 4: Four No. 1 rankings and nothing lower than third. That’s a pretty strong consensus for a team that just spent Sunday afternoon repeatedly trying to give a football game away. Buffalo turned the ball over five times against the Los Angeles Chargers, fell behind 10-0 and looked nothing like the offensive juggernaut we watched over the first two weeks. And then the Bills won anyway, 24-16. That appears to have mattered to the rankers. NFL. com’s Nick Shook was the exception, dropping Buffalo one spot from second to third behind the San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs. Even his assessment, however, acknowledged what might have been the biggest takeaway from Buffalo’s messiest performance of the young season: The Bills played terribly and still found a way to win. Across all five rankings, the Bills have an average position of 1.4, ahead of Kansas City at 2.4 and San Francisco at 3.0. Perhaps even more telling is the spread. The difference between Buffalo’s highest and lowest ranking is only two positions. And then there are the Patriots… If Buffalo represents consensus, New England represents complete chaos. Yes, you read that correctly. One outlet thinks New England is the 15th-best team in the NFL. Another thinks they’re 31st. That’s a 16-position spread, the largest disagreement among any of the 32 teams in the five rankings I compared. The Patriots are apparently either somewhere around league average, one of the worst teams in football or any flavor in between. Pick a number. Somebody probably has them there. NFL. com represents the most pessimistic end of the spectrum, dropping New England a whopping 13 positions, from number 18 to number 31, following Sunday’s 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Other rankers aren’t ready to bury them nearly that deeply. USA Today has New England 15th. ESPN has the Patriots 16th. CBS Sports has them 17th. That’s an enormous difference in how national observers are interpreting the same 1-2 football team. And perhaps there’s a reason for the uncertainty. These aren’t the Patriots everyone watched reach the Super Bowl last season. Through three weeks, New England has provided precious little consistency to suggest what exactly the 2026 version is going to become. The glaring reality of the “easiest schedule” in NFL from a year ago now has teeth. Not the same Bills Let’s be clear, this isn’t the same Bills team we watched last season either. That’s what makes Sunday’s win feels significant despite just how ugly it was. Falling behind early, turning the ball over five times, and putting together what was easily their worst overall performance of the young season. It isn’t exactly a recipe for victory. In years past, those were the kinds of afternoons when Buffalo had a frustrating tendency to let a lesser opponent, hang around, gain confidence and eventually steal game the Bills had no business losing. This time they didn’t cave. Great teams aren’t going to play great football every Sunday. Sometimes, the difference its simply whether they can survive themselves when they don’t. The biggest certainty meets the biggest question mark That’s what makes Sunday’s AFC East matchup particularly interesting through the lens of these rankings. On one sideline is perhaps the easiest team in football to place: Buffalo . On the other is the hardest: New England. Buffalo isn’t exactly entering this matchup after playing flawless football. The team has plenty to work on this week. Buffalo escaped those mistakes against an 0-3 Chargers team. Repeating them against a division rival, with everything to prove, regardless of where anyone has that rival ranked, would be asking for trouble.

full_text: Josh Allen. Christian Benford. DJ Moore. Even Deone Walker needed some additional taping. Sunday gave us plenty of reasons to worry about the next play, the next game, and the next month. But the Buffalo Bills walked — although some definitely limped — off the field with what might be only one long-term casualty. Since then, we’ve been anxiously waiting for the first injury report of Week 4. Head coach Joe Brady hasn’t offered many hints beyond saying he doesn’t worry about Josh Allen. Now we have it. And now we can all start making game plans that no one at One Bills Drive will listen to anyway. Here’s your first look at the injury report as the Bills prepare for their first divisional game of the season, hosting the New England Patriots on Sunday afternoon. The best news? Josh Allen isn’t on it at all. Wednesday injury report pic.twitter.com/FOMl4wDPFL — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) September 30, 2026 Did not practice at all: LB Joe Andreesen – knee CB Christian Benford – toe WR Keon Coleman – ankle DT T.J. Sanders – Illness Limited Practice: S Damar Hamlin – ribs WR DJ Moore – shoulder DL Deone Walker – quad Full Practice: LB Terrel Bernard – thumb OLB Brandley Chubb – thumb G Ar’maj Reed Adams – elbow LB Dorian Williams – hip What we’re watching: Christian Benford won’t play this week. The question is, when will he? Is it a minor toe injury or one that’s going to sideline him long enough to end up on IR? Rookie Davisson Igbinosun did well on Sunday, but having a freshman and a sophomore holding down your corners long term is not going to be ideal for Buffalo. __________________________________________________________________________ As for the Patriots, there is now evidence for Drake Maye’s claim that his poor play could be due to some shoulder discomfort. He’s on the injury report indicating he received medical treatment today, even if he didn’t miss any practice time. Here’s a look at what the Patriots are managing this week. Patriots Wednesday injury report for NE vs. BUF: https://t.co/3ECC6ak6ql pic.twitter.com/idSUm1L2ds — New England Patriots (@Patriots) September 30, 2026 Did not practice at all: DT Christian Barmore – Shoulder CB Christian Gonzalez – Shoulder T Morgan Moses – Toe Limited Practice: LB Christian Elliss – Chest FB Reggie Gilliam – Knee LB Dre’Mont Jones – Shoulder TE Eli Raridon – Thigh S Brenden Schooler – Back on NFI List S Craig Woodson – Shoulder Full Practice: QB Drake Maye – Shoulder What we’re watching: If Barmore can’t go on Sunday, it could be a familiar name trying to get in Allen’s face. DaQuan Jones. Also, it’s worth keeping an eye on Gonzalez. A history of shoulder injuries could mean that the Patriots will have a rookie trying to keep up with Buffalo’s improved wide receiver corps.

title: Jessica Pegula hints at wanting to help with Buffalo Bills ownership
summary: Right now Jessica Pegula is one of the best tennis players in the world — could acting owner of the Buffalo Bills be in her future? Since her parents, Terry and Kim Pegula, bought the team in 2014, Jessica has climbed the tennis world rankings all the way to No. 3 — which is her […]
full_text: Right now Jessica Pegula is one of the best tennis players in the world — could acting owner of the Buffalo Bills be in her future? Since her parents, Terry and Kim Pegula, bought the team in 2014, Jessica has climbed the tennis world rankings all the way to No. 3 — which is her current ranking. She has 11 singles titles in her career and has been a major tournament semifinalist four times. Now 32, Pegula is still clearly in the prime of her tennis career, but she was recently asked about her post-playing career in a recent CNBC interview : “I can’t say that wouldn’t be exciting if I got to help out with the organization one day. I always thought that I wanted to be in the sporting world when I was done with tennis.” Probably more importantly than Pegula’s quote is this sentence from the CNBC writer, Alex Sherman: Pegula said that despite the record high valuations and the recent team sales, she wouldn’t want her family to sell the teams they own. That, of course, is huge. Her father is 75 years old. After a tragic cardiac arrest episode, her mother Kim had to step down from her role as the CEO of Pegula Sports and Entertainment. She was very active in everything Bills and Sabres before her medical event. Technically, as one of the heirs to Bills ownership, it’s vital that Jessica is interested in future involvement in the team. She has four siblings — two brothers and two sisters. Laura, Terry’s daughter from his first marriage, started to attend league meetings with her dad as early as 2023, but her exact role with the team is unknown. While the rest of the Pegula children can be spotted around the team from time to time, there’s been nothing official or on the record about their interest in future involvement with the team. While nothing definitive, Jessica’s comments should nonetheless serve as a positive development for the Bills staying in the Pegula family long-term.

summary: Last week here at Rumblings, we wrote two articles on the potential of a Marvin Harrison Jr. trade for the Buffalo Bills, and now it’s time for an update. full_text: Last week here at Rumblings, we wrote two articles on the potential of a Marvin Harrison Jr. trade for the Buffalo Bills, and now it’s time for an update. NFL insider Jeremy Fowler wrote the following in his Week 4 intel article at ESPN.com “Teams are continuing to watch the Marvin Harrison Jr. situation closely, wondering if he would become available, as Dan pointed out last week. He would have a market, though not for a high pick (possibly a quality Day 3 pick, as one team forecasted). Harrison, the former No. 4 overall pick who has struggled in Arizona, showed a slight uptick last week vs. San Francisco with three catches for 43 yards on five targets. But tight end Trey McBride and wide receiver Michael Wilson are clearly the Cardinals’ primary options.” Right now, the Bills don’t have a receiver issue. Not anywhere close to the issue a season ago — and for probably too long of a stretch in 2024. However, I will write — I’m firmly in the “the Bills should be monitoring this situation closely” camp. There have been no reports or even insider speculation regarding the Bills and Marvin Harrison Jr. to this point, yet we will continue to write about it here at Rumblings given Brandon Beane’s trading propensity, and the fact he nearly made a trade for a receiver AND a defensive tackle before last season’s trade deadline. DJ Moore has been one of the toughest, most durable receivers in football since he entered the league in 2018. But Buffalo was very close to not having Moore or Keon Coleman a week ago against the Chargers. Both wideouts were dealing with injuries and played despite carrying questionable designations into the game last Sunday. Harrison Jr. has four catches for 73 yards on nine targets through three games. Those nine targets currently rank fifth on the Cardinals offense. Now that some trade compensation — a “quality Day 3 pick” — has been named does that change your thoughts on whether or not the Bills should pursue the polarizing young wide receiver?

title: Buffalo Bills have near historically bad day with penalties
summary: The Buffalo Bills were heavily favored to beat the Los Angeles Chargers and while they did win, it was a much bigger ordeal than anyone thought it would be. The five turnovers were a pretty big deal, but the chatter on penalties has been nearly as loud this week. That’s 100% valid too with the […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills were heavily favored to beat the Los Angeles Chargers and while they did win, it was a much bigger ordeal than anyone thought it would be. The five turnovers were a pretty big deal, but the chatter on penalties has been nearly as loud this week. That’s 100% valid too with the Bills putting up near-record numbers when it comes to my proprietary penalty rating stat. Note: As a heads up for this week, I dedicated my film and media creation time to a second penalty article on the controversial roughing the passer calls this weekend. Keep an eye out for that. Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts Right off the bat this is bad. Not near-historic as the headline suggests, but still very bad. From this perspective, the Chargers didn’t have a great game either, landing firmly on average. Though again, average was a darn sight better than where the Bills were. Penalty Yards The assessed yards plays out about as you’d expect based on count, but it’s always the true yards where things start getting interesting in my opinion. Buffalo made it very interesting impacting/negating 47 yards beyond the assessed. Buffalo negated almost as many yards as the Chargers had assessed. Penalty Harm Los Angeles Chargers When it’s all said and done though, per my Harm metric the Chargers had an alright day with 7.6 Harm total, decently below our “bad day” line of 10.0 Harm. In fact the largest spike is the 2 for Cole Strange’s count of false start flags. Every year I debate the utility of having the count of the penalty in the graph per player, and every year at least one person shows me why we need it. There’s really very little interesting to see here with Joe Alt’s offensive holding negating a nine-yard scramble by Justin Herbert being the most captivating tale by itself. If you’re into formulas and are new to this metric or forgot how it works, all yards are counted as 0.1 Harm. For Alt that’s 10 yards for the assessed and nine yards negated for 19 yards total or 1.9 Harm. The biggest impediment to their success was perhaps two false starts called with only a single play between them in the third quarter. The first one occurred on 2nd & goal at the one-yard line. Now 2nd & 6, Los Angeles tried a pass which was incomplete. And then another false start to force 3rd & 11. Rather than two or perhaps three goal line runs which likely yield a touchdown, the Chargers settled for a field goal. Buffalo Bills Dawson Knox’s offensive holding singlehandedly had higher Harm than the Chargers’ entire output for the day. Whereas yards are counted as 0.1 Harm, downs and points are all counted as 1.0 Harm for each one. In Knox’s case, his flag called back a Ray Davis touchdown or 7.0 points/Harm alone. The flag itself was 10 yards and also negated 14 yards of Davis’ 43 yard run. Potentially the most exciting play of the game tarnished. On the plus side, the play was on fourth down and the holding occurred after the first was gained, which Buffalo was able to keep. Christian Benford’s defensive holding flag was another major screw up. It gave up a free down in addition to the five assessed yards. It also wiped out an interception. Turnovers are treated as negating four downs of opportunity for your own team. Even in a three-and-out situation, the punt can drastically alter field position, hence the count of four downs lost. The Bills had a total of 26.5 Harm, not even in the same zip code as our 10.0 bad day threshold. It wasn’t the worst game since I’ve made the stat. That honors goes to the 2020 game against the Denver Broncos, that saw three touchdowns negated. But it wasn’t too far off from that record of 33.2 Harm either. A reminder that the Rousseau flag will be covered in detail in a separate article, but as a teaser I’m not a fan of that one being called. Overall, I felt the flags were warranted and the repeated attempts to hand over the game due to mistakes were genuine misfires by the Bills.
author: Skarekrow

title: Studying how much more aggressive the NFL and Buffalo Bills have gotten in end-of-half scenarios
summary: The Buffalo Bills have scored two touchdowns in the final two minutes through three games to begin their 2026 season, and of course, for the vast majority of the Josh Allen era, the team has embraced aggression in the final few minutes before halftime. And in Week 3, we saw the Ravens make a game-winning […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills have scored two touchdowns in the final two minutes through three games to begin their 2026 season, and of course, for the vast majority of the Josh Allen era, the team has embraced aggression in the final few minutes before halftime. And in Week 3, we saw the Ravens make a game-winning field goal against the Cowboys in Rio De Janeiro on a drive that began with 0:07 remaining in the contest. That highly entertaining game also featured a Brandon Aubrey field goal with 0:18 left in the first half. In watching the NFL for over 30 years now, I’ve noticed what has felt like a drastic change in league-wide philosophy when it’s come to the end of the first half scenarios for offenses. It’s seemingly had a major impact on overall coring in the NFL. Those last two minutes of the second quarter normally take forever, don’t they? I’ve wanted to study this paradigm shift for a while now to see if what I’d been feeling observationally was actually true and to what extent the perceived shift has taken place. I used 25 years of nflverse play-by-play data to finally do so. Here’s the foundational table in this investigation, which shows the amount of combined points scored in the final two minutes of games compared to overall scoring changes: Final 2:00 of 1st half points/game Total NFL points/game 2001 – 2005 4.00 41.94 2006 – 2010 4.28 43.15 2011 – 2015 4.34 45.50 2016 – 2020 4.69 46.18 2021 – 2025 4.77 45.02 That establishes a clear baseline. The 4.00 points to 4.77 points finding represents a 19.3% increase in scoring during the final two minutes over the span of the last 25 years. That’s nearly triple the percentage increase in overall scoring during that time frame. The jump from 41.94 to 45.02 is only a 7.3% increase. And this didn’t happen purely by chance. To demonstrate how much more aggressive the NFL has gotten over the past quarter century, check the gradual albeit steady growth in dropback rate in these situations in the 25-year sample: Last 2 minutes in 1st half Dropback rate No-huddle rate 2001 – 2005 74.2% 2.2% 2006 – 2010 77.5% 7.8% 2011 – 2015 81.5% 14.0% 2016 – 2020 82.4% 13.8% 2021 – 2025 80.0% 15.7% Yes, there was a bit of a dip from the 2016 – 2020 segment compared to the most recent 2021 – 2025 segment, yet a clear increase from the 74.2% at the beginning segment in this study. Only an increase of 6% points? Ehh, not much, right? Let’s dig a little deeper and narrow the scope regarding no-huddle rate, which should serve as a clear indication of play-caller aggression in these late-half scenarios. When the clock was between 0:31 and 1:00 remaining in the half, the no-huddle rate erupted from 2.9% in the 2001 – 2005 segment to 22.6% in 2021 – 2025. That’s more than a 7x increase! When zooming out, the same theme is present. Here’s NFL-wide dropback rate by time remaining in the first half: Dropback by time left in 1st Half 31-60 seconds 0-30 seconds 2001 – 2005 75.9% 77.0% 2006 – 2010 80.2% 81.5% 2011 – 2015 82.9% 84.9% 2016 – 2020 86.0% 86.9% 2021 – 2025 85.5% 87.2% Another indicator of a widespread philosophical change late in the first half. Dropback rate was up nearly 10 percentage points in the final minute of the first half across the board when comparing 2021 – 2025 to 2001 – 2025. And it the paradigm shift has generated so much more scoring in the time crunch before halftime. This is where the percentages have moved outrageously. Here are percentage of drives that ended in a score of any kind (field goal or touchdown), sorted by time remaining at time of first snap of the possession: Percentage of drives ending in score 2001 – 2005 2021 – 2025 0-30 seconds 2.6% 7.9% 31-60 seconds 16.2% 30.0% 61-90 seconds 24.4% 34.4% 91-120 seconds 25.4% 36.2% Quite staggering. How about this more narrowly focused scenario: First scrimmage snap with 45–120 seconds remaining Starts in own territory Score differential between -8 and +8 At least one offensive timeout *there were over 490 total possessions in every five-year segment First-play dropback Drive ended in score 2001 – 2005 59.6% 25.2% 2006 – 2010 65.0% 29.1% 2011 – 2015 70.5% 26.9% 2016 – 2020 68.1% 35.7% 2021 – 2025 70.4% 37.2% At this point, these percentage increases shouldn’t be surprising. More signs of aggression — first-play dropback rate rose from 59.6% in the first segment to 70.4% in the most recent segment, and it resulted in much more scoring — 25.2% of drives ended in a score in 2001 – 2025 vs. 37.2% ending in a score in 2021 – 2025. I also wanted to find the sweet spot for NFL teams, when they have started to feel the most comfortable trying to put points on the board near the end of the half compared to how it used to be. And I wanted to sort by field position, score margin, and timeouts remaining because those feel like contributing factors to coach’s end-of-half decisions, right? Here’s the data with 45–60 seconds remaining, the drive starting in a team’s own territory, game within one score, and the offense with at least one timeout. First-play dropback Drive end with a score 2001 – 2005 51.4% 23.4% 2021 – 2025 77.4% 34.0% In 2001 – 2025, teams were dropping back to pass on the first play in those scenarios almost exactly one out of every two times, and most recently, it’s happening more than three out of every four times. Enormous leap. If the scenario is tweaked to the team possessing the ball actually having a lead of 1-8 points, the first-play dropback rate went from 52.1% in 2001 – 2005 to 65.5% in 2021 – 2025 , and, more strikingly, percentage of drives ending with a score more than doubled from 22.1% in the earliest time frame to 44.8% from 2021 – 2025. That’s truly game-changing. Across the entire league. Have these trends continued early in the 2026 NFL season? And how have the Bills attacked the end of the first half? During the 2021 – 2025 segment, mostly due to the presence of Josh Allen, the Bills unsurprisingly stayed ahead of the NFL averages. In the final two minutes, Buffalo’s dropback rate was 82.1% vs. 80.0% league-wide. And its no-huddle rate was 16.5% vs. 15.7% league-wide. Fascinatingly, the Bills averaged a whopping 3.02 points per game in the final two minutes between 2021 – 2025, while their opponents only averaged 1.57 points in that scenario during that time segment. The 2026 sample is significantly smaller than the rest of the study, but the league has stayed mostly the same in all the scenarios listed above. Offenses have dropped back to pass in the final two minutes on 79.7% of their plays (vs. 80.0% from 2021 – 2025). When there’s between 31 – 60 seconds left, the dropback rate has been 88.6% thus far in 2026. That’s up from 85.5% in 2021 – 2025. League-wide scoring is slightly down (4.54) compared to the 2021 – 2025 segment (4.77) in the final minute of the half, but I expect that to change as the season progresses. As for the Bills this season, they have 16 qualifying plays in the final two minutes of the half entering Week 4. Their overall dropback rate in those scenarios is 81.3%, and they have a no-huddle rate of 18.8%. The NFL’s no-huddle rate through Week 3 was only 13.4%. They’ve scored an average of 4.67 points in the final two minutes — they have two touchdowns in the final two minutes of the first half in three games. If you’ve made it this far, you are officially as nerdy as me when it comes to the NFL. I have another, to me, equally as captivating part to this study that I’ll release in the next few weeks. But, yes, the NFL has gotten drastically more aggressive — and better at scoring — late in the first half. Compared to 25 years ago, those minutes have become entirely different, which has had a major impact on the entire game itself.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Trevor Goosby
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: ORLANDO, FL - DECEMBER 31: Texas Longhorns offensive lineman Trevor Goosby (74) protects the pocket during the Cheez-It Bowl between the Michigan Wolverines and the Texas Longhorns on Wednesday, December 31, 2025 at Camping World Stadium in Orlando, FL (Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Texas Longhorns offensive tackle Trevor Goosby. Bio Goosby (6’7”, 312 lbs.) is a third generation Texas Longhorn, following in the footsteps of his mother and her father, among other family members. Doctors found a heart defect he was born with, leading to him undergoing open heart surgery his sophomore year of high school. Since then, he has had no issues and even continued being an absolutely unreal athlete for his size. Athleticism runs in the family: his younger brother is a freshman on the Texas basketball team after being a McDonald’s All-American and his great uncle is NFL Hall of Famer Dick “Night Train” Lane. Goosby took over at left tackle in 2025, earning First Team All-SEC honors, allowing just three sacks. He has started strong so far in 2026, continuing to raise his draft stock week by week. Strengths/Weaknesses Goosby’s main trait is his athleticism, being the fastest lineman in the class. At over 300 lbs., he ran a 4.80 forty yard dash and was clocked at 21 mph via GPS in offseason workouts. He has the size to stick at tackle, especially left tackle, as he is every bit the 6’7” he is listed at while boasting an 82” inch wingspan. His run and pass blocking technique are both near the top of the class, and he has a ton of experience against SEC competition entering his second year as the full time starter at left tackle. While his technique is good, he does tend to get out-leveraged by shorter, stronger defenders. His anchor is still developing, and 312 lbs. is considered a bit light for the tackle position at the next level. Some scouts have questions about his strength, but that could be mitigated by fixing his anchor/leverage issues. Projection Goosby is probably the best athlete among the offensive line prospects in this Draft. He earned all conference honors as a first year starter as a redshirt sophomore, so he should continue to improve this season. The Panthers just spent a first round pick on an offensive tackle in Monroe Freeling, and the first round is where Goosby is all but guaranteed to go in April. With the offensive line injuries and struggles this season, the Panthers should definitely invest in getting younger and cheaper at the position. Taylor Moton’s future, Icky Ekwonu’s injury, and Monroe Freeling’s growth will all factor into how much the Panthers will want to invest there. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Trevor Goosby is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Panthers are all sorts of banged up heading into Week 4
summary: The Carolina Panthers’ week 3 loss to the Cleveland Browns couldn’t have gone much worse. They lost a game they were expected to win, the offense regressed back to the inconsistent form we’ve become accustomed to, and seemingly half the roster got hurt. Now they have to get ready to host the Lions on prime […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - NOVEMBER 16: A Carolina Panthers football helmet during the NFL game between the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons on November 16th, 2025 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers’ week 3 loss to the Cleveland Browns couldn’t have gone much worse. They lost a game they were expected to win, the offense regressed back to the inconsistent form we’ve become accustomed to, and seemingly half the roster got hurt. Now they have to get ready to host the Lions on prime time while down their top two corners among a host of other injury problems. Panthers Injury Report Jalen Coker – DNP – Quad Xavier Legette – DNP – Knee Damien Lewis – DNP – Elbow Monroe Freeling – DNP – Concussion Princely Umanmielen – DNP – Ankle Chuba Hubbard – DNP – Rest Darren Waller – DNP – Rest Jalen Coker – LP – Ankle Bryce Young – FP – Knee Nick Scott – FP – Ribs Devin Lloyd – FP – Calf There’s good news and bad news on this report. We’ll start with the good news because it’s significantly shorter. First, Bryce Young seems no worse for the wear after tweaking something late in the game. Nick Scott and Devin Lloyd are also back practicing in full, so the defense will get a couple of reinforcements to somewhat mitigate the loss of the corners. Now the bad news. The Panthers offensive line is already depleted with both preferred starting tackles working their way back from injury/health issues. Now it’s looking like they’ll be down to their third string at right tackle as Monroe Freeling works his way back from a concussion, and that rarely takes less than a week. At the same time, starting left guard Damien Lewis hurt the UCL in his left elbow and is already considered out for Sunday night. We’re getting close to a group of all backups attempting to protect Young. To make matters worse, Young’s second and third targets out wide are both dealing with lower body injuries. Jalen Coker had been playing through an ankle injury, but now he has what’s being called a minor quad strain. He might be good to go for Sunday, but I also wouldn’t be surprised if he gets held out with the bye coming up so he can get back to full health without risking a worse injury. Lions Injury Report Ben Bartch – DNP – Foot DJ Wonnum – DNP – Back DJ Reed – LP – Rib That injury report looks real nice compared to what the Panthers are dealing with. To be fair, the Lions are still without starting defensive backs Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, as both are on the PUP list. Otherwise, they’re not in a bad spot.

title: What’s next after Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson are placed on injured reserve?
summary: The Carolina Panthers have announced that Jaycee Horn (quadriceps) and Mike Jackson (groin) have been placed on injured reserve. That ends their season for at least the next four games, likely longer in at least Horn’s case. For those keeping track at home, Horn and Jackson formed one of the more formidable cornerback duos in […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - NOVEMBER 24: Mike Jackson #2 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates an interception with Jaycee Horn #8 of the Carolina Panthers during an NFL game against the San Francisco 49ers on November 24, 2025 at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have announced that Jaycee Horn (quadriceps) and Mike Jackson (groin) have been placed on injured reserve . That ends their season for at least the next four games, likely longer in at least Horn’s case. For those keeping track at home, Horn and Jackson formed one of the more formidable cornerback duos in the NFL and were the top two defensive backs on the Panthers team. Fifth year veteran Akayleb Evans, third year veteran Chau Smith-Wade, and rookie 4th round pick Will Lee III make up the entirety of the team’s current cornerback room. Evans, Smith-Wade, and Lee have all flashed higher end talent in the past. Lee earned the starting nickel corner spot this offseason as a rookie and has had a number of near-highlight worthy plays paired with his fair share of rookie blunders. They all make for good depth at this point in their careers, but look for the Panthers to seek out veteran help in advance of this week’s Sunday Night Football match up against the Detroit Lions. The veteran cornerback market is understandably thin at this point in the season. You have talented-but-injury-prone guys like Marshon Lattimore on the one hand, over-the-hill-journeymen like C.J. Goodwin (36) on the other, and guys with every other story in between. Dicaprio Bootle, who has not been on a 53-man roster since spending part of the 2024 season with the Los Angeles Chargers, may be the only veteran corner on the market currently with any direct experience with Ejiro Evero in Charlotte. Alph Other free agent options include Bene Benwikere (35), (Eric Davis (58), Chris Gamble (43), Captain Munnerlyn (38, and still in Charlotte), Josh Norman (38), Melvin White (36). Second year corner and former undrafted free agent Corey Thornton is also currently on the team’s practice squad. The long story short is that pickings are slim.

title: Panthers vs. Browns game review: Pain.
summary: Not that there are options aplenty to choose from, but Sunday’s loss to the Cleveland Browns is the worst of the season so far. The 22 point loss to the Chicago Bears was rough, but there was plenty to work with from that game that acted as the light at the end of the tunnel. […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 27: Deshaun Watson #4 of the Cleveland Browns and Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers meet on the field following the Browns 21-18 win at Huntington Bank Field on September 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Not that there are options aplenty to choose from, but Sunday’s loss to the Cleveland Browns is the worst of the season so far. The 22 point loss to the Chicago Bears was rough, but there was plenty to work with from that game that acted as the light at the end of the tunnel. Unfortunately, that light turned out to be the train and the impact of which has left the Carolina Panthers hurting. The resulting rash of significant injuries to significant players have piled up and how the Panthers pivot from here is going to be crucial to set up what the team surely hopes to be playoff run. In order to make that happen, many of the mistakes that reared their head during the match-up cannot continue to be repeated. Many of these pain points are repeat errors from previous weeks and have lingered from season to season. Some may disagree, but I almost always take the view of penalties are a symptom of a lack of discipline or abundance of aggression. However, there are plenty of examples of, well, let’s call them a difference of perspective between myself and the officials. For example, when I read “if contact by an opponent materially affects a passer… intentional grounding rules do not apply” in the official playing rules of the National Football League I think it’s straightforward and the officials think… something else. A penalty within the first 2 minutes of the game that resulted in -1.82 expected points added; rough but not something that cannot be overcome. The real back breakers for the Panthers , were two flags thrown on defensive players. Will Lee, who projects as the team’s starter with Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn both dealing with injuries, had a holding call on the opposite side of the field from the direction Deshaun Watson was scrambling/looking. A completely unforced bite on a double move that had a 0% chance of being thrown and a desperation jersey tug turned a sack on Watson on 2nd and 20 into a fresh set of downs. 1.33 expected points added for the Browns. Lastly, and a scenario that repeated itself from the aforementioned Bears loss, was a roughing the passer call on that turned a game-changing turnover into a touchdown the other way. Bobby Okereke’s roughing the passer added 1.92 expected points, the eventual touchdown was the very same one where Horn reportedly tore his quad. While penalties are frustrating, the single greatest factor that held the team back from victory was the inability to block. The pressure rate used for the Weekly Stat Reviews on this site does not factor in ‘hurries’ within the calculation. However, Pro Football Focus’ charting does include hurries and counted a whopping 30 pressures generated on 50 drop backs. If 60% of your attempts to pass the ball are significantly affected by a pass rush you’re not likely to have a good day. Young clearly wasn’t comfortable and was moving around with a noticeable limp for large stretches of the broadcast. Not ideal. It’s not all bad, though. There are areas that have improved. While the passing offense was brutal for stretches, Young still managed to throw for 291 yards which was enough to place him as the top quarterback in passing yards through the first 3 weeks. It took many attempts to get there, but frankly the odds of Young ever leading the league in this category were slim to none given the story of his career so far. Another positive area has been special teams. The Panthers are one of the top teams in the league when it comes to average opponent starting field position, and the special teams unit is the key cog in that. Kickoff coverage especially has been very strong, even causing a fumble that helped keep the team afloat when the offense was struggling to get going. The Panthers have a few days to lick their wounds before facing off in primetime against the Detroit Lions. Plenty of football still to come, so until then, keep pounding. Join the conversation! It doesn’t matter that there were obvious and—in some cases—correctable causes for the loss against the Cleveland Browns, this loss still stings. I mean, they’re still the Browns. During the loss, the team lost Jaycee Horn to a quad injury for what will likely be the rest of the season. They also lost Damien Lewis to an elbow injury for at least a few weeks. We expect to see Jalen Coker return against the Detroit Lions this week but, honestly, who’s to say he won’t walk under a piano that is being hoisted up to a penthouse by one precarious rope or trip over somebody’s shadow and fall down an open manhole? The truth of the Carolina Panthers season remains that it will only be as successful as Bryce Young can make it. Taking away his already dubious protection and threatening his weapons does not sound like a recipe for success. title: Chicago Bears Offensive Line Analysis vs. Eagles
summary: While most expected Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson to dust off the same run-heavy game plan he used last year against the Philadelphia Eagles, he pivoted to a quick passing attack that seemed to keep Philly off balance. It was brilliant strategy, as Vic Fangio and the Eagles likely didn’t expect it, especially with […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Joe Thuney #62 of the Chicago Bears in action against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images While most expected Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson to dust off the same run-heavy game plan he used last year against the Philadelphia Eagles, he pivoted to a quick passing attack that seemed to keep Philly off balance. It was brilliant strategy, as Vic Fangio and the Eagles likely didn’t expect it, especially with third-string quarterback Case Keenum forced to start. Keenum hadn’t thrown a pass in an NFL game since 2024, and at 38, it felt like they’d want to limit his exposure. But Johnson had other ideas. He knew Keenum had the experience and enough life in his arm to execute the game plan. They didn’t call many long developing passes or rollouts for him, as it was a lot of rhythm passing and play action. His average time to throw, 2.41 seconds, is the quickest of all quarterbacks this season with at least 30 attempts. Getting the ball out quickly and expertly navigating the Eagles’ blitz meant zero sacks to break down this week! There was one sack, but a penalty wiped it out, so it doesn’t count. At his postgame press conference, Keenum talked about his offensive line’s stellar pass protection and mentioned the negated sack, saying, “PFF may count those.” So with no sacks to break down, enjoy a few clips and analytics from social media about Chicago’s offensive line. title: Bears defense looking to build on strong turnaround entering Week 4
summary: There was widespread offseason speculation that the Chicago Bears defense would be a bottom-10 unit this season. The defense was also viewed as a top regression candidate, particularly because of the amount of turnovers they produced last season. Those concerns seemed valid after Week 1, when the defense gave up 37 points and 478 yards […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: D'Marco Jackson #48 of the Chicago Bears tackles Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles out of bounds during the second quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images There was widespread offseason speculation that the Chicago Bears defense would be a bottom-10 unit this season. The defense was also viewed as a top regression candidate, particularly because of the amount of turnovers they produced last season. Those concerns seemed valid after Week 1, when the defense gave up 37 points and 478 yards to the Carolina Panthers. However, the defense has looked different over the last two weeks. The Bears allowed just three points to the Minnesota Vikings in the second half of Week 2 before shutting out the Philadelphia Eagles in the second half on Monday night. According to Fox Sports , through the first three weeks of the season, the Bears defense ranks seventh in scoring defense, allowing 17.7 points per game. In total defense, they rank 15th. Seahawks – 83.1 3. Falcons – 81.6 4. Raiders – 81.1 5. Jaguars – 80.6 6. Buccaneers – 79.0 T7. Chiefs – 78.8 T7. Patriots – 78.8 T7. Bears – 78.8 10. Rams – 78.5 pic.twitter.com/EFON9I1EXk — Pro Football Network (@PFN365) September 29, 2026 After a rough showing in Week 1 followed by two strong defensive performances, the question now is which version of the Bears defense we can expect to see each week and what has contributed to its recent success. When asked about the defense’s turnaround from Week 1 to the last two weeks, Bears head coach Ben Johnson said, “We’re going to continue to get better as far as I’m concerned. We got great competition on all three levels, and I would say, still, we’re trying to define what the roles are, what the best places are for some of these guys … I think that competition is going to continue to make us better overall. I think DA is doing a great job with these game plans right now, mixing things up and making it challenging for opposing offensive coordinators to call a game.” He noted that it’s still a “small sample size,” but said that as the Bears play more games, they’ll get a better feel for the identity of the defense. title: Kyler Gordon Activated From PUP, Practice Window Open
summary: The Chicago Bears activated CB Kyler Gordon from the PUP (physically unable to perform) list on Wednesday, opening his 21-day practice window and paving the way for a return to the field. This does not mean that Gordon will play this weekend against the New York Jets. Gordon was required to miss the first four […]
full_text: The Chicago Bears activated CB Kyler Gordon from the PUP (physically unable to perform) list on Wednesday, opening his 21-day practice window and paving the way for a return to the field. This does not mean that Gordon will play this weekend against the New York Jets. Gordon was required to miss the first four games of the 2026 season given his injury designation, so the earliest he could return would be the October 11 game against the Green Bay Packers. Gordon has been sidelined with a calf injury that he sustained in offseason workouts. He missed training camp and all of the preseason due to the injury. It’s a familiar story for Gordon, who was once considered one of the top nickel cornerbacks in the NFL. He will have to earn that reputation back after playing in just three regular season games in 2025 and none so far this season. Gordon had two stints on injured reserve last year due to soft tissue injuries, though he did play in both of the team’s postseason games last January. Bears coach Ben Johnson and general manager Ryan Poles have both sounded uncertain and uncommitted about Gordon’s status when asked during media sessions, leading to a great amount of speculation about frustration within the team’s Lake Forest headquarters about the star cornerback’s status. There was also a report about frustration related to the medical personnel that Gordon has been working with outside of team headquarters. That being said, the controversies will all become background noise if Gordon is able to return to the field at his previously high level of play. Time will tell if that’s the case.

title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Won vs. the Philadelphia Eagles
summary: Welcome back to the third installment of my new series for the 2026 season, where I recap what I believe were the three reasons the Chicago Bears won or lost the previous game. In week 3, the Bears hosted the 2-0 Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night in front of a national audience and played inspired […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after defeating the Philadelphia Eagles in the game at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the third installment of my new series for the 2026 season, where I recap what I believe were the three reasons the Chicago Bears won or lost the previous game. In week 3, the Bears hosted the 2-0 Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night in front of a national audience and played inspired team football without Caleb Williams as he recovers from a hamstring injury. Here are my three reasons why they won. 1. Ben Johnson, HC With the exception of one series where I would have liked for him to kick a field goal after Rome Odunze committed his weekly drop, this time in the endzone, Ben called his best game of the season and completely outcoached Nick Sirianni AND Eagles DC Vic Fangio. The fact that he did so with 3rd string QB Case Keenum (more on him later) was even more impressive. For me, I was most pleased with the decrease in penalties as that has been hindering us the first two weeks of the season. Ben had these Bears ready to play and bounce back from a lackluster effort the week prior in their first real emotional and mental test of the season. He also seemed to relish the opportunity to do so without a 1st overall pick at QB for him for the first time in his play calling career. Overall, it was a near 50/50 split of run and pass with some of the creative genius sprinkled throughout the game and the players were ready to play. I gave him blame last week in Chicago’s loss, and he bounced back in a big way against a playoff contender. Exactly what you like to see from your head coach. 2. Dennis Allen, DC Speaking of coaches, Ben wasn’t the only one on Chicago’s sideline that was “in his bag” on Monday night. Don’t look now, but the former New Orleans Saints head coach has led this defense to two consecutive games holding Chicago opponents under 10 points per game. This week he did it with two rookies in the secondary against a Super Bowl winning team led by Super Bowl LIX MVP Jalen Hurts. Reminiscent of a vintage Lovie Smith performance, this defense played “bend but don’t break” ball all night. Though All-World RB Saquon Barkley ran for 5.5 yards per carry and consistently got the Eagles down the field, this Bears defense held the Eagles to only 7 points when they had scored 24 in each of their first two games of the season. Allen consistently seemed to befuddle Hurts with the appearance of pressure only to bring it from elsewhere or drop back into coverage. Massive hat tip to Secondary Coach Al Harris for having those two rookies ready to play as well. This team is not the same without Harris coaching the DBs, and he and Allen are doing impressive things with that group that is, without arguably its best player in Safety Coby Bryant. Don’t look now, but these Bears are for real. Even on defense. 3. Case Keenum, QB Nobody can possibly talk about this game without bringing up the performance and effort by 12 year vet Case Keenum who made his first start in over 1,000 days. Not only did Case “rush” for his first TD since 2019, but he threw for two more scores and displayed exceptional awareness all night – knowing when and where to go with the football and spreading the ball around to his playmakers. All in all, seven Bears caught passes from the 38 year old girl-dad who earned himself a game ball and post-game interview on ESPN with his daughter in his lap. Is his arm strength near elite? No, it is not, but it’s hard to argue with the results after his pinpoint accuracy and consistently elite decision-making picked apart Fangio’s defense, which has arguably the most talented defensive roster in the league. It would be easy to forget that Case has been the QB3 this entire season and off-season. Meaning, this was the first and only week that he had any work in practice with the top weapons on the team. That matters from a timing and precision standpoint, but Case trusted in his supporting cast, and they rewarded him with an unforgettable win on Monday night. Things you love to see. Take a look at some of these moments captured by Film Watchers below. These things simply don’t happen without complete trust and awareness in the game plan. In my opinion, there is no way you start anyone else next game. You gotta love it pic.twitter.com/htIJ3p4d0Q — Film Watchers (@Filmwatchers1) September 29, 2026 What about you? Who or what caught your attention on Monday night? Would you start Keenum or Bagent in week 4?

title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL, Week 3 Edition: All Hail Case Keenum
summary: 1. If that Monday Night Football game was a “true team loss” for the Philadelphia Eagles, it was no less of a “true team win” for the Chicago Bears. Head coach Ben Johnson actually had ESPN color analyst Troy Aikman saying NFL teams would take what Case Keenum—a guy who is now on his eighth […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears throws a pass against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images 1. If that Monday Night Football game was a “true team loss” for the Philadelphia Eagles, it was no less of a “true team win” for the Chicago Bears. Head coach Ben Johnson actually had ESPN color analyst Troy Aikman saying NFL teams would take what Case Keenum—a guy who is now on his eighth NFL team—did in that game over what they’re getting from their starting quarterbacks. Also, after a disgusting Week 1 performance, Dennis Allen’s defense has now held two straight opponents under 10 points. With no Caleb Williams there to generate magic on offense, it seemed like everyone earned their paychecks on Monday. (Except for Sam Roush. Come on, man.) 2. For some reason, the juxtaposition between two “go-for-it” decisions in that Monday night game felt especially poetic. Not surprisingly, Aikman spent nearly a half-quarter of action dogging Johnson’s decision to go for it on 4th-and-goal with the Bears up 7-0 rather than simply taking the points. Because there’s nothing more sacred to the older generation of former players than taking field goals over the risk of potentially failing to score a touchdown. Later, with the Eagles down by 13 and facing a 4th-and-1 from their own 49-yard line, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni opted to punt and play field position with the Bears, a decision he expressed regret for after the game . One of these coaches was trying to win the game with a backup quarterback and was willing to take risks to do it. The other was more worried about not losing, or waiting for the other team to gift them an opportunity to win. The team that played to win created their own chances and won as a result. Maybe the old heads will get it eventually. 3. Not Kyle Shanahan busting out a hook-and-ladder in the first quarter to get a score against the Arizona Cardinals. So disrespectful, and yet so clean at the same time. Deebo Samuel Sr. might not have loved the way he was used all the time during his first stint by the Bay, but he’s got to admit no one works as hard to get him the ball as Shanahan does. Also…it’s not at all crazy to say the early MVP race is between Josh Allen and Brock Purdy, who currently has nine touchdowns versus just one pick and leads the league in passer rating. MIKE EVANS FLIPS IT TO DEEBO FOR THE TD @AZvsSF on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/GOuLwblygR — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 4. I know it can’t erase the misery of last season’s ending, but seeing Baltimore Ravens kicker Tyler Loop hit that 56-yard game-winner in Rio this Sunday after blowing a kick to send Baltimore to the playoffs last season was a really cool bit of redemption. Football is a tough sport. It knocks you down a lot—both literally and figuratively. The ones who stick around in the game are the ones who keep getting up off the mat. Good on the kid. Just as cool: Lamar Jackson, who defended Loop after the aforementioned miss last year, looking (if possible) even more excited for his teammate hitting the kick than Loop did himself. That’s what being a real teammate and leader looks like. 5. We just can’t go a week without some controversial overturned call altering the outcome of a game, can we? This latest one went in the Denver Broncos’ favor when a Bo Nix interception late in the fourth quarter was undone by a questionable pass interference call that even rules analyst Terry McAulay hated . The most annoying part of the Broncos’ comeback win, though? We have to listen to more think pieces on how Nix, who is objectively mid, is somehow the best quarterback in a suddenly underwhelming 2024 class. As if Caleb Williams doesn’t exist. 6. The J.J. McCarthy trade to the Giants has made big headlines, especially with Jaxson Dart now lost for the season with a knee injury. But if we’re being completely real here, it’s not going to matter long-term. Dart is so much better than McCarthy that the idea of the latter usurping the starting role from the former feels ridiculous. Plus, if McCarthy couldn’t figure out how to get better with Kevin O’Connell, what makes you think Matt Nagy, the guy who made a healthy Patrick Mahomes look mortal the last few years, is magically going to help him figure it out? There’s a greater likelihood McCarthy isn’t on the Giants’ roster this time next year than that he’s their new QB1. 7. Good lord, the Green Bay Packers stink, and it’s a beautiful thing to behold. They can’t block anyone. They can’t tackle anyone. They just got smacked up and down the field by an Atlanta Falcons team that came into the game 0-2 and doesn’t have a quarterback, for all intents and purposes. I didn’t have Green Bay speed-running a trip to the bottom of the NFC North this early with a healthy Jordan Love, but I’m not going to turn up my nose at it. 8. Speaking of backups: Marcus Mariota did his thing against the defending champion Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, throwing for three scores and sealing the game with a patented run against one of the league’s best defenses. Look at Jameis Winston and Mariota still starting games 11 years after being the top two picks in the 2015 NFL Draft, respectively. Sure, it’s not for the teams that drafted them, and they haven’t been consistently starting-caliber guys for a while. But that’s what being a good locker room guy and a solid student can do for a guy. Mr. McCarthy, take notes. 9. I’ve heard of Super Bowl hangovers. But it seems like the New England Patriots might need to get their collective stomachs pumped. Because this is beyond a simple sluggish start. In particular, Boston media is already on the verge of either discarding Drake Maye, the MVP runner-up from last season who has been dreadful so far (one TD, eight turnovers), moving on from head coach Mike Vrabel, or both. All those good vibes from just a few months ago? Yeah…those went out the window as soon as those vacation photos hit. 10. This week’s question for the audience: whom do you want to see lose more on Thursday night—Aaron Rodgers or Deshaun Watson? I’m pretty clearly a bigger Watson hater in this case, but you’ll never catch me siding with Rodgers just because I’m hate-watching the other guy. Hopefully that game ends in a tie. It’s the closest we can get to them both losing.
author: Khari Thompson

title: Chicago Bears Midweek Musings: Phenomenal
summary: Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: I thought Week 3 was phenomenal. Started with a convincing Packers loss and ended with a convincing Bears win. Can it get any better? We’re three weeks […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears walks off the field after defeating the Philadelphia Eagles in the game at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: I thought Week 3 was phenomenal. Started with a convincing Packers loss and ended with a convincing Bears win. Can it get any better? We’re three weeks into this season but it feels like more with everything that’s already happened with this team. The Bears have a game with the most points since 1980, a bad-weather game where their ascending franchise quarterback got hurt, and a beatdown of an NFC rival with a 38-year old backup quarterback leading the way. The story of the 2026 Chicago Bears has me hooked in the first chapter. Hopefully you didn’t take Green Day’s advice and were paying attention. On to October. I was traveling on a long trip, out of my normal routine. I ate a lot of hotel breakfast food, some bad, some acceptable. I normally go for the hot dishes for some protein but I’m envious of the people starting their day at the waffle station. I like a breakfast sandwich and a breakfast burrito but they’re not nearly as good as a regular sandwich or burrito. Same goes for breakfast pizza. I continue to be impressed with the rookie defensive backs. Dillon Thieneman nabbed his first interception but more impressive to me was his presence all over the field. I’m so sad we didn’t get to see Coby Bryant start the year with Thieneman as that pair of safeties will be really fun to watch once Bryant is healthy. Malik Muhammad may have overtaken Tyrique Stevenson on the depth chart – or he’s at least someone the Bears coaches want on the field more and more. He got the start and played every snap last week. Many fans and analysts wrote off the Bears defense in the summer. I heard a lot of “worst in the league” talk. I’ve never been knowledgeable enough about every single team in the league to form an opinion that strong before a single game has been played, particularly on defense where things aren’t sticky year to year. So far, that hasn’t been the case, with the Bears defense looking incredible the last two weeks. I know there’s a lot of time between the Super Bowl and Week 1 of the new season, but there’s too much time spent trying to fully predict what the next season will look like and then being shocked when much of it is wrong. Okay, let’s get to Case Keenum. I’ve been telling Lester Wiltfong Jr. on Bear & Balanced and in many text messages that I’d want Keenum to make a spot start if Caleb Williams was going to miss one week over Tyson Bagent. I liked the idea of the veteran stepping into a big spot and crafting a game plan around his football brain and Ben Johnson sure had fun carving up Uncle Vic Fangio’s defense with the 38-year-old quarterback. It was an awesome performance as you could tell he was prepared, feeling it, and used up all the luck mana he’s stored since his last start three years ago. I loved this performance. However, I do think the Bears will go back to Tyson Bagent for next week with a full week of practice. As Ben Johnson said, there’s a reason Bagent was named the backup after training camp. Football is not a sentimental business and Johnson will game plan with the players he and his staff believe will give the Bears the best chance to move to 3-1 and I think that will be Bagent until Williams can return. That doesn’t take anything away from Keenum’s performance. Ben Johnson is awesome. I’ll take the occasional turnover on downs in exchange for his aggressive nature. I’ll take the occasional trick play that doesn’t work in exchange for the volume of explosive plays. I love this style of Bears football. It’s a dream come true to have a coach like this, at the forefront of offensive football. On a personal note, I spent two weeks out west this September. My wife and I spent time in Yellowstone National Park, Grand Tetons National Park, and the surrounding environs. We encountered elk, bison, and bears and more importantly, a lot of Bears fans, always happy to exchange a hello or a knowing nod passing each other on the trails. Every day I wore something with the Chicago Bears on it, I got a comment from a fellow fan. It’s also a great deterrent for interacting with Packers fans. I thought TJ Edwards has played some great football the last two weeks. He’s instinctual and a great team leader. Reports of his demise were greatly exaggerated. The victory against the Eagles really helps the season outlook. If the Bears can manage to beat the Jets with a backup QB at home and move to 3-1 on the year, it will take the sting out of dropping the game against the Vikings. One game at a time though because even though that team up north looms in Week 5, that’s the last thing the Bears should be thinking about. Focus on the Jets. Luckily, Johnson knows Aaron Glenn well and was almost certainly writing out his game plan the second after he yelled out “good, better, best.”
author: Jeff Berckes

title: Bears Question of the Day: Should Bagent or Keenum start vs. the Jets?
summary: Where were you for “The Case Keenum” game? This is one we are going to remember for years as Bears fans. A 38-year-old QB who was basically brought on as QB3 so he could be an assistant QB coach to Caleb Williams. A player who has admitted he was about to retire until Ben Johnson […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after a touchdown against the Philadelphia Eagles during the first quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Where were you for “The Case Keenum” game? This is one we are going to remember for years as Bears fans. A 38-year-old QB who was basically brought on as QB3 so he could be an assistant QB coach to Caleb Williams. A player who has admitted he was about to retire until Ben Johnson convinced him to come to Chicago. That man goes out there and makes his first start in over 1,000 days, a player who hasn’t started regular-season games regularly in the NFL since before the pandemic. That man went out there, turned back the block, and turned in a magical performance, leading the Bears to a 27-7 win over the Philadelphia Eagles. It’s been straightforward for two years. Keenum is QB3, Tyson Bagent is QB2, and of course, Caleb Williams is QB1. Williams is going to be out at least one, perhaps two more games. So before he returns, who should the Bears keep behind center? Should Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent start against the Jets? The Bears face the New York Jets on Sunday and, as of now, the only thing we’ve heard from Ben Johnson is, “We will have a discussion as a coaching staff and see where we need to go from here. But I said it last week, and I’ll say it again: there was a reason why Tyson ended training camp as our No. 2 quarterback.” That certainly would indicate that Johnson is leaning towards going back to Bagent, although he didn’t close the door on Keenum going again. What is the move? Should the Bears go back to Keenum, or go back to their long-time QB2, Tyson Bagent? Answer: I really want the answer to be Keenum here, but I think the answer is Bagent. I can’t get enough of the Keenum story. I’m watching every clip and every interview on social media that I can find. It’s one of the great human interest stories I have seen in football over the last few years, and it just touches on all the right notes. It was the perfect game plan, and the Bears executed it perfectly- not just Keenum, the entire offense. But with 60 minutes of tape, you would have to think that an NFL Coach (even if that coach is Aaron Glenn) would be able to put together a solid counterattack on how to defend the Keenum offense. Keenum looked phenomenal. His short and intermediate passes were excellent, but those deep balls looked shaky, to say the least. I think, with the idea that the Jets will be far more prepared to handle any kind of Keenum game plan, that it is probably smarter to go back to Bagent and be able to have a little more freedom within the body of the plan and have a QB with more mobility as well, which should open up the playbook a bit more. Bottom line for me, I’m going to support whichever decision Ben Johnson makes. The man is clearly an offensive genius, and if he says Keenum is the best man for the Jets game, I certainly won’t argue. There would be a part of me that would love to see him get another opportunity. We may not even get an answer until close to game time because Ben may want to keep the Jets off balance, but I do think that, when the dust settles and the game kicks off, Ben will go with Bagent, and I do think that’s the right call.

title: Chicago Bears News: Case Keenum Mania hits, but does he start next week?
summary: Case Keenum has made himself a Chicago Bears Legend with his strong game against a good Philadelphia Eagles team, and despite the fact that many members of the media are telling coach Ben Johnson what he “must do” the coach himself hasn’t announced his plans for Sunday’s game against the New York Jets. Johnson may […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears calls a play at the line of scrimmage during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Case Keenum has made himself a Chicago Bears Legend with his strong game against a good Philadelphia Eagles team, and despite the fact that many members of the media are telling coach Ben Johnson what he “must do” the coach himself hasn’t announced his plans for Sunday’s game against the New York Jets. Johnson may choose to pivot to Tyson Bagent, the number two quarterback on the Bears depth chart. Will he? We will see. Share your thoughts in Windy City Gridiron in the comment section below or by following this link to the Feed post. BEARSSSSSS – LATEST CHICAGO BEARS NEWS & UPDATES Case Keenum’s Monday night performance shows importance of having three quarterbacks Well, three quarterbacks all three of whom can play pro ball, anyway. Third-string QB Case Keenum leaves no doubt he should start vs. Jets, even with Tyson Bagent healthy John Lieser tells Ben Johnson what he must do for the 7,258,257th time this season. I wonder if Ben reads the Sun Times. My guess is no. Dear John, here’s a hint: It’s not loyalty, Ben will play the player who he thinks gives Chicago the best chance to win the game. This isn’t 5th grade flag football here. Even with QB Caleb Williams potentially returning, NFL moves Bears-Packers Week 5 game to noon kickoff This is all about the Packers, and none about the Bears. Eagles coach Nick Sirianni: ‘Remorse’ for screaming at Bears LB D’Marco Jackson after late hit on Jalen Hurts Sirianni would boo Santa Clause too.
