title: Cowboys discussion: What to look for as Cowboys try to bounce back at Texans
summary: Talk about mixed emotions. It was very disappointing to see the Dallas Cowboys fall to the Baltimore Ravens on a last-second field goal due to soft coverage and an unintentional bit of bad clock management to leave a second on the clock. But in a game where many of us expected Dallas to get run […]
full_text: Photo by Buda Mendes/Getty Images | Getty Images Talk about mixed emotions. It was very disappointing to see the Dallas Cowboys fall to the Baltimore Ravens on a last-second field goal due to soft coverage and an unintentional bit of bad clock management to leave a second on the clock. But in a game where many of us expected Dallas to get run over, it was also encouraging to see them come so very close to pulling it out. They went toe-to-toe with Baltimore and showed us some things that had been sorely missing in the first two games. Now, despite being 1-2, there may actually be some reasons to hope for the season. It all depends on how they do against the Houston Texans on Sunday. Our Sean Martin and Tom Ryle examine what we saw, and what we need to see. Tom – The last one came down to a very few breaks and mistakes on both sides. Had they not had a false start down on the goal line and gone up by four points instead of having to tie it, we might be in a really celebratory mood. But there are some real positives from the game that will hopefully carry forward. To begin, let’s look at the run game. Going into Rio, the concern was that Derrick Henry and Lamar Jackson would be nearly unstoppable. The Cowboys had looked unable to stop the run the first two weeks. But they held Henry to only 3.4 yards per carry, and stuffed him more than once in crucial moments. Jackson was a bit more dangerous, but they still kept him from taking over with his legs. Leading the charge was rookie Jaishawn Barham. He had seven tackles, two for a loss, and looked like a seasoned veteran wearing the green dot. The defensive line was far more effective. A glaring weakness just evaporated in Brazil. Keep that up, and we have to have new respect for Christian Parker. Just as feeble as the run defense was the Dallas ground attack those first two weeks. Javonte Williams got his groove back, just missing 100 yards and averaging an effective 5.2 yards per tote. Recent signee Tyler Goodson managed to outperform Henry, at least in YPC, with 3.7. Suddenly it isn’t all on Dak Prescott and the receivers. That is a very good thing, if it can be replicated. Sean – Yeah, it’s not time to panic yet, but for a Cowboys team that hasn’t played a playoff game in the last two years, I think fans forgot what a true gut punch game like this loss in Brazil felt like, until it was too late. To write off the 1-2 Cowboys now would also be writing off the defending AFC champion Patriots, the Packers, the entire NFC South aside from the winless Buccaneers, and the Rams. Lots of football left. You said it doesn’t feel like it’s all on the receivers anymore, but I disagree a little Tom. The next best thing the Cowboys did offensively in this game besides throw it to CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens was run the ball, and yes that was super encouraging how they gained traction on the ground after struggling the first two games. Still, any play that wasn’t in one of these two categories felt like a complete waste, yet Schotty insisted on calling them in numerous big spots. A shovel pass into traffic to Jake Ferguson that resulted in a fumble takes the cake here for dumb play calls. Then there was a real lack of creativity to free up any receivers in the red zone, both early in the game and at the very end. Points were left on the field, hardly something the “greatest offense there is” should be doing. I’ll stay optimistic with you because these things fall into the “fixable” folder for sure, but this team only going as Dak goes is certainly nothing new and I’ll have to see more before I believe these 2026 Cowboys are any different. To your note on the run game, I felt like they got it going thanks in large part to the Ravens having to respect their receivers as down field threats with two high safety looks. That’s one of the things I take away from this game to feel the best about, as they continue to work on what they can do to attack these looks that should continue to be there. Tom – Thanks for bringing up another key point, namely the lackluster job Brian Schottenheimer is doing. He keeps falling into the trap of getting cute and trying to outsmart the other team, when he probably needs to focus on what is working and force the opponent to stop the Cowboys before reaching for a poorly equipped bag of tricks. Take the very first drive of the game. Dallas had moved smartly down the field and faced a first and goal from the five, with Williams having accounted for 44 yards already. But instead of trying to pound it in against a defense that was not coming up with stops, Schotty called a pass in the area where things are compressed and it is much harder for the receivers to get open. It went incomplete. Now he felt they had to pass, a questionable conclusion, and a sack forced them to settle for a field goal. Had they just run it three times, they might well have punched it in, and barring a turnover would still likely have gotten three. I put the responsibility on the head coach/playcaller. I’ve already said that I see Parker developing as defensive coordinator, but it is hard to see a similar progression for Schottenheimer. Given that this is a team that is built to outscore the opponent rather than grind it out and hold on defense, that is something that gives me pause. Sean – Well said, Tom. I’ll add something that is also never easy to hear for fans, but patience is still warranted for Parker. And let’s just be honest about the most obvious reason why, the alternative is a non-starter. This defense has been through three scheme changes in the past three years, that trend just can’t continue. They’ve also splurged at the grocery store for Parker more than they ever did for Dan Quinn, Mike Zimmer, and Matt Eberflus to get scheme fits and commit to this rebuild. It takes time and they’re making progress, and along with the offensive line opening holes in the run game against the Ravens, the defensive line gets a thumbs up as well for the pressures Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark had. Now, Schottenheimer is a different story. I think even Jerry Jones would be the first to tell you there’s coaches you build a team and culture with and coaches you go chase the Lombardi trophy with. Jerry wants that Lombardi, but would he be willing to have a short fuse with Schotty if it comes to that? Let me be crystal clear – I’m far from wanting to move on from him yet, but he has the menu in his hands on Sundays and isn’t ordering the right things often enough. In fact, he’s had his lunch eaten by two of the three defensive minded head coaches on the schedule so far, only beating the one he coached in the same building with Dan Quinn. I think we are going to learn a lot about this Cowboys team and staff the next two weeks specifically because of their opponents. At the moment they are both winless, and will be playing with a sense of desperation that Dallas has struggled to deal with in opponents before. They need to be prepared, look the part, and execute to get two wins in a row here. Anything short of that and the tone of these weekly chats is going to change, my friend. I am off to Idaho for a Friday night, under the lights Big Sky conference game between #1 Montana State and Idaho. Enjoy the football weekend Tom, the Governor’s Cup awaits!
author: Sean Martin

title: Cowboys Week 4 opponent: Who are the 2026 Houston Texans?
summary: The Cowboys are heading back to Texas for Week 4, but their next opponent will feel very different. After opening the season with losses to Buffalo, Cincinnati and Indianapolis, the Houston Texans enter Sunday’s game against Dallas at 0-3. The Texans have scored only 54 points through three games, but their record doesn’t tell the […]
full_text: Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images | Getty Images The Cowboys are heading back to Texas for Week 4, but their next opponent will feel very different. After opening the season with losses to Buffalo, Cincinnati and Indianapolis, the Houston Texans enter Sunday’s game against Dallas at 0-3. The Texans have scored only 54 points through three games, but their record doesn’t tell the whole story of a team that has shown flashes on both sides of the ball while struggling to put it all together when it matters most. For the Cowboys, this is also a different challenge than the first three weeks. Dallas opened against the Giants, played Washington at home and then traveled to Brazil to face Baltimore. Now, after the long trip back from South America, the Cowboys have a much shorter trip south to Houston for an in-state matchup with plenty of familiarity. So, let’s take a look at who the Cowboys are facing in Week 4. The Texans are still trying to figure out their offense The biggest question surrounding Houston right now is fairly simple: Where is the offense? The Texans have averaged 349 offensive yards per game through three weeks, including only 84.7 rushing yards per game. Their rushing attack ranks near the bottom of the league, and the Texans have averaged just 3.6 yards per carry. That lack of consistency on the ground has made life more difficult for an offense that has otherwise gotten some encouraging quarterback play from C.J. Stroud. He has thrown for 794 yards through three games without an interception, although his production has varied considerably from week to week. He threw for 274 yards and two touchdowns against Buffalo in Week 1, then threw for 353 yards against Cincinnati, and completed 16 of 27 passes for 167 yards and a touchdown against Indianapolis. The problem is that the Texans have not consistently turned those passing yards into points. Against Cincinnati, Houston scored only six points despite Stroud throwing 55 passes. Against Indianapolis, the Texans gained only 233 total yards in a 19-17 loss. After the game, head coach DeMeco Ryans acknowledged that the team’s rushing attack wasn’t good enough and said Houston has to be willing to make offensive adjustments. That could mean a more pass-heavy Texans offense against Dallas, particularly if Houston gets some of its injured pieces back. What a play by CJ Stroud! @HOUvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/DeK0gTNhoG — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 Nico Collins could change the equation Which brings us to one of the biggest developments to watch this week: Whether Nico Collins returns. Collins missed Houston’s last two games with a hamstring injury after opening the season with seven catches for 75 yards and a touchdown against Buffalo. His absence has been noticeable, particularly in the red zone, where Houston, like Dallas, has struggled to finish drives. The Texans hope Collins can return against Dallas, but his status will depend on his progress during the week. Guard Ed Ingram is also expected to have a chance to return after missing the last two games with a groin injury, and he could make a plus impact for an offense that has struggled to run the football. If Collins is back, Stroud suddenly has his top outside target again, giving Houston another way to stretch a Dallas defense. If Collins cannot go, Dalton Schultz becomes an even more important part of the passing game. Schultz leads the Texans in receiving yards with 205 through three games, while Jaylin Noel has 101 and Collins has 75 despite playing only one game. What a grab by Nico Collins! BUFvsHOU on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bvCR5tqI6u — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 Will Anderson Jr. is the player Dallas has to know While the offense has struggled to find its footing, Houston’s defensive front has given the Texans something they can build around. Will Anderson Jr. enters Week 4 with four sacks through three games, including 2.5 against Indianapolis. He also forced a fumble against the Colts, continuing an extremely active start to his fourth NFL season. Anderson is not the only problem on that defensive line, either. Danielle Hunter remains one of the Texans’ most recognizable pass rushers, while Houston also has Jadeveon Clowney, although Clowney has been dealing with a knee injury and missed the Week 3 game against Indianapolis. The Texans have generated 10 sacks as a team through three games, giving Dallas another defensive front that can make life uncomfortable for Dak Prescott. That pass rush has been one of the more encouraging aspects of Houston’s start. After the Colts game, Ryans specifically praised Anderson and the defensive line for generating pressure, while also acknowledging that the next step is turning that pressure into more turnovers. That distinction matters for a Cowboys offense coming off a game in which it moved the ball effectively against Baltimore but repeatedly struggled to finish drives. Will Anderson Jr. strip sack! @HOUvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/BMCPhwCwLv — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 The Texans’ defense is still potent Anderson gets most of the attention up front, but Houston has plenty of experience behind him. Linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair leads the Texans with 31 total tackles, while safety Reed Blankenship has 22 and Jalen Pitre has 12. In the secondary, Houston still has Derek Stingley Jr., Kamari Lassiter and Calen Bullock, giving the Texans a group with plenty of athleticism and experience. Stingley has also already recorded an interception this season, although Houston has generally struggled to create turnovers. Through the first three games, the Texans have not been particularly disruptive in that area. That could come into play against Dallas because the Cowboys have shown they can produce explosive plays through CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens and Dak Prescott when the offense gets into rhythm. Plenty at stake this early in the season The Cowboys and Texans don’t play often enough for this to be a traditional rivalry, but there is always an added layer when two Texas teams meet. This year’s meeting comes with considerably more immediate stakes for Houston. The Texans are 0-3 and heading home to face a Cowboys team that is 1-2 after losing a three-point, disastrous heartbreaker in Brazil. Houston’s offense needs to find consistency; its injured players could determine how much firepower it has available, and its defense will be relying heavily on a pass rush that has already shown it can create problems. For Dallas, the challenge is different. The Cowboys have to put the Brazil trip behind them, get back on the road, and avoid letting Houston’s record obscure the fact that this is a team with legitimate talent on both sides of the ball. The Texans may be 0-3, but they have plenty of reasons to believe they can change that record. Sunday will tell us whether Dallas can keep them from doing it.
author: Jorge Guajardo

title: Broncos defense bracing for tough matchup versus versatile 49ers offense
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country. The Denver Broncos sport a 2-1 record after the first three weeks. After tough loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday Night Football to start the season, the Broncos have reeled off back-to-back comeback victories. For their Week 4 gridiron matchup, they have another tough opponent in the undefeated San […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - AUGUST 9: Head coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers and head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos interact after an NFL preseason football game, at Levi's Stadium on August 9, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country. The Denver Broncos sport a 2-1 record after the first three weeks. After tough loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday Night Football to start the season, the Broncos have reeled off back-to-back comeback victories. For their Week 4 gridiron matchup, they have another tough opponent in the undefeated San Francisco 49ers. The 49ers fell short of their Super Bowl aspirations in 2025 losing to the Seattle Seahawks in the NFC Divisional Round. This season, their goal remains the same: securing another Lombardi Trophy that has evaded them for over three decades. Their 2026 gridiron campaign is Kyle Shanahan’s tenth season leading their squad. Over the years, Shanahan has proven to be one of the most innovative minds in the NFL. That’s no surprise, given everything he was able to learn from his father Mike Shanahan and growing up in the world of football. This weekend, the Broncos’ defense will need to perform at a high level to earn their third victory of the season. Yesterday after practice, cornerback Patrick Surtain II talked about the versatility and star power of their offense. “They have a good thing going. They’re off to a hot start offensively. I think they lead the league in third-down percentage. They throw a lot of stuff at you offensively. It starts with Christian McCaffrey in the backfield and what he is able to do not only in the run game, but in the pass game as well. He’s definitely a threat coming out of the backfield,” stated Surtain. “Then you have George Kittle and Deebo Samuel Sr. and all of those guys making plays for them. They also have good perimeter players. It will be a good challenge on the horizon for us. It’s the same system that we’ve been facing these past two weeks, that same Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay system. We just have to be ready and understand how they will try to attack us,” added Surtain. The 49ers are the league’s second highest scoring team in the NFL thus far. In addition to the players Surtain mentioned, quarterback Brock Purdy has had an impressive start to the year with nine touchdowns and just one interception. Purdy has done a great job dividing his targets around with optimal efficiency. There is no doubt he has been one of the best signal callers through three weeks. McCaffrey and rookie running back Kaelon Black have been a strong duo. They’ve combined for nearly 300 yards on the ground and have an impressive 4.5 yard per carry average between the two of them. The Broncos have struggled to win the time of possession battle in their first trio of contests. On the road in San Francisco, finding a way to limit their ground game is an absolute must for victory. What would be even better is more turnovers. So far, the Broncos’ defense has notched four. They are making good on their promise with respect to that. Two of those came last week courtesy of Talanoa Hufanga, who earned AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors for his performance against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football . Maybe, just maybe, the standout safety will find a way to cause some more havoc against his former team. That’d do wonders as Denver looks to earn their third win of the season on Sunday. As always, thank you for reading. Here is today’s slate of articles for Horse Tracks .

title: Bo Nix doesn’t put pressure on himself over slow starts
summary: The question that is making the rounds this week about the Denver Broncos have been centered around their slow starts in games. Mostly that question has been directed at head coach Sean Payton, but quarterback Bo Nix got hit with one today as well when he was asked if he puts any added pressure on […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 27: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos reacts during the fourth quarter of the game against the Los Angeles Rams at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The question that is making the rounds this week about the Denver Broncos have been centered around their slow starts in games. Mostly that question has been directed at head coach Sean Payton, but quarterback Bo Nix got hit with one today as well when he was asked if he puts any added pressure on himself to get faster starts going. “Not really,” Nix said on Wednesday . “Honestly, it can lead to a couple plays I did the other day, pressing, and you just make it worse. My job is just get the ball where it’s supposed to get to, not force anything, take what the defense is giving me.” It was a good answer and entirely true. The last thing we want Nix doing is trying to force things. He’s done a little of that here and there and the results haven’t been great. Nix can create plays on his own, but that is more instinctual football than it is intentionally forcing things. No, early in games we just need to see the offense execute better on early downs and get ahead of the sticks. They do that well in the second half, but for whatever reason suck at it in the first half. title: Denver Broncos vs. San Francisco 49ers practice report: Wednesday

title: Talanoa Hufanga earns AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors
summary: Denver Broncos safety Talanoa Hufagna earned AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors for his performance against the Los Angeles Rams. Hufagna had two interceptions, a game-changing pick-six on Matthew Stafford in the second half and a game-sealing pick on the final play of the game to help deliver a Broncos a much-needed victory in […]
full_text: Sep 27, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos safety Talanoa Hufanga (9) celebrates after the win against the Los Angeles Rams at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Isaiah J. Downing-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Denver Broncos safety Talanoa Hufagna earned AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors for his performance against the Los Angeles Rams. Hufagna had two interceptions, a game-changing pick-six on Matthew Stafford in the second half and a game-sealing pick on the final play of the game to help deliver a Broncos a much-needed victory in primetime. He also had five tackles, a sack, and 3 passes defended. No doubt about it. 💪 RT to congratulate @TalanoaHufanga on being named the AFC Defensive Player of the Week! pic.twitter.com/w8mkeeDnto — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) September 30, 2026 After the primetime matchup on Sunday Night Football, Head Coach Sean Payton had high praise for the veteran safety, who earned a game ball from him for his top-tier play. “He obviously gets a game ball. The interception for the touchdown was the play, just what that does for you and the play at the very end, he’s been such a consistent performer for us and leader. I love him, I love coaching him and I went to give him the game ball in the locker room. I kind of felt that he already had the two prior, so it was more symbolic, but I was happy,” stated Payton. A free agent acquisition by the Broncos during the 2025 offseason, Hufanga has been an impact player and important player for Vance Joseph’s defense since joining the franchise. According to advanced statistics, the sixth-year safety has been targeted ten times this season but has allowed just three receptions for only 19 yards. Congratulations to Hufanga for this well-deserved accolade. Hopefully he is able to keep playing at a high level. If so, he certainly has the potential to reclaim his status as an All-Pro player in the NFL.

title: Broncos at 49ers preview: Denver hunts for another NFC West upset
summary: The Denver Broncos passed their first NFC West test. Now the Broncos (2-1) head to the Bay for the immediate follow-up against the San Francisco 49ers (3-0). And it certainly doesn’t get any easier for Denver. Bo Nix and the Broncos will use the latest thrilling, come-from-behind win to help them overcome this next challenge […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 27: Talanoa Hufanga #9 of the Denver Broncos celebrates after intercepting a pass and running for a touchdown during the fourth quarter against the Los Angeles Rams at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos passed their first NFC West test. Now the Broncos (2-1) head to the Bay for the immediate follow-up against the San Francisco 49ers (3-0). And it certainly doesn’t get any easier for Denver. Bo Nix and the Broncos will use the latest thrilling, come-from-behind win to help them overcome this next challenge in a potent offense led by Brock Purdy and Christian McCaffrey that moves the ball and scores a lot of points. FanDuel Sportsbook has Denver as the road +2.5-point underdog on Sunday. The total sits at 47.5 points, with a lean toward the under at -115. Offensive Rankings San Fran : Fifth in total offense (399.3 yards per game), sixth in rushing offense (136.3 YPG), seventh in passing offense (263 YPG), second in scoring offense (32.7 points per game). Denver : Twenty-eighth in total offense (275 yards per game), 31st in rushing offense (81 YPG), 22nd in passing offense (194 YPG), 21st in scoring offense (20 points per game). Defensive Rankings San Fran : Ninth in total defense (313 yards per game), 15th in rushing defense (105.7 YPG), 15th in passing defense (207.3 YPG), tied for third in scoring defense (16.7 points per game). Denver : Twenty-ninth in total defense (380.7 yards per game), 30th in rushing defense (143.7 YPG), 25th in passing defense (237.0 YPG), 17th in scoring defense (23.3 points per game). Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Sunday’s game. Run the ball The slow starts are the focal point for the Broncos, especially on offense. The best way to help Denver get into an offensive rhythm is by running the ball. Of the 22 offensive snaps in the first half against the Los Angeles Rams, the Broncos only had eight rushes. That needs to change against the 49ers. It not only helps bring balance to Denver’s offense, if successful, but it also helps eat the clock and keep that San Francisco offense on the sideline. Not to mention, you keep the 49ers defense on their heels a bit more, which helps set up play action for Nix. Just don’t be so predictable at the start of the game. — Ian St. Clair Make Brock Purdy uncomfortable Same as last week. This game will be determined by the pass rush. Last week, they got four sacks and made Matthew Stafford rush his decisions at times, which led to a pick-six and a game-sealing interception. They need to get Purdy seeing ghosts out there, because we all know the Broncos offense will not be getting things going until the second half again. — Tim Lynch Stop the run The Broncos need to get their running game going this weekend. They can’t continue to struggle in this regard. On top of that, they have to stop the duo of Christian McCaffrey and rookie Kaelon Black. Controlling the pace of the game on the road in San Francisco will be important for Denver to find a way to win. — Christopher Hart Win the turnover battle Three games in, the 49ers are sitting right at zero in turnover differential. They’ve lost and taken one interception and one fumble each so far. Likewise, the Broncos are at a zero turnover differential, with four interceptions and zero fumble recoveries vs three interceptions and one fumble lost. Nix needs to play his first turnover-free game of the season against one of the NFL’s five remaining undefeated teams, and the defense needs to keep ballhawking. — Taylor Kothe Play four quarters All this second-half comeback stuff is fun, but it’s not sustainable. It falls on the offense to show up early. It’s like Davis Webb needs to see what the opposing defense does for half the game before he starts calling a good game. That probably won’t work against a good 49ers defense. — Adam Malnati What are your keys to Sunday’s game?

title: Bo Nix, fourth quarter comebacks and game-winning drives
summary: The Broncos pulled off another come from behind win, which was amazing for Bronco fans, but terrible for our collective blood pressure. After a poor first half, in which the team was down 16, the Broncos roared back to tie the game at 16. Coming into the game the Broncos were 5-95-1 all-time when trailing […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 27: Denver Broncos safety Talanoa Hufanga (9) leaps before intercepting a last second pass attempt in the fourth quarter during a game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Broncos pulled off another come from behind win, which was amazing for Bronco fans, but terrible for our collective blood pressure. After a poor first half, in which the team was down 16, the Broncos roared back to tie the game at 16. Coming into the game the Broncos were 5-95-1 all-time when trailing by 15 or more at the half. So now the Broncos are 6-95-1. The generally accepted definition of a fourth quarter comeback (4QC) is when a QB leads a scoring drive in the fourth quarter with the team trailing by one score to either take the lead or tie AND the team goes on to win or tie the game. I did not realize until doing the research for this article that it didn’t count as a 4QC if the team ended up losing the game. I distinctly remember a game from 1993 when John Elway and the Broncos faced Joe Montana and the Chiefs. The Broncos were down 24-21 in the 4th until Elway led a TD drive to take a 28-24 lead. Montana then led the Chiefs on a game-winning drive in the final seconds to steal a 31-28 victory. John Elway started 231 regular season games in his career and had 31 4QC and 40 GWD (game winning drives). Tom Brady is the career leader in both categories with 46 and 58, but he didn’t get them very often. This is due to the nature of both stats. If you play for a team with a good defense and a good offense, you are not going to have many chances to lead a 4QC or a GWD. Among Hall of Fame or future HoF QBs, Johnny Unitas has the highest rate of 4QC/GS at 0.186. Brady is at 0.138 which is 8th. If you sort by GWD/GS like my tweet below, Ben Roethlisberger is #1 among HoF (or soon to be HoF) QBs with a rate of 0.215. Tom Brady is 9th. Peyton Manning is 3rd. Most Hall of Fame (or future HoF) QBs did not have to lead game winning drives very often because their teams played with leads often. Big Ben has highest rate at 0.215 GWD/GS. Among active QBs Nix leads at 0.324 (min 16 GS). pic.twitter.com/M5ph9ZzgKj — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) September 29, 2026 Bo Nix has been getting 4QC and GWD at a rate that is astounding and the 2nd best in history for a QB with 20 or more GS. Nix has essentially been leading one GWD every three starts – 32.4 percent of the time. Andrew Luck finished his career at 23.3. Big Ben finished at 21.5. Josh Allen is at 20.8. Matthew Stafford is at 20.7. Peyton Manning is second among current HoF QBs at 20.4. Game winning drives are defined as drives in the 4th quarter or OT that put the team in the lead for good. Future HoFer, Aaron Rodgers, is 125th all time at 14.6 percent. Outside of Vince Young and Bo Nix, most casual fans would not recognize any of the other names in the top 10 below. Maybe they would with Doug Williams since he led Washington to a Super Bowl victory in a game that has been erased from my memory – someone told me they played Denver. Patrick Mahomes is 41st on this list, which, to some, would invalidate this analysis, but it’s more a factor of the vagary of both of these stats. If your team is too bad or too good, you won’t have the opportunity for either. Bo Nix has been in a perfect situation where he can do this and he has been given a multitude of chances to do so in his first two plus seasons as a starter in the NFL. He already has as many GWD as former Bronco, Brian Griese, had in 83 GS. Bo Nix has 37. The hope is that the Bronco offense improves to the point where the Broncos get leads early like the mid-90s Broncos used to, and then hold that lead for the rest of the game. Like Nix, Caleb Williams has also been put in plenty of situations where he needed to lead a 4QC during his young career. He has eight 4QC in 36 GS, which is second to Nix, but interestingly, tied with Kenny Pickett at 0.222. Nix is at 0.270. Among the other big 6, Jayden Daniels is at 0.154 for 4QC and the same for GWD. JJ McCarthy is at 0.100 for both. Drake Maye is at 0.031 and 0.063. Michael Penix has zero of both in 13 career starts. Among active QBs with 30 or more starts, Drake Maye and CJ Stroud have the lowest 4QC percentage at 3.1 and 4.1 percent. I’m not sure how many opportunities these QBs have had for 4QC or GWD, but here are the worst at both among starters with 30 or more GS. What’s unreal is the draft position of those QBs. With the exception of Brissett and Purdy, they are all first round picks and only Mac Jones was late first round. If you just look at passing in the 4th quarter when trailing by one score 2024-2026, Jayden Daniels has the best passer rating at 125.6 and Bo Nix is good, but not great. JJ McCarthy did not have enough throws in these situations to qualify (min 20 throws). He only has 16. I was surprised to see how bad Patrick Mahomes has been in the 4th quarter when trailing by 8 or fewer points over the last two plus seasons. Keeping company with Cam Ward and Anthony Richardson is not good (for the Chiefs).

title: Should the Detroit Lions have made the Joey Porter Jr. trade?
summary: It’s easy to say a team should make a trade in the NFL when you don’t know exactly what the price would be. But last night, the hypothetical became reality. The Dallas Cowboys agreed to trade for Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. The price? While there is still a missing piece to this deal—a contract […]
full_text: Detroit Lions executive vice president and general manager Brad Holmes speaks during media availability at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It’s easy to say a team should make a trade in the NFL when you don’t know exactly what the price would be. But last night, the hypothetical became reality. The Dallas Cowboys agreed to trade for Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. The price? A 2028 second-round pick A 2027 sixth-round pick While there is still a missing piece to this deal—a contract extension for Porter that may or may not be coming—we now know what it would have taken for the Detroit Lions to get a deal done and add what was likely to be the best cornerback available before the NFL trade deadline. So today’s Question of the Day is simple: Should the Lions have made the Joey Porter Jr. trade? My answer: We talked about this pretty extensively on this week’s PODcast, and I am going to stand by my answer: I think the Lions should have done this. As I dug deeper and deeper into the film from Detroit’s first three games, the more and more convinced I became that the majority of their defensive problems could be placed at the hands of their cornerbacks. The defensive line is getting significant pressure, the Lions’ safeties have actually been playing okay (especially after Christian Izien got his feet wet), and while the linebacker room has been a disappointment thus far, there’s enough talent in that room to believe they’ll turn it around. But it’s hard to trust anyone in the Lions cornerback room right now because of the amount of mistakes they’re making. Whether it’s missed assignments, not being able to make a play on the ball when in position, or just straight up getting beat, opposing quarterbacks have been punishing the Lions defense mostly as a result of poor cornerback play. If you don’t trust your eyes, the PFF grades agree. The Lions rank 13th in run defense grade, fifth in pass rush grade, first in tackling grade, and 22nd in coverage grade. And here’s how Detroit’s outside cornerbacks rank individually in PFF coverage grade: D.J. Reed: 60.5 (49th out of 106 qualifying CBs) Roger McCreary: 47.7 (88th) Rock Ya-Sin: 40.8 (97th) Now, is Porter the magic elixir that will make everything better? I don’t know. There are certainly some questions about his game that many have glossed over. His coverage grades of the last three years were not extremely eye-popping: 66.6, 57.1, and 76.6. More concerning, he has tallied 38 penalties over three seasons. Assuming he’d just come in and immediately perform well is very much an assumption at this point. Still, he’s a good fit stylistically, his 2025 season was his best and extremely promising, and it’s hard not to look at his career passer rating allowed (71.5) and not crave something like that on a team that is otherwise pretty well built. The cost is the last thing to discuss, and it’s always hard to fully comprehend the value of draft picks. Losing a 2028 second-round pick doesn’t feel like a high cost until it’s draft day, though not many teams regret giving up a sixth-round pick. Ultimately, I think the Lions could very much afford to give up a future second if it means potentially having a good, young cornerback in tow for 2026 and hopefully beyond. The extension part is the missing data point to fully comprehend the value of this move. At this point, it doesn’t appear the Cowboys have a deal in place with Porter, and it’s unclear if the 26-year-old cornerback will play on the last year of his rookie deal. But this was always going to be the toughest pill to swallow for the Lions. With their tight budget and hesitancy to give massive contracts to outside players, it’s not surprising that they weren’t willing to trade for a corner who is reportedly seeking around $30 million a year. And perhaps they aren’t interested in a one-year rental after their Carlton Davis trade just left them in the same boat of needing a good cornerback the next season. Still, I think it’s about time this team took on a risk and made a play for a player who could fix a massive problem this year and potentially be a solution well beyond 2026. The cornerback problem has gone on long enough. It’s time to pay a little more for some long-term reassurance.
author: Jeremy Reisman

summary: The Detroit Lions were reportedly interested in trading for Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr., but they lost out to the Dallas Cowboys. Late on Wednesday night, it was reported that the Cowboys are sending a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick for the disgruntled cornerback. At this point, it isn’t clear if […]
full_text: Aug 17, 2024; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. (24) gestures to the crowd against the Buffalo Bills during the second quarter at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Detroit Lions were reportedly interested in trading for Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr., but they lost out to the Dallas Cowboys. Late on Wednesday night, it was reported that the Cowboys are sending a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick for the disgruntled cornerback. At this point, it isn’t clear if the Cowboys will be giving Porter, who is in the final year of his rookie contract, an extension. But there are reports he is seeking a contract north of $30 million per year , which would place him amongst the top-six paid cornerbacks in the league. Porter has three seasons under his belt in the NFL and has produced fairly solid plays. In 41 starts, he’s managed 31 passes defended, three interceptions, 165 tackles, and PFF grades of 64.3, 55.3, and 70.1 from 2023 to 2025. The former second-round pick is considered a solid man-coverage cornerback, but he has also committed 38 penalties in three years. It’s unclear how interested the Lions were in landing Porter, but several reports suggested they at least inquired about trading for him . The Lions will have to move forward with the players they currently have for now, despite early struggles that have resulted in Detroit allowing the most passing yards (299.3 per game) and the sixth-highest passer rating (110.2) through three games. D.J. Reed is likely entrenched as a starter, while the Lions are shuffling between Roger McCreary, Ennis Rakestraw, and Rock Ya-Sin for the starting job opposite Reed. Of course, the NFL trade deadline is still over a month away (Nov. 10), so it’s possible Detroit still makes a move.

title: Lions coach Tashard Choice pushing Jahmyr Gibbs vs. Bijan Robinson competition
summary: Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson are linked by many factors. The two were selected four picks apart in the 2023 NFL Draft, with Robinson going eighth overall and Gibbs going 12th. They were also linked by contract negotiations this offseason, with Robinson blinking first. He received a three-year, $66.75 million contract with Atlanta, and Gibbs […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - AUGUST 8: Bijan Robinson #7 of the Atlanta Falcons smiles with Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions prior to an NFL preseason football game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on August 8, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson are linked by many factors. The two were selected four picks apart in the 2023 NFL Draft, with Robinson going eighth overall and Gibbs going 12th. They were also linked by contract negotiations this offseason, with Robinson blinking first. He received a three-year, $66.75 million contract with Atlanta, and Gibbs received a nearly identical three-year, $67.5 million deal with Detroit. But one of the more fun connections between the two players is Lions running backs coach Tashard Choice. Gibbs first crossed paths with Choice, spending two years with him at Georgia Tech. When Gibbs left for Alabama, Choice left, too. But he headed to Texas, where he got to coach the final year of Robinson’s college career with the Longhorns. Since knowing both players, Choice has calculatedly pitted them against each other, in a fun, competitive way. After coaching Gibbs at Georgia Tech, he told Robinson, “You’ve got to be better than him.” That pushing of the buttons has continued upon Gibbs’ and Choice’s arrival in Detroit. Just last week, after Robinson put up a showcase on Thursday night against the Packers—rushing for 194 yards and two touchdowns on 29 carries—Choice texted the Falcons running back to thank him. “You put on a show tonight. You gave my boy something to aim at,” Choice recalls saying to him. Then he turned his attention back to Gibbs. “So I’m telling Jah, ‘Hey, man, they [saying] he’s better than you. You’ve got to go do something,” Choice said. Gibbs responded with a big day of his own, earning 164 scrimmage yards and finding the end zone three times against the Jets. Choice says he leans into the friendly competition because it can be hard to motivate players who are already at the top of their game. “You’ve got to nag a man sometimes, because when you’re a football player, and you have a talent, you have a chance with an organization [that] gives you what you deserve, guys get rewarded, the biggest thing for me now is to find little things to push him,” Choice said. Gibbs admits he has fun watching Robinson play and is happy for his success. But he wants to be the best too, and Robinson helps push him. “We always want to compete, and we always want to be the best,” Gibbs said. “So I mean I think that just speaks for itself.” Gibbs says that still with a sense of modesty. He’s able to appreciate other players’ games and not feel threatened by it. But while Gibbs is mostly soft-spoken, Choice is more than happy to act as his megaphone. “He wants to be the best. He’ll never say that, but his actions are going to tell you that,” Choice said. “It’s going to show so he doesn’t have to speak at all. I think that’s one of the things I’m fond of, because I was the total opposite. I probably should be quiet more, but, for me, that’s why I do the talking.” While Choice is his biggest fan publicly, he admits he’s also one of Gibbs’ biggest critics behind the scenes. He can’t let Gibbs get complacent, and so he continues to badger him on the biggest areas of improvement. “Trying to get him motivated, trying to find something to poke at, because when everybody tells him he’s good, I tell him he’s the sorriest player,” Choice said. “Like he has a big game, and I’m on his head about every single little thing that he didn’t do. That’s what I have to be for him, and I’ve always been that way, and I think that’s why he respects me, because I ultimately just want to see him do better.” One of those areas is pass protection. Against the Jets, backup running back Sione Vaki stepped up in a big way, taking some of the load off of Gibbs. And while Choice admits it’s important to take some of those hits and blows off of Gibbs’ shoulders, they can’t afford Gibbs to be a liability in pass protection, either. “It’s one thing to take some loads off people; that’s what you want to do sometimes. You want to take blows, and having Vaki out there sometimes to take blows, we’ll do that,” Choice said. “But Jah has to block. At the end of the day, from me to him, that’s the biggest thing. That’s the growth.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

full_text: Detroit Lions edge rusher DJ Wonnum (98) celebrates a sack of New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith (7) during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (2-1) will take on the Carolina Panthers (1-2) on “Sunday Night Football” in Week 4, and while the Lions were on the practice field, the Panthers held a walkthrough. The Lions have only a handful of names on this week’s initial injury li st—including two new additions—but the Panthers are dealing with several injuries suffered over the past few weeks, including needing to place both starting corners, Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, on injured reserve . Let’s take a look at Wednesday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . Injured list updates RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back) — IR, expected to be out until December C Cade Mays (Wrist) — IR, eligible to begin practicing in Week 5 OL Giovanni Manu (Undisclosed) — NFI, eligible to begin practicing in Week 5 S Brian Branch (Achilles) — PUP, eligible to begin practicing at any time S Kerby Joseph (Knee) — PUP, eligible to begin practicing at any time S Thomas Harper (ankle) — IR, eligible to begin practicing in Week 7 Mays will need to sit out at least one more week due to injured reserve-return rules, but coach Dan Campbell believes the Lions starting center should be available to practice by the Lions bye week (Week 6). “He’d be ready to play in the bye week. That was kind of always the goal was, man, can we get him after the bye? And he’s doing a good job right now, but I don’t want to put a timetable just yet on it.” Harper was placed on injured reserve ahead of last Sunday’s game, and while he’ll be eligible to return to practice in Week 7, Campbell said there was too much unknown about his injury at this time to project when he’ll be available. “We’ll see on that. I just know he won’t be here for four weeks for sure.” N o practice G Ben Bartch (foot) EDGE DJ Wonnum (back) — NEW Addition Bartch missed all of last week’s practices with a foot injury that has apparently carried over into this week as well. With eight other offensive linemen on the active roster and Christian Mahogany settling into the starting left guard role, the Lions can take their time with Bartch. Wonnun didn’t appear to injure himself in last Sunday’s game against the Jets, and didn’t seem bothered by an injury in the locker room after the game either. With not much known about his absence, we won’t have a clear understanding of his status until we see Thursday’s injury report and speak with Campbell on Friday. Limited practice D.J. Reed (rib) — NEW addition Like Wonnum, Reed played a full game and didn’t appear to suffer a known injury, so fans will need to be patient while we learn more about his rib injury. Full practice None No longer on the injury report LG Christian Mahogany (hip) RT Blake Miller (knee) RG Tate Ratledge (elbow) EDGE Ahmed Hassanein (illness) LS Hogan Hatten (wrist) The players in this section were on last week’s injury report but are now healthy enough to no longer be on the daily injury report. The interior offensive line looked sharp against the Jets, and their injuries didn’t appear to be a factor. With them all off the injury report, they’re all expected to play again on Sunday night. title: Lions coach Dan Campbell weighs in on reviewable pass interference
summary: It seems like every week in the NFL, there’s a game that is heavily impacted by a controversial pass interference call. This past week, the Los Angeles Rams fell victim to a controversial call against the Denver Broncos. Rams cornerback Josh Wallace intercepted a Bo Nix pass in the red zone with just over a […]
full_text: New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) makes a contested catch that was later called a touchdown after pass interference was called against Detroit Lions cornerback D.J. Reed (4) during the second half of the NFL game at Ford Field in Detroit, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It seems like every week in the NFL, there’s a game that is heavily impacted by a controversial pass interference call. This past week, the Los Angeles Rams fell victim to a controversial call against the Denver Broncos. Rams cornerback Josh Wallace intercepted a Bo Nix pass in the red zone with just over a minute left, but he was called for pass interference, extending what would become the game-winning drive. Upon replay, it appeared, if anything, it should have been called offensive pass interference on Broncos receiver Pat Bryant. You be the judge: NBC rules analyst Terry McAulay did not believe Rams CB Josh Wallace should have been flagged for pass interference, in what may have otherwise been an interception. The Broncos went on to score what would serve as the game-winning TD. pic.twitter.com/A0YDJ8ZmZl — Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) September 28, 2026 Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell wasn’t asked specifically about this play, but whether he believes the penalty should be reviewable. “I’m all good with it not being a challenge anymore,” Campbell said. “Those guys have got to make the call, and you’ve got to live with it.” Campbell has an interesting perspective on the topic, as he was part of the coaching staff when the New Orleans Saints were impacted by one of the biggest non-calls in playoff history. In the 2018 NFC Championship Game, Rams cornerback Nickell Robey-Coleman clearly hit Saints receiver Tommylee Lewis before the ball arrived, but no flag was thrown. It turned out to be a critical no-call with less than two minutes left in a tie game. New Orleans would lose in overtime. But the play was so high-profile that it led the league to adopt—on a one-year basis—a rule that allowed coaches to challenge pass interference. That year, the rule change was largely considered ineffective. Of the 81 calls that coaches challenged that year, only 13 were overturned . Campbell believes that didn’t make the situation any better, and only delayed the game further. “I just know when we tried to do this whole thing, it just gets muddy, man,” Campbell said. “It’s so subjective, is what happens. And I think what you run into is the same thing that we’re running into with catch, no catch. There is a— it’s told this is what it is. But yet, man, if it’s 50-50, they’re going to go with what’s been called. And now you do enough of these, now the game gets extended, you’re waiting to figure out what they’re going to say.” The Lions themselves have been on the bad end of pass interference calls more than most teams. Through three weeks, Detroit has been called for a league-high five defensive pass interference penalties, although three of those were declined. While Campbell isn’t in favor of making pass interference reviewable, the Lions franchise did propose a rule related to the topic. In 2025, they sought to remove the automatic first-down stipulation for illegal contract penalties, but it did not pass .
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: 5 Lions vs. Panthers thoughts after watching Carolina’s loss to Browns
summary: To begin my scouting of the Detroit Lions’ next opponent, I like to watch their most recent game played. For the Carolina Panthers, that means checking in on their 21-18 loss to the Cleveland Browns in Week 3. I took notes during the game, and here are my five biggest takeaways on what it may […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 27: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers attempts a pass against the Cleveland Browns during the fourth quarter at Huntington Bank Field on September 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images To begin my scouting of the Detroit Lions’ next opponent, I like to watch their most recent game played. For the Carolina Panthers, that means checking in on their 21-18 loss to the Cleveland Browns in Week 3. I took notes during the game, and here are my five biggest takeaways on what it may mean for Lions vs. Panthers, along with some data to support those observations. The Panthers defense can get to the passer… but they have to get aggressive Against the Browns, the Panthers posted a 38.5% pressure rate, but that dropped significantly when just rushing four. Here are their pressure rates in Week 3 with and without blitz: Blitzing: 55.6% pressure rate (fourth highest), 2.76 seconds to pressure (29th) No blitz: 33.3% pressure rate (10th), 2.93 seconds to pressure (22nd) When the Panthers don’t send extra blitzers, they generate their pressure utilizing the speed of their edge rushers. Princely Umanmielen is second in pressures on the team, only trailing Jaelen Phillips, and his speed and bend were on display against Cleveland. But the Lions dealt with a pair of speed rushers last week against the Jets and held up very well. That said, they’ve got some interior players with some pass rushing skills, including Derrick Brown (7.0 sacks last year). That could be the bigger threat against Detroit’s young interior. Bryce Young’s arm talent is a problem Man, Bryce Young is fun to watch when you’re only looking at arm talent. He can make any throw. And while the deep shots are what get most of the national attention, I’m impressed with the throws he can make on the perimeter in tight windows. Just look at his passing chart against the Browns and how he utilized every inch of the boundaries: It takes a ton of arm talent to drive that ball all the way to the sidelines, and he is not afraid to do so. He is also not afraid to air it out deep. He currently holds the longest intended air yards per pass attempt in the league (10.2) and leads the league in passes of 20+ air yards (17). The accuracy is a bit up and down, but there’s more good than bad there. And while we’re on the topic of Young, his mobility is obviously something defenses need to be aware of. He can extend plays with his legs and his pocket presence is clearly improving. However, interestingly, he is much less inclined to run and scramble. Against the Browns, he passed up several opportunities for easy yards to try for the big play. For the season, he has attempted just three rushes for 16 yards and a touchdown. Panthers’ standard run game struggled, but came alive late For the season, the Panthers run game has been fairly ineffective. They rank 21st in DVOA, 23rd in EPA, and 23rd in success rate. However, they do have the ability to wear teams down as the game continues. Against the Browns, Carolina had just 22 yards on 11 carries through three quarters. But in the final quarter, they ran the ball down Cleveland’s throat, rushing for 76 yards on just 12 carries (6.3 YPC). With a pair of bruising backs in Chuba Hubbard (6-foot-1, 210) and AJ Dillon (6-foot, 247), they can wear you down—but they are not explosive. The Panthers’ longest run of the season is 24 yards by… Kenny Pickett. The running backs don’t have a run over 16 yards. Detroit may need to defend all four downs Panthers head coach Dave Canales is not afraid to get a little aggressive on fourth down. Twice in the first half against the Browns, Carolina opted to go for it near midfield. Here were the two opportunities: 8:38 left in the second quarter: 0-0 tie, fourth-and-3 from the Browns’ 43-yard line 3:40 left in the second quarter: 3-0 Browns, fourth-and-1 from the Panthers’ 40-yard line The Panthers failed both attempts, and it immediately led to two Browns’ scoring drives and a 10-0 deficit. If Detroit can stand their ground on fourth down (Lions currently have stopped zero of three fourth down attempts), it could be a game-changer. For the year, the Panthers are just 1-of-6 on fourth down. Last year, they attempted the second most fourth downs in the NFL (40), converting on 27 of them (67.5% conversion rate, fourth best). Panthers run defense maybe better than advertised If you look at the season-long stats for Carolina’s run defense, they look god awful. They’ve allowed an NFL-high 5.7 yards per carry, 193.3 rushing yards per game, and they rank 23rd in run defense DVOA. However, I think three things are happening: the data is being swung by a terrible Week 1 performance against the Bears, they’re being disproportionately hurt by mobile quarterbacks, and they’ve also just made some clear progress. Against Chicago, the Panthers allowed 291 rushing yards and 7.5 yards per carry. It was a truly awful performance, led by D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai, who combined for 224 yards and four touchdowns on 28 carries (8.0 YPC). The following week wasn’t great, but it was a marked improvement: allowing Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson to combine for 123 yards on 27 carries (4.6 YPC). Against the Browns, the Panthers allowed 132 rushing yards on 4.4 yards per carry—but Quinshon Judkins managed just 70 yards on 18 carries (3.9 YPC). In total, of the 580 rushing yards the Panthers have allowed, 146 (over 25%) have come from quarterbacks. That won’t be an issue this week. Particularly, when it came down to needing their defense to stop the run, they did. The Browns had an opportunity to put the game away late with a single first down clinching it. Despite facing a second-and-2, the Panthers were able to get three straight stops on runs to give the offense one more shot. That is reflected in their overall run success rate allowed (35.6%), which is actually ninth best in the NFL Now, the Browns’ rushing attack (31st in DVOA) is way worse than the Bears (ninth) and Falcons (sixth), and the Lions have one of the best in the NFL (second). But I still think the early numbers are skewing a run defense that can hang.

title: Jared Goff clears up ‘controversy’ about Ben Johnson’s mobility comment
summary: There was a very mild controversy involving the Detroit Lions following the Chicago Bears’ win over the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night. Bears coach Ben Johnson was asked about the night of third-string quarterback Case Keenum, and how to coach a game with a much different skill set than their normal quarterback Caleb Williams. “I’ve […]
full_text: Aug 28, 2022; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (left) and offensive coordinator Ben Johnson (right) talk on the field before the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-USA TODAY Sports There was a very mild controversy involving the Detroit Lions following the Chicago Bears’ win over the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night. Bears coach Ben Johnson was asked about the night of third-string quarterback Case Keenum, and how to coach a game with a much different skill set than their normal quarterback Caleb Williams. “I’ve got a little history with that, calling plays for someone not so mobile,” Johnson said with a smile. “Now, I don’t have a history with someone that’s not a No. 1 pick, though, so that was currently a big deal. But Case came through; he played lights out.“ Some took offense to that claim, viewing it as an insult to Lions quarterback Jared Goff . Goff addressed that situation in his appearance on the “St. Brown Brothers” podcast this week , downplaying the situation. “Ben can’t seem to get out of his own way when he’s talking to the media,” Goff said with a smile. “So I know there was no ill intent to that. He seems to be a lightning rod for them. They pick up everything he says.” This isn’t the first time Johnson’s comments have been construed as an insult to Goff. Back in 2025, Johnson made another comment about Goff’s mobility , drawing a response from Lions safety Kerby Joseph. This time, however, Goff said he has already received a call from Johnson, further clarifying that he did not intend to insult the Lions quarterback. “He called me this morning and was like, ‘Dude, you know that means nothing,’” Goff said. “I’m like, ‘Yeah, dude. You’re good. Don’t worry about it.’” That said, Goff joked that he may throw some shade back at Johnson as revenge. “But I’m saving something. I’ll have to throw something his way at some point, where I’m like, ‘Oh, yeah, whatever. But like playcaller, blah, blah, blah,’” Goff said. “And I’ll call him and be like, ‘Dude, you know I’m just kidding. You know I mean nothing by it.’” Goff even admitted that what Johnson said was accurate. “Probably the lower end of the league,” Goff said, describing his mobility. “But I don’t think he was telling any lies when he said I wouldn’t be considered mobile. Am I more mobile than Case? I sure hope so. I love you, Case, but he’s in year whatever-he’s-in, and I’m a bit younger and hopefully a bit more mobile than him.” So there is obviously no real controversy here, other than fans being overprotective of their team’s players.

title: Lions mailbag: What’s with Jack Campbell’s slow start?
summary: A lot of the Detroit Lions’ struggles on defense were predictable from the start. Many correctly pointed out concerns with the Lions’ cornerback room after the team failed to add significant talent this offseason and lost the promise of young cornerback Terrion Arnold. Missing their two top, Pro Bowl safeties was going to hurt, even […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jack Campbell #46 of the Detroit Lions jogs off the field after an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images A lot of the Detroit Lions’ struggles on defense were predictable from the start. Many correctly pointed out concerns with the Lions’ cornerback room after the team failed to add significant talent this offseason and lost the promise of young cornerback Terrion Arnold. Missing their two top, Pro Bowl safeties was going to hurt, even if they had confidence in their offseason replacements. But what no one could have predicted was a rough start from All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell. Against the Buffalo Bills, Campbell appeared to commit several missed assignments, he struggled in coverage, and was extremely upset with his own performance . He was better against the New York Jets on Sunday, but we’ve still yet to see him make a huge impact. Through three weeks, PFF has credited him with a 44.2 overall grade (52nd out of 57 qualifying LBs) and has him allowing receptions on 12 of 14 targets for 145 yards, two touchdowns, and a 149.4 passer rating. So… what the heck is going on? How has Campbell gone from the best linebacker in the NFL to one of the worst through three games? On this week’s Midweek Mailbag, we try to provide some answers. Some of his struggles can likely be explained through a pretty significant change in role. With Alex Anzalone gone, Campbell has taken a bigger load in coverage thus far. He’s averaged nearly 43 coverage snaps per game thus far compared to just under 36 last year. Additionally, the Lions’ coverage scheme has drastically shifted, going from one of the most man-heavy teams in football to a bottom-half man-coverage team through three weeks. There’s also clearly a trust issues that coach Dan Campbell has referred to many times. “We got to get our trust level back,” Campbell said after the Bills game. “We got to start back from ground level, get back to the basics of what we do. And man, just do your job. Trust it. You got to trust it.” Watching the film, it certainly seems like Jack Campbell is hesitating more than he has before. Whether that’s an adjustment to some schematic changes or a doubt in his teammates, that half-second is often costing him proper positioning. We dive deeper into the topic on this week’s show. Other topics on this week’s show include: What are some clear schematic changes the Lions made out of the mini-bye and were they effective? Did Detroit provide enough pass rush against the Jets? What should the Lions do with Juice Scruggs when Cade Mays gets back? Should they consider a trade? Would a Joey Porter Jr. trade really solve most of Detroit’s secondary problems? Do you think the Lions are even willing to make that move? Have the Lions already put aside money for Porter, hoping they’d give that money to Terrion Arnold? When Brian Branch is healthy, what will the starting secondary look like? Who is in most danger of being cut: Roger McCreary, Rock Ya-Sin, or Devin White? How will Sione Vaki’s improvement impact the offense going forward? Thoughts on the NFC North after three games Catch the full show on your favorite podcasting platform by searching “Pride of Detroit,” or you can just use the Spotify embed below: As always, we have a ton of bonus content from each week’s podcast available in the video version of the show. For all of that, head over to our YouTube page or Twitch channel, where the length of the show is essentially double . We’re also just over 300 YouTube subscribers away from 20,000, so please consider following us there !

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Can the Carolina Panthers offense be contained?
summary: Back under the lights, the Detroit Lions hit the road for “Sunday Night Football” as they take on the defending NFC South champion Carolina Panthers. This’ll be Detroit’s second of four primetime games this season, and it won’t be a pushover. Despite their 1-2 record, the Panthers are an improved football team. So far, their […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 27: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers attempts a pass against the Cleveland Browns during the first quarter at Huntington Bank Field on September 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back under the lights, the Detroit Lions hit the road for “Sunday Night Football” as they take on the defending NFC South champion Carolina Panthers. This’ll be Detroit’s second of four primetime games this season, and it won’t be a pushover. Despite their 1-2 record, the Panthers are an improved football team. So far, their injury luck hasn’t been kind and has certainly played a factor in how this team is performing, coming off a Week 3 loss to the Cleveland Browns. Their offense has taken a step forward, while the defense still has work to do. Let’s take a deep look at the Panthers and how much they’ve changed ahead of Week 4. Carolina Panthers 2025 season 8-9 record (1st in NFC South) 27th in points for, 15th in point allowed Overall DVOA: 25th (25th on offense, 22nd on defense) 2025 was an inconsistent season for the Panthers. They started the year 0-2, then got on a short win streak to reach 4-3, but they never seemed to find their footing to be a playoff threat. They limped into the playoffs, winning the division with an 8-9 record. In the NFC Wild Card round, they almost held off the Los Angeles Rams but ultimately failed, losing 34-31. Quarterback Bryce Young had his best season so far in the NFL, which was a big factor in the Panthers’ playoff push. He threw career highs in yards (3,011) and touchdowns (23), and an offensive line only allowed a career-low 27 sacks helped. At running back, Rico Dowdle took over the starting job from Chuba Hubbard after Hubbard missed two games in Weeks 5 and 6 and didn’t look back. Dowdle ran for 1,076 yards and six touchdowns, while Hubbard managed 511 yards and one touchdown. The receiving game saw rookie wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan take over and win NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year after finishing with 70 catches for 1,014 yards and seven touchdowns. Behind him, the talent dropped off, as the next three receivers didn’t match McMillan’s output: Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette, and tight end Tommy Tremble combined for 1,006 yards and eight touchdowns. The defense was led by its secondary as cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Michael Jackson combined for nine interceptions and 27 pass deflections. The duo made life hard for opposing quarterbacks to find an open receiver. The defensive front seven also made things difficult, as defensive tackle Derrick Brown and linebacker Nic Scourton each had five sacks, leading the team. EDGE D.J. Wonnum also had three sacks, along with safety Tre’von Moehrig. 2026 offseason Key additions: LB Jaelan Phillips, LB Devin Lloyd, LT Rasheed Walker, QB Kenny Pickett, RB A.J. Dillon, TE Darren Waller Key losses: DT A’Shawn Robinson, C Cade Mays, RB Rico Dowdle, EDGE D.J. Wonnum, QB Andy Dalton (trade) 2026 NFL Draft picks Round 1: OT Monroe Freeling Round 2: DT Lee Hunter Round 3: WR Chris Brazzell II Round 4: CB Will Lee III Round 5: C Sam Hecht Round 5: S Zakee Wheatley Round 7: LB Jackson Kuwatch Coming off their first divisional crown since 2015, the Panthers didn’t want to waste their opportunity to improve. They beefed up the defense with linebackers Jaelan Phillips and Devin Lloyd—a pass rusher who can get in the backfield and a coverage linebacker who can create turnovers. They also got more help on offense, signing left tackle Rasheed Walker to a one-year deal to fill the void left by Ikem Ekwonu while he recovers from a torn patellar tendon. After trading Andy Dalton at backup quarterback, they brought in Kenny Pickett and upgraded at backup tight end with Darren Waller. With running back Rico Dowdle leaving in free agency, the Panthers signed A.J. Dillon to add valuable depth at the position alongside Hubbard and Jonathon Brooks. The Panthers lost two of their starters to the Lions in center Cade Mays and Wonnum, while defensive tackle A’Shawn Robinson went to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. In the draft, the Panthers got some help everywhere. They drafted right tackle Monroe Freeling in the first round to compete for the starting job. They replaced Robinson with defensive tackle Lee Hunter in the second, then added wide receiver Chris Brazzell II in the third to boost the offense. The defense got most of the attention in the remaining picks, adding depth at linebacker and in the secondary, while drafting center Sam Hecht to be their new backup. 2026 season thus far (1-2) Week 1: Lost to Chicago Bears, 59-37 Week 2: Defeated Atlanta Falcons, 34-3 Week 3: Lost to Cleveland Browns, 21-18 Stats: 5th in points scored, 26th in points allowed Overall DVOA: 12th (15th on offense, 17th on defense, 4th on special teams) This season has been a bumpy ride for the Panthers. In their opening contest against the Chicago Bears, they put up 37 points on offense, but their defense couldn’t stop the Bears from scoring 59. Then, against a lesser opponent with a third-string quarterback starting for the Atlanta Falcons, the Panthers’ defense clamped down and held them to just three points, while their offense stayed on par with the previous week. In Week 3, Carolina took a step back both ways, getting held to under 20 points for the first time this season and failing to stop the Browns offense. Overall, the offense is doing a solid job, especially Young. He’s leading the NFL in passing yards (939) and tied for fifth in passing touchdowns (seven). His improved receiving corps has been crucial, and Young is really growing as a player and finally becoming the quarterback the Panthers envisioned. After losing his starting job last season, Hubbard has bounced back well, rushing for 184 yards, averaging 4.5 yards per carry, and scoring a touchdown. He’s also one of Young’s favorite threats in the passing game, getting nine catches for 77 yards and two touchdowns. Speaking of receiving, Coker leads the team in receiving yards (222) and catches (18) and is tied with Hubbard and Waller for touchdowns (2). Waller has also assisted Young greatly in the passing game with 10 catches for 112 yards. With McMillan gaining more attention, it’s opening doors for others to make plays and having opposing defenses worry about them. Losing two starters on the offensive line has made life a little difficult for Young, who has been sacked seven times so far this season. With both tackles, Taylor Moton and Ekwonu, on either NFI or PUP, they’re relying on Walker and Freeling to carry the weight. Walker has been about average according to PFF, posting a 70.6 pass-blocking grade, while Freeling is a bit behind (61.3 pass-blocking grade) and has been tagged for allowing two sacks, most out of any of the five linemen. On defense, there are a lot more problems on that side of the ball. Carolina is dead last in the NFL in rushing yards allowed (580), yards per carry allowed (5.7), and is tied with the Green Bay Packers for the most rushing touchdowns allowed (six). Their linebackers are doing the heavy lifting, leading the team in sacks and interceptions. Philips is tied with Princely Umanmielen for most sacks with two, while Lloyd leads the team with two interceptions, returning one for a touchdown. If the defense can’t figure out its run defense soon, it’ll be a big reason it can’t repeat as divisional champions. Injury notes Key players ruled out : RB Jonathon Brooks (IR), LB Nic Scourton (IR), RT Taylor Moton (NFI), LT Ikem Ekwonu (PUP), DT Tershawn Wharton (PUP), CB Jaycee Horn (quad), G Damien Lewis (UCL) Key players to monitor : WR Xavier Legette (knee), WR Jalen Coker (quad/ankle), LB Devin Lloyd (calf), S Nick Scott (rib), CB Mike Jackson (groin), QB Bryce Young (lower body) This is the first team that Detroit faces that has already been hit hard by the injury bug, and it’s only Week 4. Multiple starters will miss this game on both sides of the ball, and the list…

title: Packers Injury Report: Jayden Reed goes on injured reserve
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ big injury news on Wednesday was that the team placed receiver Jayden Reed on the injured reserve list to make room for the addition of guard Kevin Zeitler, bringing the Packers’ offensive line total in practice to a league-leading 15 players. According to head coach Matt LaFleur, Reed notified him yesterday […]
full_text: (Photo by Nick Wosika/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ big injury news on Wednesday was that the team placed receiver Jayden Reed on the injured reserve list to make room for the addition of guard Kevin Zeitler, bringing the Packers’ offensive line total in practice to a league-leading 15 players . According to head coach Matt LaFleur, Reed notified him yesterday that he will be having surgery on his neck. Per LaFleur, this is expected to end Reed’s 2026 campaign, but is not considered to be a career-ending injury. Either way, prayers up for Reed and his family as he recovers from a spooky injury — neck issues are always dicey. Beyond the Reed news, four players in practice on Wednesday were non-participants: left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe), right guard Jacob Monk (quadricep), defensive lineman Karl Brooks (illness) and defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (ankle). Banks and Campbell did not play last week, so those are not surprises. Monk dropped out of action late against the Atlanta Falcons, but he was never given a status by the team — clearly, he’s banged up as we’re nearly a week removed from game action. Brooks’ illness was not reported on before practice. Limited participants for the Packers today were defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf/groin), linebacker Edgerrin Cooper (shoulder/concussion) and edge defender Lukas Van Ness (shoulder). This was Brinson’s first practice since he was injured in pre-game warmups leading up to Week 2 of the preseason, but reporters on the scene for individual drills and warmups today (the portions of practice open to the media) stated that Brinson “appeared to go down and was receiving medical attention.” Worth noting: Brinson has never had a groin status on his injury report before today, so it’s possible that he could have suffered a second injury on Wednesday. Warren Brinson (calf) returned to practice but then in the first individual period appeared to go down and was receiving medical attention. Eventually got back up as the open portion ended. Not practicing: Jayden Reed, Jacob Monk, Aaron Banks, Anthony Campbell, Karl Brooks. — Rob Demovsky (@RobDemovsky) September 30, 2026 The good news is that Cooper, who dropped out against the Falcons, is already a limited participant in practice. Generally, a player who suffers a concussion on a Thursday Night Football game is cleared for the next Sunday’s action, but concussions can be tricky. If Cooper can’t go, it will be Isaiah McDuffie — both the backup Mike linebacker (behind Zaire Franklin) and backup Will linebacker (behind Cooper) — who starts in his place. For what it’s worth, the “starting” offensive line with both Banks and Monk out, plus Zeitler still learning the ropes, was Jordan Morgan, Laken Tomlinson, Sean Rhyan, Donovan Jennings and Anthony Belton (left to right). LaFleur said Zeitler will play when ramped up. Banks and Monk are hurt. pic.twitter.com/c8oL5C8Hbr — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) September 30, 2026 Below is the full injury report, which includes seven non-participants for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Packers’ Week 4 opponent, and four more limited participants.
