title: Packers Roster Update: No NFL team has more offensive linemen than Green Bay
summary: The Green Bay Packers are using an incredible number of their roster spots on offensive linemen, as they attempt to right the ship after three straight poor performances from the unit to start the season. Just this week alone, they signed Kevin Zeitler and Laken Tomlinson to the 53-man roster, along with adding Mekhi Becton […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are using an incredible number of their roster spots on offensive linemen, as they attempt to right the ship after three straight poor performances from the unit to start the season. Just this week alone, they signed Kevin Zeitler and Laken Tomlinson to the 53-man roster, along with adding Mekhi Becton Sr. to the practice squad (which was offset by the release of Cordell Volson). Currently, 15 of the team’s total 70 roster spots (when you include the 17-man practice squad with the 53-man roster) are being spent on offensive linemen, good for 21 percent of the team. That leads the NFL and is 50 percent more roster spots committed to the position than the league’s slimmest offensive line room — the Pittsburgh Steelers, who have eight players on the 53-man roster and just two practice squad players at the position. The Packers are the only NFL team that has committed 11 roster spots on the 53-man roster to offensive linemen as of Wednesday, September 30th. Here’s the league-wide breakdown: 11 linemen: 1 team (Packers) 10 linemen: 10 teams 9 linemen: 16 teams 8 linemen: 5 teams For the full 70-man roster, including the practice squad, here’s the league-wide roster count for linemen: 15 linemen: 1 team (Packers) 14 linemen: 1 team (Ravens) 13 linemen: 8 teams 12 linemen: 16 teams 11 linemen: 5 teams 10 linemen: 1 team (Steelers) The average NFL team is spending nine 53-man roster spots on the offensive line, a number the Packers are going above and beyond by two. Including the practice squad, the average NFL team is spending 12 70-man roster spots on offensive linemen, a number the Packers are going above and beyond by three. So not only is the team “oversigned” on the active roster, but they’re also “oversigned” on the practice squad, too. At a minimum, the front office is giving the coaching staff options to figure out how to salvage the season. Below is the full count of the Packers’ current offensive linemen: Jordan Morgan (preferred starting left tackle) Aaron Banks (presumably still the preferred starting left guard when healthy) Sean Rhyan (preferred starting center) Kevin Zeitler (head coach Matt LaFleur stated he will be the starting right guard when he’s caught up on the system) Anthony Belton (preferred starting right tackle) Laken Tomlinson (worked as the starting left guard in practice on Wednesday with Banks out) Donovan Jennings (worked as the starting right guard in practice on Wednesday with Zeitler still not caught up) Jacob Monk (backup interior offensive lineman) Jager Burton (backup interior offensive lineman) John Williams (backup left tackle) Travis Glover (backup right tackle/right guard) Mekhi Becton Jr. (backup right tackle/right guard, practice squad) Dalton Cooper (backup tackle/guard, practice squad) Dillon Wade (backup interior offensive lineman, practice squad) Josh Gesky (backup guard, practice squad) For what it’s worth, Green Bay signed two more practice squadders on Wednesday, receiver Coleman Owen and defensive lineman David Blay. That gives the Packers the following practice squad, which is now full: QB: Kedon Slovis RB: Pierre Strong Jr. WR: Isaiah Neyor, Quincy Skinner Jr. and Coleman Owen TE: Drake Dabney OL: Mekhi Becton Jr., Dalton Cooper, Dillon Wade and Josh Gesky DL: David Blay ED: Nyjalik Kelly and Arron Mosby LB: Kristian Welch CB: Domani Jackson S: Kahlef Hailassie K: Lenny Krieg (international exemption) P: None LS: None Below is a list of visits/tryouts the team has had since the cutdown deadline: QB Jack Plummer QB Cam Miller RB Phil Mafah (signed by Giants) RB Damon Bankston (signed and released by Packers) RB Ian Wheeler WR Nick Nash WR Bryce Oliver (signed by Texans) WR Quincy Skinner Jr. (signed by Packers) WR Coleman Owen (signed by Packers) WR Dontae Fleming TE Cody Hardy OL Cordell Volson (signed and released by Packers) OL Mekhi Becton (signed by Packers) OL Robert Jones (signed by 49ers) OL Kevin Zeitler (signed by Packers) DL Zxavian Harris ( they got in trouble for this ) DL Eric Johnson II (signed and released by Packers) DL Jalen Hunt DL Gabe Hall DL David Blay (signed by Packers) ED Cruz Smith ( international exemption player from Australia, per sources ) CB Ambry Thomas S Sanoussi Kane S Kahlef Hailassie (signed by Packers) S John Saunders Jr. (signed by Jets) S Chris Edmonds S Wande Owens S Juanyeh Thomas

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers trying to dig out of a hole
summary: You’ve got no shortage of bad things to choose from during the early days of the season, but one of the worst things about the Packers stumbling out of the gate is that everyone else in the NFC North has as well. The Vikings lost their starting quarterback early in Week 1, but the Packers […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers reacts against the Atlanta Falcons during the fourth quarter of the game at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images You’ve got no shortage of bad things to choose from during the early days of the season, but one of the worst things about the Packers stumbling out of the gate is that everyone else in the NFC North has as well. The Vikings lost their starting quarterback early in Week 1, but the Packers couldn’t take advantage — as we well know. They let the Vikings survive, and now they’re 3-0. The Bears, meanwhile, lost their own quarterback a week later, dropping a game to the Vikings as a result. They managed to keep things afloat the following week, but they remain vulnerable. The Lions, for their part, have staggered to a 1-2 start, the same as the Packers. All of this, of course, was avoidable. The Packers went into the season with a patchwork offensive line — and we’re being offensive to patchwork quilters with that description. They have more self respect than the Packers showed trotting out that bunch. But that’s beside the point. It didn’t have to be this way. They’re taking steps now to fix it, but there was no need to wait. Kevin Zeitler was sitting at home for all of training camp, as was Mekhi Becton. Laken Tomlinson’s been chilling on the Cowboys’ practice squad, too. Sure, there have been some unexpected bumps in the road — nobody planned for Aaron Banks to battle an injury for weeks and weeks and weeks, and nobody expected Zach Bako-Bewele’s knee to implode — but there was plenty of opportunity to mitigate those possibilities before things turned into a disaster. Now the Packers have dug themselves a hole. They’re trying to dig out, but it’s better to not put yourself in a hole to begin with. title: The Packers’ offensive line renovation is wild and unprecedented
summary: I can’t talk about the Packers’ offensive line renovations without using hyperbolic language. You generally want to avoid descriptors  like “desperate” and “panicked” and “last-ditch attempt to save their season and their jobs,” when trying to write anything resembling sober, reasoned analysis of a team. For one thing, it’s rarely that serious. For another, it […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - DECEMBER 28: Kevin Zeitler #70 of the Tennessee Titans signals at the line of scrimmage during a game against the New Orleans Saints at Nissan Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Nashville, Tennessee. The Saints defeated the Titans 34-26. (Photo by Wesley Hitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images I can’t talk about the Packers’ offensive line renovations without using hyperbolic language. You generally want to avoid descriptors like “desperate” and “panicked” and “last-ditch attempt to save their season and their jobs,” when trying to write anything resembling sober, reasoned analysis of a team. For one thing, it’s rarely that serious. For another, it paints you as the kind of person who can’t be trusted to react appropriately to things. But seriously, how else would you describe what the Packers have done over the past few days? After a truly apocalyptic start to the year, the Packers have signed three different replacement offensive linemen, raiding the Cowboys’ practice squad for Laken Tomlinson and picking up Mekhi Becton and Kevin Zeitler off the street. That’s a flurry of activity virtually unprecedented in the corners of Packers history I’m aware of. I’ve been writing about this team in some format for about 20 years now and was a fan for long before that, and I can’t recall any kind of in-season renovation at a position group like we’re seeing now. The Packers have added notable in-season free agents before, but it’s usually one at a time. They’ve tried late-career mercenary signings with guys like Snacks Harrison and Whitney Mercilus. They added Cedric Benson just before the start of the 2012 season to fix a moribund running back room. The most famous example of all is probably Andre Rison, claimed off of waivers late in the 1996 season. But those are all one-off moves. This is entirely different. Tomlinson, Becton, and Zeitler could all start for the Packers. Two of the three, in some combination, will probably be starting sooner than later. Given how the injury bug has infected the Packers’ offensive line, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see all of them in the starting lineup at some point. That’s not normal! You don’t just sign three new starting offensive linemen during the season! It’d be noteworthy enough to be remarkable had they done it in the offseason, but we’re sitting here in late September discussing three new linemen joining the team. That’s bananas! We can only speculate as to what caused the sudden flurry of activity. The need for help was obvious to anyone with eyes, but neither Brian Gutekunst or Matt LaFleur seemed overly inclined to do anything about it for the first three weeks. We watched Donovan Jennings get shoved up and down the field for most of two weeks before Lafleur even tried Jager Burton at left guard, for goodness sake, and prior to the spending spree of the last few days, Brian Gutekunst’s big move was signing Cordell Volson to the practice squad. Did Ed Policy throw a fit? Did he give the recently extended pair of Gutekunst and LaFleur a “fix it or you’re fired” ultimatum? It’s hard not to conclude something happened behind closed doors, because we’ve all lived through a very un-Packers-like few days since they farted out an embarrassing home loss to the Falcons on Thursday Night Football. Whether or not these moves end up helping is anybody’s guess, but we’re certainly going to find out. But whether it works or not, the Packers are making unprecedented moves. Who knows what caused it, but we can’t avoid the words that accurately describe what it is. It’s desperate, it’s more than a little panicky, and it could still all be for naught.

title: Packers sign Wisconsin native Kevin Zeitler in latest OL move
summary: A prodigal son is coming home. Kevin Zeitler, a 14-year veteran and Pro Bowl right guard, is returning back to the state of Wisconsin to sign with the Green Bay Packers. ESPN’s Adam Schefter reports that the Packers are signing Zeitler on Wednesday, one day after he worked out for the team. Zeitler, who comes […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 05: Kevin Zeitler #71 of the Detroit Lions plays against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on December 05, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images A prodigal son is coming home. Kevin Zeitler, a 14-year veteran and Pro Bowl right guard, is returning back to the state of Wisconsin to sign with the Green Bay Packers. ESPN’s Adam Schefter reports that the Packers are signing Zeitler on Wednesday, one day after he worked out for the team. Zeitler, who comes out of unofficial retirement with the signing, becomes the third veteran guard and second former Pro Bowler to sign with the Packers since the team’s Week 3 loss last Thursday night, joining Laken Tomlinson (signed to the 53-man roster) and Mekhi Becton (practice squad). Zeitler, a Waukesha native, played for the Wisconsin Badgers during some of their finest seasons in recent memory, serving as the team’s starting right guard from 2009 to 2011. The Badgers won double-digit games in each of those three years and made two Rose Bowl appearances, while Zeitler earned first-team All-American honors as a senior in 2011. He then became a first-round draft pick in 2012, selected 27th overall by the Cincinnati Bengals. In his 14 NFL seasons, Zeitler has played for six different teams, but has remained a quality, steady player at every single stop. Most recently, he started 16 games for the Tennessee Titans in 2025 while on a one-year, $9 million contract. Unlike Tomlinson and Becton, Zeitler likely will draw a significant salary for the remainder of the season. The move was telegraphed a bit by Becton changing his jersey number almost immediately after signing earlier in the week: Zeitler’s lone Pro Bowl appearance came at age 33, earning the honor for the 2023 season as a member of the Baltimore Ravens. He then signed a one-year, $6 million deal with the Detroit Lions for 2024, making 16 starts, before landing in Tennessee a year ago. This is easily the highest-profile and most significant of the three signings this week, however. Once up to speed with the Packers’ offense, Zeitler should be an immediate upgrade over Jacob Monk at right guard while the Packers continue working to sort out the left guard position with a battle between the likes of Tomlinson, Aaron Banks, and others. UPDATE: Zeitler’s contract is for a surprisingly low amount of money, given rumors that had put him at between $6-8 million. According to Ian Rapoport , the deal is only a one-year, $4.05 million contract with incentives that could take it to a maximum of $5 million.

title: Houston Texans NFL Power Rankings: Week 4
summary: The Houston Texans started this season with Super Bowl ambitions, and a large percentage of the NFL viewing public was behind them. Three weeks and three losses later, and this dream seems almost comical in hindsight. But, remarkably, the 12-5 squad from last year was in the same exact apocalyptic position at 0-3, and they […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans reacts after a 19-17 defeat against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans started this season with Super Bowl ambitions, and a large percentage of the NFL viewing public was behind them. Three weeks and three losses later, and this dream seems almost comical in hindsight. But, remarkably, the 12-5 squad from last year was in the same exact apocalyptic position at 0-3, and they went on the win nine straight! So, even though an 0-3 start is close to a death sentence, the Texans are technically not out of the race quite yet. But, was does their 0-3 really say about this 2026 Texans team? How does it compare to last year’s squad? Well, going back to my Week 4 Power Rankings of last year, I had a lot of similar things to say: Punt after punt after punt (six in total for this game), hope deflated out of Texans fans like a balloon and was refilled by discontent and confusion. Why are so many receivers not getting open? Why is Stroud still getting pressured nearly every down? Why can’t the Texans get a rhythm going on offense? What in the WORLD are all these penalties about? – NFL Power Rankings Week 4 (2025) Failing to get an offensive rhythm? Stroud getting pressured on every down? Sounds a lot like the complaints about Houston we’ve been hearing recently, but this doesn’t tell the whole story: In the first three games of the 2025 season, the Texans scored a total of just 38 points and failed to gain over 300 yards of offense in any of those contests. By contrast, the 2026 Texans have scored a total of 54 points in three games and have already broken the 300-yard mark twice so far. At first, this might yield some optimism on the Texans’ outlook for this season, but to still be 0-3 despite the modestly improved offense means the three losses may be more complicated, and not so easily repaired. The interior offensive line remains the primary culprit of Houston’s suffering, but the defense this season has not been quite as dominant as they were last year (at least so far), and combined with questionable time management by the coaching staff creates a recipe for a disastrous start to the season. Juice Scruggs was labeled a massive bust in Houston Nick Caserio has been crushed for trading up in 2nd Rd of 2023 draft for taking Scruggs & he was “unplayable” for #Texans Playing as top C this year for #Lions . Texans scheme is garbage. https://t.co/XP1mb9qIAU — Patrick Creighton (@PCreighton1) September 29, 2026 Houston fell out of most pundits’ top ten after their first loss, then they dropped into the middle of the standings after the second loss, and now following a third loss, the Texans may see their stock fall to its lowest point of the CJ Stroud/DeMeco Ryans era. This is going to be like ripping off a band-aid: here’s where the Houston Texans are ranked following their Week 3 loss to the Indianapolis Colts: NFL.COM : 24. Houston Texans (0-3) The Texans have serious problems offensively that are painfully familiar. They can’t run the ball, lack difference-makers at receiver and still can’t consistently sustain drives. After a six-point output in the Week 2 loss to Cincinnati, the Texans were nearly as dreadful Sunday in Indianapolis, save for one urgent drive to briefly take a late lead. It’s unrealistic to expect the defense to carry Houston on a weekly basis, and until offensive coordinator Nick Caley finds some solutions, the Texans will remain mired in these struggles. – Nick Shook ESPN: 21. Houston Texans (0-3) Week 3 result: Lost to the Colts 19-17 Week 3 ranking: 15 Fantasy surprise: RB David Montgomery After scoring 28.9 fantasy points in Week 1, Montgomery has only 11.2 in the past two games combined. He averages 0.5 yards before contact — an abhorrent number for a rushing attack. Any hope for an improvement in Montgomery’s fantasy production starts with better play from the offensive line. That unit is a big reason the Texans are winless and averaging 11.5 points over the past two weeks. – DJ Bien-Aime SPORTS ILLUSTRATED: 16. Houston Texans (0–3) Last week’s ranking: No. 13 Last week’s result: lost to Colts, 19–17 This week: vs. Cowboys When you get as involved in a team’s success as I did , the absolute breakdown of its most vulnerable unit—the one you believed would look brand new—feels especially difficult to stomach. But I would like to be a fly on the wall during the next phase of offensive meetings for the Houston Texans. Where is the machine coming unplugged? – Conor Orr BLEACHER REPORT: 27. Houston Texans (0-3) Last Week: 16 Week 3 Result: Lost at Indianapolis 19-17 The good news is that the Texans are in familiar territory. The bad news is that familiar territory is up a creek. This marks the second straight season that the Texans have started 0-3. Last year, they rebounded to make the postseason and won a playoff game. The Texans also started 0-3 and made the playoffs in 2018. But no team has made the playoffs after an 0-3 start in back-to-back seasons, and right now the Texans do not look the part of a contender—at all. Houston’s offensive line play and rushing attack have been all but non-existent—against a Colts defense that entered Week 3 with the AFC’s worst defense, the Texans had 70 rushing yards and averaged less than 3.5 yards per carry. C.J. Stroud had his worst game of the season throwing the ball in Indianapolis. Houston’s defense can’t do it all—and right now the offense isn’t doing much. – Gary Davenport CBS SPORTS: 27. Texans (0-3) (Last Week: 24) At 0-3, their season is on the line against the Cowboys this week. The offense just isn’t good enough right now. – Pete Prisco USA TODAY: 25. Houston Texans (18): While he’s been hindered by key offensive absences, C.J. Stroud does not look like a quarterback deserving of a, say, $55 million-a-year contract. – Nate Davis YAHOO! SPORTS: 24. Houston Texans (0-3, LW: 19) The Texans were 0-3 last season and went 12-5. So Houston can turn this around. But only six teams in NFL history, not counting the 1982 strike season, have made the playoffs after an 0-3 start, according to Josh Dubow of the Associated Press . “0-3 is where we are right now,” Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans said, via Texans Wire . “The only way we can do anything about it is to go through it. We’re going through it right now, it’s adversity, it happens. For me, it starts with me. I have to do a better job of getting our guys ready to roll.” The offense has been a problem. It has failed without Nico Collins , who has missed two games with a hamstring injury. Against a Colts defense that had allowed the most points and yards in the NFL through two weeks, the Texans had 93 yards through three quarters. And 68 of those yards, and seven of their eight first downs, came on one drive. Even with Collins out, it shouldn’t have been that hard to sustain drives. QB C.J. Stroud is looking for a contract extension , and the start to this season shouldn’t be providing the Texans any optimism that he’s worth the massive raise he’s seeking. – Frank Schwab THE ATHLETIC: 22. Houston Texans (0-3) Last week: 17 Sunday: Lost to Colts 19-17 QB confidence: Falling, again It’s been a roller-coaster ride for Houston fans and C.J. Stroud. In his first 23 games, Stroud was 15-8 with 26 touchdowns, five interceptions and a 101.7 passer rating. In the next 21 games, he was 9-12 with 11 touchdowns, nine interceptions and an 86.2 passer rating. Then another climb, seven straight wins that included nine touchdowns and four interceptions and a 91.5 passer rating. But now, Stroud has lost four straight games, and the Texans have started a second straight season 0-3. Up next: vs. Cowboys, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET – Chad Graff & Josh Kendall PRO FOOTBALL TALK: 17. title: Value of Things: Is it time to panic?
summary: Last year I introduced something called the stages of suck. The higher ups didn’t respond well to the headlines, but I am going to go with the same concept now that the Texans are 0-3 for the second year in a row. This brings a number of questions to the forefront. Is it too early […]
full_text: Last year I introduced something called the stages of suck. The higher ups didn’t respond well to the headlines, but I am going to go with the same concept now that the Texans are 0-3 for the second year in a row. This brings a number of questions to the forefront. Is it too early to give up on the season? How concerned should we be? The more important question is who should take the blame for the team’s struggles? The way that the stages of suck worked is that some people in the organization get the benefit of the doubt and some don’t. It depends on the culpability we think that they have. So, we will be evaluating three men in key positions on the Texans. The Texans have played back to back solid defensive games, so Matt Burke is off the hook. Instead, we will look at DeMeco Ryans, Nick Caserio, and Nick Caley. Essentially, the either get the benefit of the doubt for now, side eye (meaning we have them under the microscope), and the pitch fork stage which means we want them gone. Nick Caserio This exists on two levels. The first level is obviously the players on the field. The second are those that are on the coaching staff. Ryans and Caserio get to share the criticism there. In terms of the player, we have seen Caserio in Houston since 2021. He has tried to build and rebuild the offensive line every year since then. The model seems the same. He has used the same modus operandi in each season. He trades away expensive players like Laremy Tunsil and Tytus Howard and tries to bring in a collection of guys with the hopes they can cobble a line together. It has not worked yet. A part of that is key misses in the draft and in free agency. It includes Kenyon Green and Juice Scruggs. The jury is still out on Blake Fisher, but it isn’t look good there either. Then there are the Cam Robinsons, Wyatt Tellers, and Shaq Masons of the world. We would have to count Ed Ingram as a win last season, but he hasn’t been there for the most part this season. Airontae Ersery looks okay and Keeland Rutledge could be a good one too, but the other three slots appear shaky at best. That is the beginning. We could also look at the inability to surround Nico Collins with enough skill position talent to make up for when he is out. However, the biggest problem has been the selection of Nick Caley as an offensive coordinator. The decision has his fingerprints all over it as he has a New England backgroun and he is a John Carroll University alum. All of this adds up to some serious side eye. You generally don’t fire a general manager that has won 32 games in three seasons. So, he probably gets the benefit of the doubt for now, but this season might be his one warning. DeMeco Ryans Ryans has not been here as long, so he does not have the same track record. Every coach has criticism when they lose. This Sunday, Ryans did not handle the end of the game well as the Texans left too much time for the Colts to score and did not use their time outs to give themselves another chance. However, every coach has come under pressure at one point or another for their decisions. In a big picture sense, there is very little to criticize Ryans for in terms of how he runs the team on game day. You can complain how much or how little he involves himself in the offense, but that would be relatively minor. The bigger question with him is how much he has input in the coaches. In particular, Caley and the offensive line coaches appear to be Caserio buddy hires. Ryans has more juice in this organization than anyone and should have pounded the table more. I am willing to overlook that as a learning experience. Ryans feels like a Mike Tomlin kind of coach that could stick for a decade or more. He is having growing pains and clearly needs to look more closely at what is being done on his behalf. So, he gets the benefit of the doubt for now. Nick Caley I went by the moniker vballretired for awhile because I am a retired volleyball coach. I coached varsity for a few seasons and my teams were never good. So, I fully understand the idea of being outgunned on a court or field. A coach’s job is to get as much our of his or her players as they can. Sometimes that means losing but you can go down fighting or go down meekly. So, I can sympathize with those that think Caley simply doesn’t have the horses. However, that ignores other teams that are equally as devoid in talent or worse and yet somehow manage to gain more yards and score more points. They do that in two ways. First, they know what their players do well and they accentuate that. Secondly, they see what does not work and don’t go back to the well. If I see one more off tackle run on third or fourth and short I’m going to puke. It hasn’t worked. This is usually where some macho guy ssys “if you can’t get a push to gain a yard then you don’t deserve to win.” Sure Grandpa. That works at the end of the bar, but in real life teams adjust and do something different. This is simple. You are thinking about paying C.J. Stroud and you can’t figure out whether he is worth it because this offense sucks. So, there is no on the job training. You either figure it out or you don’t. Every coach has their level just like players. I was not really cut out to be a varsity coach. I was a lot happier teaching younger kids. Caley might be happier as a position coach. Some guys just don’t have the imagination. The pitch forks are out for Caley and he probably doesn’t have much time.

title: Colts’ Week 3 QB Analysis: One Step Back
summary: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. […]
full_text: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) People often describe a quarterback’s performance as “good enough to win.” If that’s considered a valid critique, then this week I would say that Daniel Jones played bad enough to lose. And here’s a bunch of graphs to back that up. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: arsr , edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , qbsr , epa/p , adj/p Run game efficiency was about average, but the Colts leaned heavily on the pass in early-down situations. (18th ARSR; 2nd EDP) Jones faced a lot of pressure, but got the ball out fairly quickly with average depth. This points to an O-line that struggled to protect. ( 9th PR% , 21st TIP; 19th TTT; 17th ADOT) The passing game did not generate much after the catch or turn those completions into yardage. (25th AY/C; 20th YAC; 26th YCOE; 26th YD/C) Jones’ completion rate was OK, but the completions themselves weren’t especially productive. (15th AC%; 19th CPOE; 23rd AYPA) Four sacks, only one scramble and one throwaway meant too many pressured plays ended badly rather than being salvaged or discarded. (23rd SCR%; 25th TA%; 5th SCK%; 16th AA%) That left Jones toward the bottom of the league in net yardage efficiency and first-down generation. (27th NY/D; 26th NY/P; 23rd 1ST%) The biggest problem was the damaging plays: Jones produced only one passing touchdown while turning the ball over three times — an interception and two lost fumbles on sacks. (27th TD%; 3rd TO%) Overall, he was about average at sustaining positive plays, but the negative plays pushed his total value much lower. (17th QBSR; 23rd EPA/P) mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p Jones never really found a strength to build around. His completions were relatively short and produced little after the catch, keeping the passing production modest. Efficiency could have been salvaged with a very high completion rate, but his wasn’t that great. From there, the negative plays became the bigger problem, with sacks and turnovers dragging down an already limited performance and leaving him with a well-below-average EPA per play. Jones had plenty of positive plays, but the damaging negatives overwhelmed them. His 20 successful plays on 43 QB plays produced a 46.5% success rate, but four sacks, an interception and the late fumble created several of the biggest negative plays of the game. Those high-cost mistakes turned a performance with a reasonable number of successful plays into poor overall value. Jones’ recent trend continues to move in the wrong direction. His ability to consistently produce successful plays has fallen from where it was last season, while both his overall value and net yardage have also declined. Week 3 continued that pattern. HOW FAR? Jones had trouble getting going, with a string of incompletions keeping the passing game from establishing any early rhythm. He eventually settled in and put together a more productive stretch, but the improvement didn’t hold, as the negative plays piled up later in the game. Jones struggled to generate much downfield production. His completed air yards stayed relatively short throughout the game, and even when he connected deeper, those gains were isolated rather than part of a sustained vertical passing attack. Jones passing short is fine, but not making up for it with YAC and a high completion rate is not. TO WHO? Jones spread the ball around well with Downs, Warren and Allen having similar target volume. Warren was the most reliable target, catching 9 of 10 passes, but of course those were much shorter throws. Downs is by far the most targeted but catching 14 of 24 is not exactly thrilling. Nothing really of note here as the wide receiver depth and value are near or above average. On the season, both Allen and Warren are too low value-wise. HOW ACCURATE? Accuracy (CPOE) was fine, but with shorter than average throws, I would have liked to have seen a higher-than-average completion rate. HOW FAST? Jones’ release time is pretty good. Adjusting for depth, he gets rid of it a little quicker than expected, so he’s processing well and not holding on to the ball too long. TO WHERE? He had a lot of success toward the right side of the field and on the left side, not so much. On the year I see a lot of bad, a lot of meh, but not much good.

title: For the Colts to win, Daniel Jones must be better
summary: Quarterbacks turn the ball over. Houston’s defense causes turnovers. Because of that, it makes total sense that a quarterback facing the vaunted Texans’ defense would turn the ball over, and that is exactly what Daniel Jones did on Sunday. If he and the Indianapolis Colts hope to create a winning streak, however, he will have […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts fumbles the ball while being tackled during the fourth quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Quarterbacks turn the ball over. Houston’s defense causes turnovers. Because of that, it makes total sense that a quarterback facing the vaunted Texans’ defense would turn the ball over, and that is exactly what Daniel Jones did on Sunday. If he and the Indianapolis Colts hope to create a winning streak, however, he will have to be better. Jones had three turnovers on the day. Two of them were unacceptable. When the offensive line can’t block Will Anderson or Danielle Hunter, it makes it hard on a quarterback, so the first fumble can be forgiven. It’s the interception to start the third quarter that creates concern. The Colts had a chance to extend their lead to two scores, but on third down, with a defender barreling towards him, Jones chucked the ball into the air. It was intercepted and kept the Texans needing only a touchdown to take the lead. That wasn’t the worst of it, however. The Colts had control late in the fourth quarter. They were up six and driving on the Texans’ side of the field, looking to put this one on ice. With less than five minutes remaining, Jones changed the play and had Jonathan Taylor open in the flat. Instead of getting it to him in space, of which there was plenty, Jones held the ball and was stripped. The Texans marched down the field and scored the go-ahead touchdown. Of course, we all know the ending, but that doesn’t mean all’s well that ends well. There was no guarantee the Colts would get into field goal range or that Spencer Shrader would make the game winning 53-yard field goal. It worked out, but that doesn’t mean it always will. Daniel Jones must take better care of the ball if the Colts want to win.

title: How good do you feel about the Colts’ first win?
summary: In football, we judge our teams by wins and losses. It makes sense, otherwise we’d have something like figure skating or the X Games where you get scored by judges, or like the old college football polls deciding a national champion. Careers can be defined by the amount of wins your team can amass, so […]
full_text: In football, we judge our teams by wins and losses. It makes sense, otherwise we’d have something like figure skating or the X Games where you get scored by judges, or like the old college football polls deciding a national champion. Careers can be defined by the amount of wins your team can amass, so anytime you get one, you should feel good about it. We got one of those valuable wins on Sunday and added it to the divisional and conference win total by knocking off a rival, during Rivalry Week. With Rivalry Week, comes a new uniform concept. In theory and maybe even on the runway, I liked the look. I hope that those blue helmets make more appearances. However, when coupled with the roof being open on game day, I spent most of the time wondering just who did what? I relied on the announcers much more than I prefer and found it hard to determine who was getting playing time. I might like them with the roof closed, or if they were on the road, but I have to go thumbs down after one game. Check back if we somehow find ourselves 5 – 0 in them, or we win a big playoff game. If that were the case, I might just get one for myself. I don’t have a prevailing sentiment on the game, other than a win is a win. The much maligned defense showed much better, but I have to wonder if the same folks who said our offenses feasted on weak teams last year, will say that the D had a good day against a bad offense. I did think we tackled better, but I am concerned that we got zero pass rush when it was needed most. Shouldn’t you accidentally force a turnover each game? We have one in three games. I think we would win a lot of games if we held opponents to 17 points each week, but I’m going to need a bigger sample size before I ease up on Lou. As far as the offense goes, I think ball security from DJ is worrisome. We need to figure out a way keep the edge rushers from collapsing the pocket. I think Jones is better when he can get outside, so try to force the rush to the inside, or be able to ride them far enough outside that there is a lane in that vacated spot. He just doesn’t feel that pressure from his blind side consistently enough. Other offensive suggestions: We have to take our deep shots. Trust your WR to make a play. We need to loosen up those shorter routes and the way that teams swarm to JT, there has to be some one-on-one matchups. Could we mix in some No Huddle possessions? Figure out what their D likes, personnel wise, on 1st down and script some plays that work against it, while keeping our same players on the field. It doesn’t have to be the first series, but something that you can go to. Also, why does Jones need a wrist band? This is a guy that was accepted into Princeton. We lose a little time on the play clock and take away time for our QB to make adjustments, by adding that extra step. I thought we found a way to get Warren more involved, but we shouldn’t forget that Cox and Ogletree are capable receivers as well, who do not get the same attention as 84. My last thought is that I still don’t think Steichen understands the difference between FG “range” and a chip shot. While still outside of “range” we huddled, with less than two minutes left. It eventually made the Texans use a TO, but if you playcall that series well, they never see the ball again. If you are that concerned that your QB will not make a good call at the line, you either are not confident in your guy, or you are too confident and controlling with your own abilities. Are you afraid DJ will turn the ball over? If so, you have a different kind of problem. This didn’t come out as I expected as an optimist after a divisional win, but we definitely have some things to clean up.

title: Chiefs News: Tyreek Hill continues to hint at a comeback
summary: The 3-0 Kansas City Chiefs are in a strong position to return to the playoffs this year. The team can certainly improve, and it has 14 regular-season games to do so. As the team has done multiple times in past playoff seasons, a midseason acquisition is on the table, whether it’s a trade or a […]
full_text: (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 3-0 Kansas City Chiefs are in a strong position to return to the playoffs this year. The team can certainly improve, and it has 14 regular-season games to do so. As the team has done multiple times in past playoff seasons, a midseason acquisition is on the table, whether it’s a trade or a free-agent signing. A former All-Pro Chiefs wide receiver is on the open market. Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device! For Apple devices, click here . For Android devices, click here . The latest Kansas City Chiefs news Chiefs’ Tyreek Hill Speculation Becomes Red Hot After ‘Cold Weather’ Hint | Heavy Sports And now, the rumor mill has reached red-hot levels after Hill pronounced on Wednesday that he is “ready for some cold weather” in a post on X. “Cold weather” does not necessarily imply that KC is the only possible destination. The Buffalo Bills would also be a potential contender for his services that matches the “cold weather” description, the same for the Baltimore Ravens. What Eric Bieniemy’s return has brought to the Chiefs offense | The Athletic Veteran Mike Caliendo said it can be as small as harping on offensive linemen to “cover downfield” at the end of plays. That emphasis — telling blockers to hustle upfield after a pass is completed — could result in an offensive lineman coming away with a critical fumble recovery downfield or making the final block to spring the play an extra few yards. Remigio, meanwhile, believes the passing offense also has gained something from Bieniemy’s specific teachings. Micah Parsons shares what he’s spotted from the Chiefs that he got all ‘wrong’ | HITC “They’re playing really good football offensively and defensively right now. I can admit when I’m wrong. I was wrong when I didn’t think they were going to have the year they had,” said Parsons. “Patrick Mahomes came back from the ACL and LCL, playing good ball, not turning the ball over. Kenneth Walker came in, and he’s going crazy. It’s like they had a plan, and that’s what I mean. What is the plan for when you’re signing these free agents? What placement are they going to be in? The guys they drafted are playing really good for them. They’re making a difference in their lineup. They knew what they were doing.” Chiefs’ defense knows its No. 1 priority ahead of visit to 3-0 Las Vegas Raiders | The Kansas City Star “They find different ways to get him involved in the offense,” Bolton said. “Spread him out, screen game. We have to be aware of where he’s at.” Bowers was the first-target read on almost half of Cousins’ 33 pass attempts last weekend. And that sounds like the sort of attention Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce received in his prime years. “There are definitely some similarities,” Bolton said. “He’s a little bit smaller than Kelce, a little more twitchy. I guess you could say (he’s) a younger ‘Kels’. But (he’s) definitely good with the ball, good ball skills, able to run all the routes.” Chiefs Celebrate With Borrowed Barcelona Flair | Yahoo! Sports During a Week 2 game against the Indianapolis Colts, Xavier Worthy found the end zone on a 1-yard catch. Right after that score, Kenneth Walker III met him there to perform a very specific move. The Chiefs even showed respect to the original creators. On X, the team posted, “Thanks for the celly inspo @FCBarcelona 🤞,” according to reports. It is great to see players connecting with different sports. This isn’t just about random movement, either. Raphinha previously stated that the gesture originated from teammates simply adopting the motion as a greeting method. Around the NFL Sources: Steelers to trade Joey Porter Jr. to Cowboys | ESPN The trade marks the end of a monthslong saga that stretched throughout the offseason as Porter, one of the Steelers’ 2023 second-round picks, awaited an extension and was sidelined by a back injury. The heart of the dispute was the guaranteed money within the contract’s structure, sources told ESPN, and the sides never made meaningful progress on agreeing to terms despite talks as late as hours before kickoff of the Steelers’ Week 1 game against the Atlanta Falcons. The Steelers then stopped talks because they don’t negotiate during the regular season as a longstanding organizational principle. Patriots’ Drake Maye: Shoulder not impacting throws; no rift with HC Mike Vrabel | NFL.com Maye was asked on Wednesday if his shoulder is impacting how he’s throwing the football. “No, it hasn’t,” Maye said. “I don’t think it impacts my decision-making, and that’s what makes and breaks play for quarterbacks.” Maye instead redirected the attention toward the team’s turnover issues, which he admitted are holding them back. Broncos WR Pat Bryant comes clean on whether he flopped on controversial pass interference call vs. Rams | CBS Sports Nevertheless, Bryant, who caught both of his targets on Sunday for 44 yards and a touchdown, is sticking to the ruling on the field, but did acknowledge that he did “sell it just enough.” “It was a little pass interference,” Bryant told Romi Bean of CBS Colorado. “I did sell it just enough, you know what I’m saying, to get the flag. He definitely gave me a little nudge that I felt, and I felt like I couldn’t get the ball, so it was either the ball or call, and we ended up getting the call.” In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride The Chiefs are using play action as well as anyone in the NFL The one thing missing is a receiver who can beat press and play on the outside. That’s what the Chiefs are asking Xavier Worthy to do right now, and he’s just not good at that. It’s been true for three years now. If they can improve that spot at the trade deadline, the Chiefs’ offense could become the best in the league. title: ‘Which’ Wednesday: Is talent or coaching driving the new-look Chiefs offense?
summary: In 2026, the Kansas City Chiefs are off to a hot start with an offense that looks different than recent years. Running back Kenneth Walker leads the NFL in rushing yards through three weeks, and the Chiefs have been highly effective on play-action passes. Walker and rookie Emmett Johnson have brought a much-needed boost to […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images In 2026, the Kansas City Chiefs are off to a hot start with an offense that looks different than recent years. Running back Kenneth Walker leads the NFL in rushing yards through three weeks, and the Chiefs have been highly effective on play-action passes. Walker and rookie Emmett Johnson have brought a much-needed boost to the talent in the backfield, but the whole unit is now being coached by offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy, along with veteran receivers coach Chad O’Shea and former All-Pro running back DeMarco Murray, who is directly teaching Walker, Johnson, and second-year back Brashard Smith. So which side of the coin deserves more credit for the effective offense: the coaching staff refresh or the upgraded talent in the backfield? Let us know in our poll on The Feed. Head coach Andy Reid was asked about Kansas City’s success using play action this season compared to last year during his press conference on Wednesday. “We’ve got a good running back — a couple of good running backs there, and we’ve been running the football,” Reid said. “So obviously, that’s going to fit in with that. Pat’s doing a nice job with it; [the offensive line] is doing a nice job with it.” Through three weeks, the Chiefs rank second in the NFL in total yards. That’s a familiar ranking for a unit led by Bieniemy. Here are Kansas City’s total-yards rankings by year and coordinator in the Mahomes era. Bieniemy 2018: 1st 2019: 6th 2020: 1st 2021: 3rd 2022: 1st Matt Nagy 2023: 9th 2024: 16th 2025: 20th So which side do you want to credit more for revamping the Chiefs’ offense? The talent or the coaches? Let us know!

full_text: (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Heading into Week 4 of the NFL season for the Kansas City Chiefs , one question has lingered from before the season and into preparation for the team’s fourth game: the status of left tackle Josh Simmons (Back). At the podium before Wednesday’s practice, head coach Andy Reid revealed that Simmons has been dealing with a bulging disk in his lower back. “[Josh] is making progress,” Reid began. “He’s had a bulging disk in his lower back, and it has kind of hindered the strength of his leg, but he’s working through it; he’s here every day grinding away.” “The positive is that he is making progress and getting stronger,” Reid added. “Which is important with those backs, as well all know backs can be kind of tricky.” On September 2, just under two weeks from the season opener this year, Reid told local media that Simmons’s back flared up . “He had the back checked, and there’s a spot in there that flared up,” Reid said. “Now, you have to sit here and wait until that thing calms down. He has been here working out and doing the rehab stuff, so we’ll see where it goes.” Now, looking ahead to the fourth game of the season, Simmons is still not on the practice field. Reid explained that the Chiefs “didn’t have to make any roster moves, so we didn’t have to put him on [the Reserve/Injured list] or anything.” He added further context on Simmons staying on the active roster through the first four weeks of the schedule. “The timeline- that would be the other half of not putting him on IR; you just never know with these things,” Reid said. “We just hang with it; the positive is that he’s here, he’s working, and he’s getting better. The exams that he has had, he’s making progress, which is the biggest positive of everything.” The head coach was asked about the possibility of surgery, since this was the first report of Simmons having a “bulging disk.” “I think we’re heading in the right direction here, where that shouldn’t happen,” Reid shared. “We’ll see where it all goes. I think we’re going to be, knock on wood, we’re going to be in a good place with time here.” In Simmons’ place, rookie left tackle Kahlil Benson has been filling in, but opponents have figured him out more each week. Against the Miami Dolphins , he allowed three quarterback hits, according to Pro Football Focus . By all accounts, he will continue to man quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ blind side, but we will provide updates on Simmons’ status as this week’s injury reports come out.

title: The Chiefs are using play action as well as anyone in the NFL
summary: Coming into the season, the conversation about the Kansas City Chiefs‘ offense focused on what would change. They ran into a wall with the previous version of the offense and needed to make changes. This offseason, their only meaningful addition was signing running back Kenneth Walker. Signing a good running back was the easiest way […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Coming into the season, the conversation about the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ offense focused on what would change. They ran into a wall with the previous version of the offense and needed to make changes. This offseason, their only meaningful addition was signing running back Kenneth Walker. Signing a good running back was the easiest way for the Chiefs to boost their offense. They couldn’t generate explosive runs last year and got nothing from their running backs. Any semblance of a run game would improve the offense. Another benefit of having Walker is that the improved run game has opened up the Chiefs’ play-action calls, which have been wildly successful this year. Chiefs play-action passing yards: 2025: 396 in 17 games (last in the NFL) 2026: 312 in 3 games (most in the NFL) — Matt McMullen (@KCChiefs_Matt) September 29, 2026 According to Next Gen Stats , Mahomes has had 36 dropbacks on play action this year. On those plays, he has a 71% completion rate, 348 passing yards, 3 TDs, and 1 interception, with a 69% success rate. He has thrown 11 passes over 20 yards. That is absurd efficiency that easily tops the NFL. So, what is driving Mahomes’s success with play action? Let’s dive into some of his best plays of the year: Film Review One of the best ways to get Mahomes going is to get him on the run, and the bootleg lets him do that. Kansas City has done a good job protecting the backside of the bootleg to keep Mahomes clean, and he can make any throw on the run. Getting Rashee Rice to the middle of the field is how he’ll succeed, and play action has helped. The Chiefs can get him on crossers. Condensing the formation means he doesn’t have to beat press, and he can get a leverage advantage. He can stay off contact, and Mahomes can throw a fastball to get Rice going in space. Moving to this style of offense seems to have unlocked something in tight end Travis Kelce. He’s been great running routes and finding soft spots, but even deeper downfield than before. He also benefits from being closer to the line of scrimmage more, where he can get free releases and find soft spots between linebackers. Condensing the formation makes it hard for teams to play man coverage against you, and the Chiefs have won the leverage advantage every week with their passing concepts. This is one of the best corner-route throws you’ll ever see. Mahomes short rolls, runs himself into the defensive lineman’s vision, and throws a fade-away on a 24-yard downfield throw. It’s pristine accuracy and touch. Mahomes’s accuracy on these downfield throws off play action has been insane. He can hit any throw on the field from any angle. Mahomes can hit Rice with a fastball, but he can also lob it up and still hit him. As I mentioned above, Mahomes’ touch has been insane this year. Every downfield pass hits a player in stride, and the ball is never in conflict. He’s making it very easy on his receivers to make plays. The Bottom Line When I watched these clips, the comparison for how Mahomes is playing right now was Matthew Stafford last year with the Los Angeles Rams . Stafford was unbelievable using play action last year, and it won him an MVP. He could hit any blade of grass with either a fastball or touch. He had great chemistry with everyone. Mahomes has that right now, but he also has more mobility than Stafford did. The Chiefs can boot Mahomes more and get him on the run, which puts even more stress on a defense. They can change the angles and launch points and create misdirection. It’s also a great fit with the Chiefs’ current personnel. Rashee Rice and Travis Kelce need free releases to be successful, and going under center more often helps you do that. Walker and Emmett Johnson are good checkdown guys that can create in the passing game. Thornton does a good job on the vertical clearout routes that are essential to opening up space. The one thing missing is a receiver who can beat press and play on the outside. That’s what the Chiefs are asking Xavier Worthy to do right now, and he’s just not good at that. It’s been true for three years now. If they can improve that spot at the trade deadline, the Chiefs’ offense could become the best in the league. The New York Jets are playing pretty well this year and already have three first-round picks next year, so I doubt No. 1 receiver Garrett Wilson becomes available. The guys who might become available are guys like Marvin Harrison Jr. of the Arizona Cardinals , Brian Thomas Jr. of the Jacksonville Jaguars , or Jordan Addison of the Minnesota Vikings . Those are three guys whose teams aren’t going to pay and who might want some value. If any of those guys become available, I think the Chiefs should really look into it. All three of those players haven’t been great in the NFL, but they would be an upgrade over Worthy. At the very least, that helps your offense. If you get lucky, you could tap into their upside, and they could become a long-term core piece. But even if that doesn’t happen, they would immediately improve the room. The Chiefs’ picks are always going to be near the end of the rounds anyway, and they have an extra third-round pick this year. I think this would be a good year to get aggressive at wide receiver and see if you can find someone. If the Chiefs can find one more functional wide receiver, they could have the best offense in the NFL, with Mahomes, a great run game, and Kelce and Rice filling key roles. We’ll see if that receiver becomes available.

title: Chiefs’ defense struggled on third downs in win over Dolphins
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Miami Dolphins 24-10 on Sunday to improve to 3-0. Despite the two-score win, Kansas City had its fair share of struggles and let the Dolphins stick around until the end. The defense, in particular, struggled to get off the field on third down, allowing a 50% conversion rate (Miami […]
full_text: (Photo by Alie Skowronski/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Miami Dolphins 24-10 on Sunday to improve to 3-0. Despite the two-score win, Kansas City had its fair share of struggles and let the Dolphins stick around until the end. The defense, in particular, struggled to get off the field on third down, allowing a 50% conversion rate (Miami went 8 for 16), which led to extended drives for the Dolphins. Overall, the third-down defense has been fine this season—37.50%, 11th best in the NFL—but with tougher competition on the horizon, they will need to fix these issues before the trend goes the wrong way. Early issues The Dolphins started the game with a lengthy 17-play drive in which they converted four third downs, two in the air, one on the ground, and one by way of a penalty. The Chiefs tried to bring pressure, but Miami’s well-timed plays took advantage of loose secondary coverage. On the snap, the Chiefs brought pressure with five, while dropping defensive lineman George Karlaftis into coverage as safety Christian Roland-Wallace and cornerback Nohl Williams came off the right side of the offense. Linebacker Nick Bolton and Karlaftis pick up the shallow crossing routes, while the rest of the defensive backs drop into a quarters look. Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis is under pressure, and the rush nearly gets home, but at the last second he finds a target downfield and fires off his back foot. Rookie Mansoor Delane plays loose coverage and gives up outside leverage to the receiver. Playing head up with his back to the sideline, the receiver makes one quick cut and comes back for the ball. The catch is made, and it was a quick first down for the Dolphins despite good pressure. In the red zone, the Dolphins used a tremendous draw play to keep the sticks moving and set up a touchdown. On third and long, an obvious passing down, the Dolphins took advantage of the alignment and caught them looking for the quarterback. With the Chiefs in double three-techniques up front and both linebackers wider than normal, the Dolphins brought Ollie Gordon into the backfield on a motion and ran a quick trap draw look, pulling both Chiefs defensive tackles upfield and quickly putting the interior offensive line at linebacker level. Gordon builds speed and takes the Chiefs defense for a ride, finally being dragged down inside the five. These early conversions helped the Dolphins build momentum and stay in the game. Mid-game trouble The Dolphins would continue to attack on third down, and in the middle of the game they kept drives alive. After being the most-sacked quarterback in the NFL through two weeks, Willis was very cognizant of the pressure and ripped the ball as quickly as he could find open targets. The Dolphins set Willis up for success with quick routes built into their third-down packages and quick three-step drops out of shotgun; they made sure the ball was out of his hands before the pass rush could feasibly get home. Rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas came close a few times, but could not get home on third downs. Pre-snap, Gordon’s motion pulls Bolton out wide to help in coverage. Bolton taps Delane to move him off the line, but the move gives the wide receiver enough space to create separation on a slant, leading to another first down. The Dolphins made easy work of the Chiefs’ third-down defense early, but with adjustments and quick on-field thinking, the Chiefs overcame these issues. Late-game adjustments In the second half, the defense found ways to take away the quick routes, forcing Miami to look further downfield to convert late downs. Pre-snap, the Chiefs show multiple defenders across the line of scrimmage, giving the impression that a blitz is coming. On the snap, only four rushers come after Willis, and the Chiefs strategically drop into coverage to take away quick routes. Hicks and Thomas take away the tight end on the short side of the formation, while Sneed takes away the flat route, and Tranquil covers the deep route over the middle. The in-cutout of the bunch formation might have been open, but Willis sped up because of the pressure show and thought he had his man deep. Tranquill gave a good effort to stick on the deep route till the last minute, while Alohi Gilman was there to clean up the mess. The pass should have been picked off, but the play still got the defense off the field. Late in the game, the Chiefs would put the game away for good. On this snap, the Chiefs do bring pressure and drop into man coverage against the Dolphins’ bunch. Both outside corners quickly get to the receivers, taking away the quick throwing lanes. The Chiefs bring seven against a six-man protection, and Willis quickly drops back to the middle. Anticipating the quick release, Nick Bolton slows his rush and jumps, batting down the pass and stopping the Dolphins. Even if the pass had been delivered, Delane clung to the tight end and was in position to break it up. The bottom line The Chiefs’ mistakes were correctable, but against a better team, they could be the difference between winning and losing. The lack of pass rush, compounded by quick throws, allowed Miami to take advantage early. The schedule will only get harder, and over the next few months, they will face some of the league’s best teams at converting on third down.

(Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s not just the Chargers fan base that’s starting to freak out about Justin Herbert and the Chargers offense. ESPN insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano got together to discuss the latest around the NFL and part of that was discussing the panic meter for several underperforming quarterbacks. Of course, Justin Herbert was among that small group that included Cam Ward and Drake Maye. With more picks than touchdown passes through three games, Herbert’s too easy of a selection not to be discussed. “ Jumping to Herbert, his play is inexcusably bad, but he’s in Year 7 with 98 career starts, with most of those played at a high level,” says Fowler. ‘‘He has proof of concept more so than Maye or Ward. The jumbled offense under offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel hasn’t helped. And I’m not exactly sure where they turn next. ” Graziano’s opinion unfortunately did not differ much from Fowler. “Yikes. Talk about disconnect between player and scheme. Everything looks “difficult and exhausting” for Herbert, using the words of one evaluator I spoke to last week. There was so much talk in the offseason about how Herbert and his immense natural talent would flourish under McDaniel, but it’s clearly not clicking. A fresh wave of offensive line injuries that happened as the season was getting underway certainly didn’t help. But the run game can’t get going, the receivers haven’t taken the jumps we were promised, and Herbert has looked confused and overwhelmed by whatever it is he’s being asked to do out there.” “A lot of people have theories on what the Chargers need to do in terms of simplifying things so they can just start having success to build on. But there’s also concern that the personnel doesn’t fit what the offense is built to do, which might be difficult to overcome.” Despite it all, Fowler believes the old Herbert is still in there somewhere. ‘‘Look, Herbert has excelled as a true pocket passer, whereas McDaniel thrived having Tua Tagovailoa throw with anticipation to spots. Either Herbert struggles to do both or McDaniel isn’t putting him in a position to show that he can. I still think Herbert has good football in him, but that’s harder to sell by the week. And your point about mismatched personnel is a good one.” And now for today’s links. title: The Rams defense isn’t the problem
summary: Defense was a significant problem for the 2025 Los Angeles Rams. Fast forward a year later and they might actually be a defensive-first team. Through three weeks the Rams are currently the seventh-ranked defense in EPA per play. Further, LA is 10th-best in Pro Football Focus (PFF)’s success rate allowed, fourth in explosive play rate […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 27: Trent McDuffie #22 of the Los Angeles Rams talks to teammates in a huddle during the second quarter of the game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Defense was a significant problem for the 2025 Los Angeles Rams. Fast forward a year later and they might actually be a defensive-first team. Through three weeks the Rams are currently the seventh-ranked defense in EPA per play. Further, LA is 10th-best in Pro Football Focus (PFF)’s success rate allowed, fourth in explosive play rate allowed, and third in missed tackle rate. Even more impressive are the Rams’ numbers in the pass game. They are the third defense in EPA per play, sixth in passing rate success allowed, second in yards per attempt allowed, and third in completion percentage allowed. Of course, LA has faced two underperforming quarterbacks in Jameis Winston and Bo Nix. They also played the NFL’s best quarterback in nearly every statistical category, Brock Purdy, in Week 1. While Los Angeles is 23rd in run defense in terms of EPA per play, they are limiting explosive plays and rank eighth in this category. Similar to their high ranking in missed tackle rate, the Rams are allowing just 2.5 yards after contact per carry—good for 10th. The defense isn’t creating many zer0-yard runs or tackles for loss. They are 31st in the frequency of such plays. At the same time they aren’t letting opposing offenses rip off long gains on the ground. The silver lining is that the Rams have accomplished these rankings without the best defensive player in football, Myles Garrett, at 100% health. He’s missed the entirety of two games. Their fellow acquisitions of Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson are paying significant dividends. Moving forward, LA will still be without Garrett for a few weeks. Watson is expected to be sideline for this weekend’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles. It’s a concern whether Josh Wallace can adequately replace Watson; however, there are very encouraging signs about this group’s capabilities once they return—if they ever return—back to full force. Most will look at the inept performance in Australia against the 49ers and a second-half collapse against the Broncos and blame Chris Shula’s defense. This group also held a weak Giants offense to just six points sandwiched between those contests. The defense is doing its job. The offense needs to be more consistent, score more points, and take care of the football. Special teams most do its part and be a value add instead of a hinderence. It will take help in all three phases in order to pull the wagon and dig out of a 1-2 hole. At least the defense looks ready through three games.

full_text: The Los Angeles Rams have had two major wide receiver questions in 2026, one surrounding the impending free agency of superstar Puka Nacua, and the other centering on the team’s decision to draft Ty Simpson instead of a pass catcher. Some people believe that you should not extend a receiver for over $40 million per season because there are so many exciting players in the draft ever year, and others believe that the Rams should have never foregone the chance to draft Makai Lemon. Lemon — who the Rams will face when they take on the Eagles this week — has to avoid joining many recent examples for why receivers like Nacua are truly generational . Because the annual pre-draft report that “this receiver class is loaded!!!” seems to become more of a lie every year. Makai Lemon advanced stat rankings entering Week 4 (of 147 receivers): 146th in total EPA (-2.37) 79th in target share (11.11%) 78th in YAC (21) 131st in targets per route run (0.10) 135th in yards per route run (0.42) 108th in YBC/reception 118th in ADOT (6.56) — Tommy Jaggi (@TommyJaggi) September 29, 2026 NFL fans have been promised a new wave of “generational” wide receivers in the draft practically every year during this decade. So where are they? Surprise, surprise, it turns out that every year isn’t “the best class we’ve ever seen before” and that finding starting wide receivers in the draft isn’t as simple as picking a great athlete and plugging him into any offense. In fact, wide receivers have probably been much worse first-round draft picks than running backs recently. While running backs like Saquon Barkley, Christian McCaffrey, Bijan Robinson, and Jahmyr Gibbs have more than justified their top-12 draft slots, an inordinate number of early-pick receivers aren’t living up to the hype. As such, receivers like Marvin Harrison, Jr. and Brian Thomas, Jr. are rumored to be on the trade block. Harrison’s reported price tag is only a day three pick, per ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, less than three years after he was the fourth overall pick in the draft. Teams around the league are continuing to monitor Marvin Harrison Jr.’s situation with the Cardinals, with one team forecasting his market value as “possibly a quality Day 3 pick”, per @JFowlerESPN . Harrison Jr., the No. 4 pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, only has four catches for 73… pic.twitter.com/IoUEnY5XsA — Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) September 30, 2026 If you think the Rams can just trade Puka Nacua and be fine with “next year’s draft picks”, good luck with that plan. (And no, the Rams won’t have a pick high enough to take Jeremiah Smith.) 2021 PFF called 2021 “one of the best receivers classes we’ve ever seen,” headlined by Ja’Marr Chase, Jaylen Waddle, and DeVonta Smith. By those three names, the receiver class exceeded expectations, right? Well, what if you DIDN’T have a top-10 pick? The Eagles traded up for Smith and now we know why. The next 10 receivers off of the board could be classified as “busts” on one level or another. On the high end are guys like Rashod Bateman, and he has only had more than 515 yards once (756 yards in 2024) and he’s basically just a complement piece. Nothing teams can’t replace. It’s the same story with Josh Palmer and Dyami Brown. It’s not until you hit Nico Collins that the Houston Texans got very luck at pick 89. A star emerged in the fourth round when the Lions picked Amon-Ra St. Brown, but him and Collins are the only two starters drafted after pick 10! Just those two! 2022 The 2022 class had six first-round picks and the results are very mixed. Chris Olave is probably the best of the first three. Olave, Drake London, and Garrett Wilson are all Pro Bowl-level receivers, but not in the same tier as Nacua and Chase. London’s lack of high-end speed does really limit his ceiling. Then there’s Jameson Williams, the most talented receiver in the class. His injury history and a suspension for gambling have limited his production and now he’s only averaging 42 yards per game so far this season. Can you replace Puka or Davante Adams with Jameson? I don’t think so. Jahan Dotson and Treylon Burks are busts. The second round produced four starters (Wan’Dale Robinson maybe a borderline guy) and three busts. The one-dimensional quality of a George Pickens, Alec Pierce, or Christian Watson really stands out. Watson is currently fifth in the NFL in yards, so we’ll see if this is his big year or not. The third round produced nobody. Day three produced Khalil Shakir and Romeo Doubs. Okay. 2023 Ironically, 2023 was not as highly touted as the previous few years or the years after it. And yet it produced Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Puka Nacua, the reigning Offensive Player of the Year and the third-place finisher in the same category. So there’s those two. Then Zay Flowers is really good and Jordan Addison is above-average. The other first-rounder is Quentin Johnston and he’s a bust. The second-round produced four receivers (Jonathan Mingo, Jayden Reed, Rashee Rice, and Marvin Mims), whereas the third produced six (Dell, Hyatt, Tillman, Downs, Michael Wilson, and Tucker). Hyatt and Tillman are rather notorious busts, but Wilson is good. Tank Dell gets hurt too often. Josh Downs and Tre Tucker are useful. Day three produced Puka and Parker Washington and not much else. 2024 Also cited as a “generational” class , just two and three years after the last generation, people got overly excited by Malik Nabers after one season, and crowned Harrison before he ever actually did anything. Sell Malik Nabers. Sell low. Get anything you can. https://t.co/J8uuuiJpFo — Katz (@jasonkatz13) September 29, 2026 Nabers suffered a devastating knee injury in 2025 and he hasn’t been good this season. Maybe that will change after more time to adapt, but he’s bad right now. Harrison has always been bad. Rome Odunze is mediocre. Brian Thomas got overrated based on a productive rookie season and he’ll probably never be that good again. Three more receivers snuck into the first round: Xavier Worthy, Ricky Pearsall, and Xavier Legette . Out of seven receivers, what has the 2023 first-round actually produced going into year three? Best case scenario is probably that Nabers rebounds and maybe one other guy has a mid-career breakout. Ladd McConkey is surrounded by three busts in the second round, and McConkey is just pretty good. And there’s nobody really special in the rest of the rounds either. Including guys who were really hyped as steals, like Malachi Corley and Jalen McMillan. Just not much at all, including Jordan Whittington. 2025 Travis Hunter was hyped as the rarest type of player: a two-way starter at corner and receiver. Now in year two, the Jaguars have almost exclusively moved him to cornerback. Hunter has one catch for eight yards this season. The rest of the first round is up in the air, with Tetairoa McMillan, Emeka Egbuka, and Matthew Golden all off to fairly good starts. Egbuka is probably lagging behind the other two now. Outside of the first round, Luther Burden is maybe the only other receiver in the entire draft who consistently looks like a starter in the NFL. Most missed tackles forced among WR this season Luther Burden 6 Malik Nabers 4 Dohnte Meyers 4 Jalen Coker 4 Malik Washington 4 Ja’Marr Chase 4 Chris Godwin 4 pic.twitter.com/CHFwCoQIwr — PFF (@PFF) September 29, 2026 And in 2026, Carnell Tate is on one of the worst offenses in football, Jordyn Tyson is injured, and Makai Lemon is maybe not on the same page with Jalen Hurts or Philadelphia’s coaching staff just yet. It’s early to say. So how bad is this really? The NFL’s leading receivers are JSN, Olave, Adams, CeeDee Lamb, and Watson in the top-five for yards so far. Golden is actually eighth. But it’s not just about who is leading, it’s the hit rate for drafting wide receivers that has become the most deceptive thing about planning to replace a receiver in the draft next year. Those plans often fail . Even top-10 picks are no guarantee, but top-15 picks have been far more…

(Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Odell Beckham Jr. was released by the New York Giants, should the Los Angeles Rams give Beckham a shot to contribute for them in 2026? The last time Beckham and the Rams were together they won a Super Bowl, but that was a long time ago in football years. It’s unclear that Beckham can make the impact now that he did then. Or maybe it is clear which is why the Giants released him. Then again, the Rams don’t seem to have much offense outside of Davante Adams and Kyren Williams. Tyler Higbee had a great Week 3, but will that keep up? The tight end room for L.A. is wounded, and it’s unclear if their wide receiver room has enough depth. If the Rams want to give Beckham a shot, that’s fun, but if Beckham couldn’t stick on the New York roster, it doesn’t seem likely he’d make the L.A. one, but we’ll see. Giants release fan favorite Odell Beckham Jr. (espn.com) “Beckham, 33, is not expected to be added to the Giants’ practice squad at this time, a source told ESPN. The three-time Pro Bowler was hoping for a better result as he attended to some “unfinished business” with the franchise that drafted him 12th in 2014. Instead, Beckham played 19 snaps in three games and did not record a single catch.“ Broncos WR admits he ‘did sell’ the DPI that erased Rams’ interception (ramswire) “It was… it was a little pass interference,” Bryant said. “I did—I did sell it just enough, you know what I’m saying, to get the flag.
