title: Three potential returns could change Washington Commanders game plan
summary: The Commanders could be getting a significant boost in Week 4. Dan Quinn announced on Monday that Jayden Daniels, Frankie Luvu, and Chig Okonkwo will all travel to London and participate in practice this week ahead of Washington’s matchup with the Indianapolis Colts. Having all three back would give offensive coordinator David Blough and defensive […]
full_text: The Commanders could be getting a significant boost in Week 4. Dan Quinn announced on Monday that Jayden Daniels, Frankie Luvu, and Chig Okonkwo will all travel to London and participate in practice this week ahead of Washington’s matchup with the Indianapolis Colts. Having all three back would give offensive coordinator David Blough and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones more options in their game planning, but the impact could be especially significant at two position groups that have been hit hard by injuries. The question is: if only one of them can return this week, who matters most? The tight end position has yet to provide much production through three games, looking remarkably similar to the group Washington had in 2025. Okonkwo’s debut against the Philadelphia Eagles wasn’t particularly productive, but his skill set gives the offense something the current group has struggled to consistently provide: explosiveness, versatility, quick targets and yards after the catch. Through three games, John Bates, Colson Yankoff and Ben Sinnott have combined for just six receptions while averaging seven yards per reception. Adding Okonkwo back into the rotation could give Blough another weapon to move around the formation and create opportunities in the middle of the field. Luvu’s potential return could be just as important for Jones. With Leo Chenal out for the season and Jordan Magee already on injured reserve , Washington’s linebacker depth has become a legitimate concern. Behind Sonny Styles are Kain Medrano and Ale Kaho, neither of whom has significant NFL experience. At the same time, Medrano’s defensive debut provided a glimpse of what this defense could look like with younger players taking on larger roles. A rotation featuring Styles, Luvu and Medrano could give Jones another combination of athleticism and versatility as the defense continues to establish its identity. Then there’s Daniels. His availability is obviously the biggest question surrounding Washington heading into Week 4. Is this a legitimate ramp up toward playing against Indianapolis, or is the goal to get Daniels closer to 100% before the Week 5 home game against the New York Giants? There are still plenty of questions surrounding Daniels’ recovery and how the Commanders will manage his return. For Washington, the balance will be finding a way to get its franchise quarterback back on the field while limiting the risk of further injury. On the latest Trap or Dive Podcast, we break down all three potential returns, including a debate over which player Washington would rather have back this week if onl y Luvu or Okonkwo were available . We also look at what Washington’s win over Seattle means for the bigger picture. After an uneven start to the season, the Commanders are showing signs of an identity on both sides of the ball. We’re also taking a closer look at whether that development can carry Washington forward — and what these potential Week 4 returns could mean for the team. Podcast : View Link YouTube: Comment and let us know which of Chigg Okonkwo and Frankie Luvu you would rather have this week . Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

title: Here's why NFL players risk CTE despite knowing the dangers
summary: We asked over 30 NFL players about CTE concerns, and their answers ranged from fear to resignation.
full_text:
ON A HOT summer day, with sweat dripping from his nose and his body decked out in football pads from head to toe, Will Fries catalogs every step he takes in hope of avoiding chronic traumatic encephalopathy, the progressive, degenerative brain disease known as CTE.

 A diet heavy in fish and omega-3 fatty acids. 

 Glasses that block blue light. 

 Never getting less than eight hours' sleep. 

 Fries, a 28-year-old Minnesota Vikings guard in his sixth NFL season, was 17 years old when the movie "Concussion" was released in 2015 and 18 when NFL executive Jeff Miller sat in front of a congressional committee and acknowledged a link between football and CTE.

 "Your football life is short," Fries recently told ESPN, "and then you've got the rest of your life to live."

 Researchers believe CTE is caused by repeated subconcussive hits to the head, the kind that occur on nearly every play at every level of tackle football and in other contact sports. There are no specific symptoms or treatment for CTE, in part because it can't be diagnosed until after death.

 Studies of CTE, the brains of athletes and the effects of head trauma increased dramatically after links between the disease and football began to emerge alongside reporting that the NFL had led a two-decade campaign to deny such a link before Miller's comments in 2016.

 A study published this summer in the British Medical Journal determined that at least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE at the time of their deaths. A study published in January found that suicide rates among former NFL players were 2.6 times higher than among NBA and MLB athletes from 2011 to 2019. A 2024 study reported that nearly a third of former NFL players believed they had CTE. That group was five times more likely to have suicidal thoughts than those who reported they did not believe they had CTE.

 Ahead of this season, ESPN asked more than 30 active and retired players how the increased attention on brain trauma has affected their lives and career decisions. All were aware of CTE to at least a small degree, an advantage that thousands of their predecessors did not have. Some acknowledged that CTE has become a topic of dark humor, including Pittsburgh Steelers safety DeShon Elliott : "Sometimes you might draw a blank and forget something from last week and you go, 'Oh my god, it's that CTE.'"

 Like Fries, some players follow what they consider best practices to minimize their chances of getting CTE. NFL rules changes and attempts to improve equipment -- such as Guardian Caps -- instill confidence in some players. Others consider brain health out of their hands and ultimately an acceptable tradeoff for the benefits of an NFL career.

 

 "I think [for] any football player, that crosses your mind," said 26-year-old Arizona Cardinals receiver Michael Wilson , who's in his fourth season. "But also, that is so far down the line and ... the legacy, the financial gain that you can carve out for yourself to me outweighs the risk of CTE, especially as a wideout.

 "How cool would it be to leave a legacy that generations of my family, the Wilson legacy will talk about? And if CTE is a consequence of that, then so be it. But I also could sleep good at night knowing that I was the one person in the Wilson family that ended up changing our financial, socioeconomic class, like you can point it back to me and say, 'Michael's the one that did it.' So for my kids' kids' kids' kids, they can always look at me, and if CTE is a consequence of that, then I'm willing to bet on myself that hopefully I won't get it, but if I do, then I made a decision and I chose that."

 Weeks after the interview, Wilson signed a three-year, $75 million extension.

 "A lot of guys want to have families, and that's a goal of mine," the Vikings' Fries said. "Would I trade football for anything? Absolutely not. I love putting in the work and I know the risks of it, and I'm doing everything I can."

 Retired players, especially those who played before the connection between CTE and football was recognized, react to such views with varying emotions.

 Matt Hasselbeck, an NFL quarterback for 17 seasons who announced his retirement on March 9, 2016 -- five days before Miller's appearance at the congressional hearing -- recently announced he will donate his brain for CTE study after his death. In an interview with ESPN, Hasselbeck had pointed words for New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo , who when asked this summer on a podcast whether CTE was real, said: "No, it's an excuse." Skattebo later apologized , saying his response was a "tasteless joke."

 "CTE is a very real thing," Hasselbeck said. "And we have guys who are very conscious of it. We also have guys who are whatever the opposite of that is. We have guys that are rookie running backs slamming their heads into everything with their helmet. And then they're making light of it and they're making jokes of it. And they're, like, 'I don't care. You only live once.' And then they have to come back and apologize.

 "I'm thinking of Cam Skattebo this year. And I played with tons of guys like that. And it's funny in the moment. Teams like it because you're like, 'Oh, you're a warrior. I'll go to battle with you any day.' But it doesn't need to be that way. And there's a balance there where you can't live in fear, but also this is a real thing."

 The NFL's efforts to reduce concussions through major rules changes, helmet technology and technique changes have been well-documented. Regarding CTE, the NFL's chief medical officer Dr. Allen Sills, who has been in his role for over nine years, said the league is following three precepts.

 "We have to continue to do the research to try to understand how these pathologic changes might be caused in life symptoms," Sills said. "No. 2, we have to make sure that people don't self-diagnose and that they get properly evaluated, and that we treat symptoms that we know we can treat. And No. 3, we just double down on our efforts to reduce and prevent head contact where we can."

 In a statement this summer, the NFLPA said in part: "We all share a responsibility to advance research, improve access to care, develop better treatments, and support those affected by the long-term impacts of the game."

 Finances play a part in risking CTE 
 FOR MANY NFL players, the movie "Concussion" marked the introduction to the risks of long-term brain injuries from playing football. Among other events, the film dramatized the discovery of CTE in former Steelers center Mike Webster, who died in poor physical and mental health in 2002 at age 50.

 One NFC defensive lineman said CTE was "a tough thing to think about." An NFC defensive end remembered watching the movie in high school with his mother and said: "It was one of the reasons she didn't want me playing football."

 

 The reminders have continued this summer, most recently when researchers in July determined former Dallas Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland had CTE when he died by suicide eight months prior.

 And the family of former San Francisco 49ers star Aldon Smith , who died suddenly at the age of 36 in June, is awaiting the results of testing after donating his brain to the Boston University CTE Center to determine whether CTE played a role in his death.

 For some players, a concern for CTE and other long-term health risks prompted them to end their careers earlier than expected. One of the top rookies in 2014, linebacker Chris Borland, retired after just one season at age 24 citing concerns about head trauma . Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers offensive lineman Ali Marpet retired in 2022 at the age of 28. In an interview with ESPN earlier this month, he described it as "one of the hardest decisions I've made in my life."

 He added, "For me, my personal value system [prioritizes] health. And if that's going to be the case, I want to live authentically and in line with those values. And if…

title: NFL Week 4 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips
summary: Alarm bells for Justin Herbert and Drake Maye? More QB trades on the way? Growing injury concerns for the 49ers and Panthers? Here's the latest for Week 4.
full_text:
We're onto Week 4 of the  2026 NFL season , and insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 Drake Maye and the Patriots had an ugly game Sunday , but Maye is hardly the only quarterback with a concerning start to the season. Dan and Jeremy asked around the league to get a sense of which QBs land on the early-season panic meter. And after J.J. McCarthy kicked off trading season Monday in going to the Giants , our insiders poked around on more QB trades that could be on deck. Any other passers potentially switching teams?

 Additionally, is the league buying the 3-0 start from the Raiders, who have already matched their win total from 2025? Can Las Vegas keep this up? And which teams -- 3-0 or otherwise -- are getting hit particularly hard with injuries? It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 4.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 QB panic meter | QB trades 
 Raiders' start | Injury impact 
 Fantasy football advice 
 More notes, intel 

 
 

 Which QB currently sits atop the league's panic meter? 
 Fowler: Three come to mind here -- Drake Maye , Cam Ward and Justin Herbert . All three garner varying degrees of panic, but I'm putting Maye on top for now. The Year 3 regression is startling. He looks shaken right now. Mike Vrabel's comment after the 35-6 loss to Jacksonville was blunt: "My concern level is very high for this football team." Maye is a big part of that after six interceptions in three games. The next day, Vrabel questioned whether the Patriots' offense needs to scale back its game plans a bit, essentially to do less but do it better.

 

 Still, the notion that Maye's play can improve is there. He was considered one of the cleanest quarterback prospects of the past half-decade when he entered the 2024 draft. He played at an MVP level less than a calendar year ago. And to be sure, the Patriots have not played well around Maye and have not adequately protected him, and wide receiver A.J. Brown 's absence is deeply felt. The passing game was designed to feed him the ball often. Josh McDaniels' scheme is also considered to be complex for young passers.

 But dating to last year's playoffs, Maye's seven-game production line is 120-of-200 passing for 1,413 yards, seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions. Those are 1970s QB numbers -- and jarring for a quarterback seemingly on the door of superstardom (to be fair, four of those seven were playoff games against top-shelf defenses).

 So, I'm leaving the door open for Maye to fix it, but the panic can be found in Vrabel's voice right now. I mean, this team was in the Super Bowl last season, so the expectations couldn't have been higher. Perhaps last season's soft schedule masked a quarterback who was still very much in development.

 Graziano: It went largely unnoticed during their run to the Super Bowl, but Maye did not play well during the playoffs last season. And many of the issues that surfaced then have carried into this season. What I'm hearing is that it's not that Maye is a consistently poor decision-maker, it's that he's an occasionally disastrous one, and the mistakes are exceedingly harmful. Through three quarters of the season opener in Seattle, you'd have said Maye was playing well, demonstrating poise in difficult circumstances and putting his team in position to win. Then he fell apart completely in the fourth quarter.

 There are ups and downs with young players, but Maye's downs have been way too far down. And without Brown, the Patriots don't have enough around Maye to overcome the errors. His protection also hasn't been consistent. But while I don't get the sense that people think Maye has regressed, there is concern that we aren't seeing advancement in some of the young-player areas that should be improving for a quarterback who finished second in MVP voting and played in the Super Bowl.

 Fowler: After some conversations this week, I feel certain that Tennessee wants to give Ward more time despite his 3-17 record as a starter. Accuracy and decision-making are issues, but the Titans hope he will build off the late-game growing pains. He also isn't turning the ball over at a high clip (one interception through three games) and the team values his makeup and work ethic. Adjusting to Brian Daboll's offense has taken time, but averaging 12 points can test a front office's -- and locker room's -- patience only for so long.

 Graziano: The sense I get from Tennessee is that things are out of whack there and haven't gotten on track at all. I'm talking about the overall environment around the team, not just Ward. There's an obvious disconnect between Ward and the coaching staff, or at least the scheme, and the time to address and adjust those things was the spring and summer. How do the Titans fix lingering structural issues with their offense and with Ward's development during the season? There's still widespread belief that Ward has the character and the ability to weather early-career struggles and come out stronger for it. But there's also a sense around the league that it should look better than it does right now, and there's curiosity about what's preventing the improvement from happening.

 Fowler: Jumping to Herbert, his play is inexcusably bad, but he's in Year 7 with 98 career starts, with most of those played at a high level. He has proof of concept more so than Maye or Ward. The jumbled offense under offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel hasn't helped. And I'm not exactly sure where they turn next.

 

 Graziano: Yikes. Talk about disconnect between player and scheme. Everything looks "difficult and exhausting" for Herbert, using the words of one evaluator I spoke to last week. There was so much talk in the offseason about how Herbert and his immense natural talent would flourish under McDaniel, but it's clearly not clicking. A fresh wave of offensive line injuries that happened as the season was getting underway certainly didn't help. But the run game can't get going, the receivers haven't taken the jumps we were promised, and Herbert has looked confused and overwhelmed by whatever it is he's being asked to do out there.

 A lot of people have theories on what the Chargers need to do in terms of simplifying things so they can just start having success to build on. But there's also concern that the personnel doesn't fit what the offense is built to do, which might be difficult to overcome.

 Fowler: Next up for the Chargers: at Seattle , vs. Denver , at Kansas City , then a much-needed bye before the Rams , Texans and Ravens await. Oof. Not many get-right games on that schedule.

 Look, Herbert has excelled as a true pocket passer, whereas McDaniel thrived having Tua Tagovailoa throw with anticipation to spots. Either Herbert struggles to do both or McDaniel isn't putting him in a position to show that he can. I still think Herbert has good football in him, but that's harder to sell by the week. And your point about mismatched personnel is a good one.

 

 
 True or false: J.J. McCarthy won't be the only QB traded before the deadline. 
 Graziano: True! A lot of these situations are going to change drastically by midseason. Jacoby Brissett could struggle and prompt the Cardinals to want to see third-round rookie Carson Beck , which could lead to Brissett or veteran backup Gardner Minshew II being dealt. We heard talk in the offseason about the Bears looking into trading Tyson Bagent , and maybe someone gets interested if he gets a start or two during Caleb Williams ' absence and looks good.

 We also heard about the Eagles dealing  Tanner McKee , and they could still do so if they're comfortable with Andy Dalton as QB2. They could also deal Dalton. Joe Flacco is still in the league and always seems to appeal to someone, though I believe Cincinnati values him highly as a fallback should something…

title: Are we seeing more NFL quarterback injuries than normal this season?
summary: There have been eight QB injuries through three weeks of the NFL season, up a little bit from recent years. Is it a trend or just an outlier -- and is there a clear reason?
full_text:
It happened again. Just when it looked like we might get through a Sunday without an NFL quarterback getting injured for the first time in 2026, Tampa Bay's  Baker Mayfield went down in pain against the Vikings . On a day when Mayfield was sacked six times and knocked down on four more dropbacks, a glancing blow proved to be the most painful hit, as the Bucs starter suffered a dislocated thumb while trying to get the ball out on fourth down. The injury is expected to cost Mayfield about three weeks, which only makes life harder for the winless Buccaneers, who will now turn to Jalon Daniels in the meantime.

 Then, on " Monday Night Football ," both teams dealt with quarterback injuries. The Bears started Case Keenum after Caleb Williams injured his hamstring and Tyson Bagent spent most of the week in concussion protocol . The Eagles briefly lost Jalen Hurts to a concussion check of his own, and while he quickly returned to the game, he was out of the lineup just long enough for Andy Dalton to throw a critical interception in the end zone to end an Eagles drive.

 Depending on who you define as each team's primary option, Mayfield was somewhere between the sixth, seventh, eighth or even ninth starting quarterback to go down so far this season. The Bears likely would have started Bagent if not for the time in concussion protocol, but he didn't actually miss any action. Hurts was back quickly, as Dalton threw only one pass. You could argue that the Falcons would have started either Tua Tagovailoa or  Michael Penix Jr . in Week 1; both were injured, leaving them to start Cooper Rush instead.

 The NFL made it exactly zero drives without a starting quarterback going down this season, as Sam Darnold suffered a glute injury before the end of Seattle's opening possession in the season opener. He's already back after missing a couple of weeks, as is Kyler Murray , who left quickly in Week 1 because of a concussion .

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 The news was good on Jayden Daniels  ( elbow ) and Williams, who luckily avoided long-term injuries. Giants fans were less fortunate, as early suggestions that Jaxson Dart would be OK eventually turned more ominous. Dart underwent knee surgery to end his season last week. He's currently the only starting quarterback lost for the year.

 So, to recap: Seven quarterbacks have been forced out of games by injuries through the first three weeks of the NFL season. Is that a lot? Is it a problem that's getting worse? Are QBs getting hit more often? Are we seeing more backup quarterbacks than ever before? Should teams be investing more in those QB2s as a result? These are all legitimate questions to ask. So, I actually did the research this week to try to figure out how often quarterbacks get hurt early in the season.

 Going back through 2002 -- when the league expanded to 32 teams -- I looked at where every team and their preferred starting quarterbacks stood through the first three weeks of the season. I looked at every team that had two or more quarterbacks throw at least five passes through those first three weeks to see how often teams had been forced to turn to their backups for even a modest number of snaps. Let's see what history says about all these quarterback injuries.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Are we seeing more QBs than usual? 
 Are there more QB injuries than usual? 
 Why are so many QBs getting hurt? 
 Are QBs getting hit more than ever before? 
 Should teams invest more in QB2s? 

 
 

 Are we seeing more quarterbacks playing than usual? 
 Not really. Through three weeks, 41 quarterbacks have thrown at least five passes. That's up from a year ago, when 40 quarterbacks were on the board through three weeks, and tied for where we were in 2024. There was a four-year stretch between 2020 and 2023 when we saw fewer quarterbacks than normal, including just 35 passers appearing through three weeks in 2022.

 Since 2002, though, the average has been just over 39 quarterbacks with at least five pass attempts over the first three weeks of the season. And that number hasn't even changed all that much since the league emphasized roughing the passer rules heading into the 2018 season. Teams have averaged 38.9 quarterbacks through three games over that span.

 

 If it seems like we see more backup quarterbacks on a weekly basis than we might have 20 or more years ago, that's likely a product of simply seeing more football overall. Over the first three weeks of the season, the NFL put on 10 primetime "island" games to go along with widely available access to Sunday Ticket via streaming. In 2006, there were eight island games through three weeks, and Sunday Ticket was available only via satellite. In 1986, the league had five island games through three weeks, with no way to watch otherwise out-of-market games. We see more of every kind of quarterback than we did in the past.

 Yes, 41 quarterbacks is slightly more than the historical average but hardly out of line with what we've seen during the 32-team era. And if you go back even further into the past, coaches were cycling through QBs on an even more regular basis. In 1999, for example, 47 different signal-callers threw at least five passes through the first three weeks of the season despite the fact that there were only 31 teams in the league at the time. The same number popped up again in 1995, when the NFL had 30 teams. Was that a product of an era when defenses had more latitude to hit quarterbacks or coaches trying to find a better answer under center?

 

 
 Are we seeing more quarterback injuries than usual? 
 Yes. This is the most injured season through three weeks we've seen from NFL quarterbacks in recent memory. Defining an injury depends on your methodology, but in terms of quarterbacks who would have been in the lineup if healthy but weren't able to make a start, or backup quarterbacks who were forced into the lineup to throw at least five passes because the quarterback ahead of them on the depth chart wasn't healthy enough to play, the league has dealt with eight injured passers through three games. (While he hasn't yet thrown five passes, I'm counting Jalon Daniels as a backup who has been forced into the lineup, because we know Mayfield will be out for a few weeks because of his thumb injury.)

 Again, the evidence suggests that while the league is on the higher side relative to historical averages, it's not an outlier or indicative of a broader trend. Eight injuries to quarterbacks through three games is up from five in 2025 and four in 2024. The 2022 season was an outlier, with just two injuries through three weeks, but that's the lowest figure we've seen since 2002.

 The last time eight quarterbacks were unavailable by our criteria through the first three weeks of the season would have been all the way back in 1999. There were seven quarterbacks sidelined through three weeks of the 2019 season, a grouping that included Andrew Luck, who dealt with a calf injury all summer and then shockingly retired because of the ailment just before the start of the campaign.

 Over the course of the past 25 seasons, an average of almost exactly 5.0 quarterbacks have been injured by the end of Week 3. You can split that up into 4.6 quarterbacks who have been hurt during the regular season and an average of 0.4 quarterbacks who were injured and unavailable heading into Week 1.

 

 Depending on whether you consider Penix or Tagovailoa the preferred starter in Atlanta, we would have had either zero or one injured starter heading into the season, which isn't always the case. In 2016, for example, Teddy Bridgewater and Tony Romo suffered serious injuries before the season began. (These numbers don't include situations involving players who were holding out to begin past seasons, such as  Deshaun Watson and Carson Palmer, or players who were suspended to open the season, such as Watson and Ben Roethlisberger.)

 Since 2018, the NFL has ended Week 3 with an average…

title: Lamar Jackson, Ravens looking for first home win since before Thanksgiving
summary: Once among the most dominant teams at home, the Ravens have lost four straight games in Baltimore.
full_text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- Toward the end of his media session Wednesday, Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry made it clear that Sunday's game is more than his reunion with the Tennessee Titans . 
 
 "We need to win at home," Henry said. "We need to protect our home turf and that's got to be the emphasis. That's got to be the focus for us to go out there and do that on Sunday." 
 
 When the Ravens play the Titans on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, CBS), Baltimore will be looking for their first win at M&T Bank Stadium since before Thanksgiving. Once among the most dominant teams at home, the Ravens have lost four straight games in Baltimore, which is one shy of tying a franchise record. 
 
 It's gotten so bad at home that offensive tackle Roger Rosengarten recently acknowledged that he couldn't remember the last time the team had won in Baltimore. The answer: Nov. 23 against the New York Jets . 
 
 Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson said "there's a lot of urgency" to start winning at home. 
 
 "[It's] very disappointing to not just us but Flock Nation," Jackson said. 
 
 
 
 There was a time when the Ravens enjoyed one of the best home-field advantages in the NFL. From 2000 to 2024, Baltimore was 141-54 (.723) at home, which was the third-best mark in the league. Only the New England Patriots (144-50, .742) and Green Bay Packers (140-52-2, .727) had better home records during that span. 
 
 Now, since Week 13 of last season, there are only two teams who haven't won at home: the Ravens and the Arizona Cardinals . 
 
 "Personally, it bothers me a lot," Rosengarten said. "We have a very passionate organization and fan base, and you want to perform well in your home territory. To not come away with wins, it really stings. It's very upsetting and annoying. So, I'm ready to flip that narrative." 
 
 During this skid at home, there has been plenty of blame to go around. 
 
 In a 32-14 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals on Nov. 27, Baltimore turned the ball over five times. Jackson threw one interception and lost two fumbles. 
 
 In a 27-22 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Dec. 7, an overturned touchdown cost the Ravens. With about three minutes left in the game, tight end Isaiah Likely 's 13-yard touchdown catch -- which would have put Baltimore ahead 28-27 -- was ruled an incompletion after replay ruled the ball was ripped out of Likely's hands before his third foot was down. 
 
 In a 28-24 loss to the New England Patriots on Dec. 21, Jackson was knocked out of the game in the second quarter with a back contusion just before Baltimore was about to tie the game at 10. Backup quarterback Tyler Huntley then managed 58 yards passing in the second half. 
 
 In a 24-17 loss to the New Orleans Saints on Sept. 20, the Ravens allowed two touchdowns in the fourth quarter and Jackson's final pass was intercepted with 13 seconds left in the game. 
 
 During the four-game home losing streak, Jackson has not looked like his MVP self, throwing two touchdown passes and three interceptions. The only time in the Ravens' 31-year history that they have lost five consecutive home games was 2021 to 2022. 
 
 Heading into the Ravens' home opener in Week 2, Ravens coach Jesse Minter opened a team meeting by talking about the importance of protecting the home turf. This week, Minter has decided not to use winning at home as motivation. 
 
 "We want to chase the best version of us," Minter said. "We are a team that needs to really, really just focus on us and take care of us, clean up things that we can do and that we have major control over. And if we do that, we will live with the results."

title: What's level of concern for Panthers' notable injuries before Week 4 vs. Lions?
summary: Ahead of its first primetime game of the season Sunday, Carolina has seven noteworthy injuries to monitor.
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers (1-2) will be without their top two cornerbacks for the foreseeable future, and even with two-time Pro Bowl defender Jaycee Horn (quad) and fellow starter Mike Jackson (groin) on injured reserve, the team is monitoring injuries for seven other notable players ahead of Week 4's primetime matchup against the Detroit Lions on "Sunday Night Football." ( 8:20 ET, NBC ).

 "No one can replace Jaycee Horn," Panthers coach Dave Canales said Monday. The task for the team's other cornerbacks is to "do their jobs" in relief. But with Jackson also on the injury list, the Panthers' secondary will be tested against the Lions and beyond.

 Cornerback is not the only position group facing a challenge with injuries piling up for the Panthers.

 

 Following Carolina's 21-18 Week 3 loss to the Cleveland Browns , the Panthers are overseeing the injury statuses for several players, including starting quarterback Bryce Young and No. 1 wide receiver Jalen Coker . The MASH unit formed within the Carolina locker room has created issues as the Panthers try to finish the first quarter of the season with a .500 (or better) record for the first time since 2021.

 "It's a challenge because you want to know what your [game-day roster] is going to look like on Sunday so that you can have a significant game plan for your guys," Canales said Monday. "At a minimum, we start with the opponent and we say, 'Structurally, these are the things we do well -- how we want to attack.' ... So, we have to be able to look at all of those things and make assumptions based on the information that we have today and tomorrow to get that game plan going. But it presents its challenges."

 While the Panthers could see a potential upswing in reinforcements following their Week 5 bye, they still need to contend with a formidable 2-1 Lions squad first.

 Here's a look at seven of the Panthers' most notable injuries as of Wednesday's injury report, listed in order of significance to the team:

 
 

 Bryce Young , QB 
 Injury: Knee
 Wednesday's walk-through status: Full

 What happened: Young limped off the field after he was sacked by Browns DT Mason Graham  in the second quarter of the Week 3 loss at Cleveland. He returned on the next drive but went to the blue tent during the third quarter before making another immediate comeback. Following the game, Canales said Young was dealing with "something," but the QB said everyone is dealing with "something" in the NFL.

 Level of concern - Minor: Canales said Monday that he expected Young to play against Detroit. However, he also said the QB would undergo testing on his lower-body injury. Young led the offense in practice Wednesday without issue.

 Biggest issue for Week 4 (or beyond?): Through three weeks, the Lions have 57 QB pressures, which is tied for second in the league with the Atlanta Falcons , according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Detroit also has 12 sacks, which ranks as the second most in the league. Young has dealt with constant pressure over the past three weeks, so a hobbled version of the QB could be in trouble against the Lions' front.

 

 

 Devin Lloyd , LB 
 Injury: Calf
 Wednesday's walk-through status: Full

 What happened: Lloyd missed Week 3 after injuring himself during his epic Week 2 performance against the Falcons. Lloyd was replaced by Tyrel Dodson in the starting lineup against Cleveland.

 Level of concern - Minor: Canales said Monday that he expected Lloyd to return this week. The linebacker backed that claim a few minutes later, saying he was ready to go and nearly returned for Week 3. He returned to practice Wednesday.

 Biggest issue for Week 4 (or beyond?): The Panthers weren't particularly strong against the run with Lloyd sidelined in Week 3. Cleveland picked up 132 yards on the ground against Carolina, and even with QB Deshaun Watson factoring into that math, it wasn't a banner performance for the Panthers' front seven. Lloyd is a better run defender than Dodson or Bobby Okereke , and with Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs coming to town, his return to the field is notable.

 

 

 Monroe Freeling , OT 
 Injury: NFL concussion protocol
 Wednesday's walk-through status: DNP

 What happened: Freeling spent Wednesday's practice working with a trainer. Freeling played all 77 snaps against the Browns, but Canales said Freeling felt symptoms on Monday. The coach said he is hopeful Freeling will be cleared Thursday.

 Level of concern - Moderate: Freeling being on the field Wednesday isn't insignificant. It means he has gotten relatively deep into the concussion protocol process. However, with left guard Damien Lewis (elbow) out for Sunday's game, losing their fill-in starting right tackle would only make matters worse.

 Biggest issue for Week 4 (or beyond?): The Panthers would need to rely on Stone Forsythe in Freeling's spot if the rookie can't play Sunday. Forsythe had an up-and-down camp this summer after having an underwhelming season with the Las Vegas Raiders as a fill-in starting left tackle in 2026. Undrafted rookie Albert Reese IV would be Carolina's other option. Neither has played significant snaps in the first three games.

 

 

 Damien Lewis , LG 
 Injury: Elbow
 Wednesday's walk-through status: DNP

 What happened: Lewis was forced from the field in the second quarter of the Week 3 loss. However, he returned in the first half and played the rest of the game.

 Level of concern - Moderate: Lewis, who completed the Week 3 game, is arguably the team's top lineman over the past three seasons. The Panthers re-signed guard Saahdiq Charles to the practice squad for insurance, as ESPN reported earlier this week that Lewis is expected to miss Week 4.

 Biggest issue for Week 4 (or beyond?): The Panthers' offensive line has struggled mightily to begin the season. Against the Browns, Young was pressured on 51% of his dropbacks, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. The run game has also been inefficient, and with Lewis most likely down for at least Week 4, the Panthers will need to rely on recent waiver claim Corey Bullock (or newly promoted Charlotte native Torricelli Simpkins III ) to replace him.

 

 

 Jalen Coker , WR 
 Injury: Quad
 Wednesday's walk-through status: DNP

 What happened: Coker started the second half of the loss to the Browns on the sideline. After battling through an ankle injury during the previous two weeks, Canales said Coker's quad "lit up" on him during the game. He didn't return.

 Level of concern - Moderate: Coker said he didn't believe the quad injury was significant. A league source told ESPN's Ian Rapoport that Coker was considered questionable this week. Coker's history of soft tissue injuries, dating back to his rookie season in 2024, makes this a tad more concerning than a one-off ailment.

 Biggest issue for Week 4 (or beyond?): The Panthers could use another playmaker opposite Tetairoa McMillan . Despite missing half of last week's game, Coker still leads the Panthers with 222 receiving yards and all Carolina wide receivers with two touchdowns. If Coker can't play against the Lions, the Panthers will rely on Brycen Tremayne , John Metchie III and David Moore (who was promoted to the 53-man roster Wednesday) opposite McMillan.

 

 

 Xavier Legette , WR 
 Injury: Knee

 Wednesday's walk-through status: DNP

 What happened: Legette hurt his knee during the Week 2 win and missed Week 3's loss to the Browns as a result.

 Level of concern - Moderate: Legette had as many catches in Week 3 as he did in Week 1 -- 0. The difference is Legette played 35 snaps on opening weekend. Legette is a role player, and his absence is a run-of-the-mill issue in the NFL.

 Biggest issue for Week 4 (or beyond?): Like with Horn and Jackson, having two players hobbled at one position can be a major problem. With Coker banged up, Legette's participation is at least noteworthy. He could be replaced (again) by Tremayne and Metchie in the lineup against Detroit.

title: How to bet Steelers Browns on TNF: Analysis, tips and top prop plays
summary: Odds, bets and analysis to help you bet Steelers-Browns on "Thursday Night Football."
full_text:
The surprising 2-1 Cleveland Browns host the (maybe not so surprising, but still notable) 2-1 Pittsburgh Steelers on "Thursday Night Football" in a matchup I broke down in depth in my column earlier this week. I love the Steelers' ability to get to heavy personnel and run a variety of concepts, and perennially underrated back Jaylen Warren is seeing the field well behind his retooled offensive line. New starting right guard Brock Hoffman and rookie right tackle Max Iheanachor give the Steelers a five-across that can hang with anyone.

 

 But the Browns have a fast and aggressive front featuring second-year defensive tackle Mason Graham , free-agent linebacker Quincy Williams and trade acquisition Jared Verse . Cleveland's offense has been nothing special, but the defense can create short fields and keep games close. Against an immobile quarterback like Aaron Rodgers , the pass rush has a chance to really shine.

 Significant injuries in this game include cornerback Jalen Ramsey , who may try to go despite a broken wrist. His absence would dramatically impact the Steelers' pass rush and run defense approach, as they've been playing Ramsey in the box as part of their disguised looks. Browns center Elgton Jenkins looks unlikely to go, which is a particularly big deal against a Steelers defensive tackle room loaded with waves of talent ( Cameron Heyward ,  Keeanu Benton , Derrick Harmon and Yahya Black ). Starting guard Teven Jenkins did not practice Monday but was limited Tuesday, which is a good sign for his availability. The status of Joey Porter Jr ., the Steelers' star corner in need of a new contract, is as always uncertain.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 
 

 The Steelers offense had a peak day against the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 3, but they still bring into this contest a bottom-10 offense by success rate (29th), EPA per play (30th) and points per drive (29th). The Cleveland offense has been a little better, but the Browns have played easier defenses and remain bottom 10 in all three metrics. It is hard to trust either unit to move the football consistently, though both defenses have been liable to surrendering explosive plays. This does not feel like a night to take player prop overs, but some longest reception or rush props may be in play as one-offs.

 The Steelers are 2.5-point road favorites with heavy juice, which is appropriate given their advantages in the offensive trenches and at quarterback. If this is, as expected, a low-scoring game (total of 38.5), it's fair to side with the Steelers to grind out more positive runs and with Rodgers to avoid the backbreaking turnover that may swing this one.

 The pick: UNDER 38.5 total points (-115) 

 Without turnovers and short fields, it's hard to see many touchdown drives in this game. Neither offense is consistent enough down-to-down to turn red zone appearances into seven points, and they'll have to rely on explosives to hit paydirt. I also expect a fast clock, with the Steelers leaning on their running game against a penetration-heavy Browns front and the Browns doing the same to protect their weaker offensive line from dealing with the Steelers' group in pass protection.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 

 Quinshon Judkins rushing attempts OVER (-112) 

 Eric Moody: Judkins finished with 18 carries last week against the Carolina Panthers . The Steelers have allowed the eighth-fewest passing yards per game this season, which could push Cleveland to lean more heavily on the run. The efficiency may not be there for Judkins, but the volume should be.

 

 KC Concepcion 5+ receptions (+147) 

 Solak: Concepcion is only the ninth receiver in the last 26 seasons to have at least 20 targets and under 80 receiving yards through the first three weeks of a season. He is a high-volume player (95% route share last week!) who has yet to have a high-volume day because of quarterbacking failures. His role is far, far too juicy to not take the over of 4.5 receptions at +147. Todd Monken clearly wants to get Concepcion the football, and with Deshaun Watson struggling to do so, I'm anticipating that Monken will begin manufacturing easier touches for the exciting rookie receiver.

 Harold Fannin Jr . receiving yards OVER 40.5 (-111) 

 Moody: Fannin has seen at least six targets in his last two games and cleared this line in both. Watson's ability to extend plays helps, because when things break down, he has shown a tendency to look Fannin's way. Pittsburgh has defended tight ends well, but its zone-heavy scheme should give Fannin chances to settle into open areas underneath and over the middle.

title: Browns' QB situation takes a turn as Deshaun Watson finds his footing
summary: Cleveland's 2-1 start and the QB's late-game performances have helped to shift the conversation around the future of the position.
full_text:
DESHAUN WATSON JOGGED toward the tunnel leading to the  Cleveland Browns ' locker room at Huntington Bank Field surrounded by cheers last Sunday -- a stark contrast to the loud boos he received the last time he played in front of the hometown fans.

 Waiting outside the locker room for the Browns' starting quarterback was general manager Andrew Berry, who smiled broadly. The two shared a handshake and hug. With Berry's arm around Watson's shoulder, they turned, ready to celebrate with the team.

 The sequence leading to that scene and the change in reception from fans was a game-winning touchdown drive to defeat the Carolina Panthers  21-18 in Week 3. The win marked Watson's second fourth-quarter comeback in as many weeks, which seemed implausible after a late August preseason game, when Watson struggled in the second half, was loudly booed, and later lashed out at fans in the postgame news conference.

 

 That preseason discontent seemed like the final chapter for a player who received a five-year, fully guaranteed $230 million contract in March 2022 but was crumbling under high expectations in Cleveland. Through four seasons, 19 mostly underwhelming performances were sandwiched between an 11-game suspension after more than two dozen women accused him of sexual assault and inappropriate conduct during massage sessions, and multiple significant injuries since Cleveland traded three first-round picks to the Houston Texans for Watson.

 Entering the 2026 season, the consensus view among Cleveland spectators was that the Browns might finally part ways with Watson at the end of the regular season, taking an exorbitant $86 million dead cap hit while possibly turning to the 2027 NFL draft -- with the Browns holding two first-round picks -- to solve the franchise's perpetual quarterback conundrum. Such a conclusion would render playing Watson pointless.

 Instead, Watson emerged as the starter following a monthslong competition. His late-game performances and the Browns' 2-1 start have added another wrinkle to the NFL's most confounding quarterback dynamic: Cleveland enters its "Thursday Night Football" home game against the Pittsburgh Steelers ( 8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video ) with first place in the AFC North on the line.

 "[Watson] is playing pretty well. At least give him enough of a sample size to see what he can do," an NFC executive told ESPN.

 While team sources indicated that Watson's performance through three games hasn't convinced the Browns to consider Watson the long-term answer, Cleveland's surprising start has shifted the conversation inside the building to whether the 31-year-old passer and the Browns can build short-term momentum.

 "I feel like I have a lot of football left in my game, in my career, and that's how I approach the game," Watson said last week. "That's how I approach my preparation on and off the field. I feel like I'm 10 years in, but still got a lot of football to play, definitely for myself."

 

 
 THE BROWNS HAVE selected three quarterbacks in the past two drafts -- 2025 picks Shedeur Sanders and Dillon Gabriel (who is currently on injured reserve), and 2026 sixth-round pick Taylen Green -- but first-year coach Todd Monken named Watson the winner of a quarterback competition with Sanders that stretched from offseason workouts in April into the first month of training camp in August.

 Monken faced questions about his decision to tab Watson as QB1 despite an inconsistent training camp and preseason in which he threw more than a dozen interceptions. Monken explained that Watson's full body of work, experience, and athleticism gave Cleveland's offense the best chance to succeed. He added that he expected Watson to improve with more reps and that the QB conversation wouldn't be a weekly query. However, with two road games to begin the season before the home opener, Watson's first two starts since tearing his Achilles in October 2024 almost felt like an audition to keep the starting job.

 When Watson struggled in a 34-10 Week 1 blowout loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars , the Week 2 matchup against former Browns quarterback Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers looked like a potential inflection point for a QB change and an opportunity to evaluate Sanders.

 Monken continued to back Watson, who delivered one of his best moments in a Browns uniform in Tampa. Watson rallied Cleveland from a 10-point second-half deficit and threw the game-winning touchdown in a 23-19 victory , securing his first win as a starter since September 2024.

 Watson's second game-winning drive this season against the Panthers seemed to vindicate Monken's decision-making, and it gave the quarterback more runway to remain Cleveland's starter. Sanders, who entered in for one play on the game-winning drive after Watson took a big hit, remains the backup.

 

 Monken has said he wants the Browns' quarterback play to reach a level in which he doesn't have to face weekly questions about who will start.

 "Do I love dealing with it every week? Of course not," Monken said two weeks ago. "You guys keep asking, which is a lot of fun, but the reality is, of course. Of course. And I'm happy for Deshaun, the way he's played, and I expect improvement, and I expect continued improvement.

 "There's a lot of football left in him; he just hasn't played in a while. And learning our system and trying to get him consistent with his drops and his reads is part of the process. He's like every player. I see him as a young player. I know people don't want to see it that way, and I haven't been here, but I see him as still a very young player that is going to continue to grow."

 The QB questions have ceased -- at least for a week -- with production from Watson that has been modest but also clutch in key moments. Watson has completed 68.3% of his passes for 587 yards, five touchdowns and one interception. His 62.3 QBR, his highest single-season mark in Cleveland, ranks 15th out of 30 qualifying quarterbacks. Watson, though, has been at his best in high-leverage situations; his fourth-quarter QBR rises to 95.1, the fifth-highest mark in the league.

 Despite two surgeries to repair a torn right Achilles tendon, Watson has used his legs effectively; his 105 rushing yards are the fifth most among quarterbacks.

 Team sources said Watson's ability to move past negative plays and stretches instead of compounding them has stood out.

 Watson's recent play still hasn't matched the standard of a contract with a fully guaranteed value exceeded by only two players: Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen and Dallas Cowboys QB Dak Prescott . Team sources acknowledged that expectations for Watson were uncertain after his 22-month layoff. Nonetheless, he has delivered his best two-game stretch in a Cleveland uniform. It's the second time Watson, who has an 11-11 record as the Browns' starter, has won consecutive games since joining Cleveland.

 "There's never a scenario where you pull a healthy QB you're paying $40-46 million a year within the first six weeks of the season to tank," the aforementioned NFC executive said. "Especially if [the team is] showing signs of life. If it's Thanksgiving and they stink and Watson stinks, then that's different."

 
 

 WITH A DEFENSE returning to form under new coordinator Mike Rutenberg, the big question in Cleveland is whether Watson's play is sustainable and can be improved. The Browns have won their past four home games against the Steelers, but none has come with Watson under center. Watson is 0-3 against the Steelers in his career, including two games as a member of the Browns in which he completed 59.4% of his passes and threw three touchdowns with three interceptions.

 While Watson has delivered in late-game moments, he and the Browns' offense, which ranks 24th in scoring (18 points per game), have started slowly in each game this season. Watson has thrown for 334 yards in the first three quarters of Cleveland's three games, and his 30.9 QBR before…

title: NFL trade deadline grades: Joey Porter Jr. to Cowboys, J.J. McCarthy to Giants
summary: Can Joey Porter Jr. clean up the Cowboys' defense? Will J.J. McCarthy improve the Giants' QB situation? We're grading NFL trades ahead of November's deadline.
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline , which will pass on Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for the first two deals of trading season:  J.J. McCarthy  to the Giants and  Joey Porter Jr . to the Cowboys. Check back right through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

 

 

 Steelers trade CB Porter to Cowboys 
 Cowboys get: CB Joey Porter Jr . 
 Steelers get: 2027 sixth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

 Cowboys grade: B 
 Steelers grade: C+

 This is the Cowboys' third trade with the Steelers in the past 18 months ( George Pickens  and  Broderick Jones ), and it's their third trade involving a star defensive player after acquiring Quinnen Williams at the trade deadline last season and shipping Micah Parsons to Green Bay last offseason.

 It's easy to see what the Cowboys are doing here. DaRon Bland , who first broke onto the scene as a slot corner, was playing on the outside given Dallas' lack of depth. By acquiring Porter, Bland can move back inside, which will allow the Cowboys to relocate 2026 first-round defensive back Caleb Downs , as well. He has been playing the slot, but his natural position is at safety. These are options, not guarantees. Bland might stay outside as the Cowboys instead pursue a strong 1-2 punch at outside corner, with Porter shadowing WR1s.

 The salient point is this: Porter can have a rising tide impact on the Cowboys secondary, clarifying the roles of other players and enhancing the whole unit in the process.

 Porter is not as tricky of a scheme fit in Dallas as people think, too. His strengths are certainly his length and physicality, such that he can line up in press -- but he has been in press alignments on only 30.6% of his snaps over his career, just above the league average for cornerbacks (24.1%). Porter is a much better man coverage defender than he is in zone, as his passer rating allowed in man coverage over the past four seasons is better than all but Derek Stingley Jr . But the Cowboys are actually running more man coverage (24.8%) under first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker than the league average (23.2%) over the first three weeks.

 

 Of course, early-season rate stats can be noisy. Parker's Vic Fangio-inspired defense will require Porter to play from greater depth than he did in Pittsburgh, and the communication and keys required in that match-heavy system will take some getting used to. But Porter has a valuable and rare skill set in his press-man ability, and premium picks should be spent on players with premium traits. The Cowboys got much, much better in the secondary -- though the move is not without risk.

 Acquiring Porter does not solve all their deficiencies; linebacker is still a big problem for this team, and the edge rush isn't far behind. But if the secondary needs less schematic help now that Porter is in play, more coaching tools can be used to hide those other weak spots.

 For the Steelers, Porter's recurring back ailments seemed incurable without an extension or a relocation -- what can you do? It's frustrating that GM Omar Khan invested more in third-contract players like Jalen Ramsey and T.J. Watt over a younger, second-contract player like Porter -- Ramsey and Watt will hit their athletic wall far sooner than Porter. Jamel Dean , another third-contract player signed to play corner opposite Porter, now has to cover WR1s alongside Asante Samuel Jr . and 2026 third-round pick Daylen Everette . Corner is no longer a strong position on Pittsburgh's depth chart.

 Porter reportedly had contract demands up at the top of the cornerback market, where Devon Witherspoon and Christian Gonzalez recently reset elite deals to clear $33 million annually. I'm not sold that Porter is a top-tier corner deserving of that top money. But because the Steelers let this go on for so long and bleed into the regular season, they were only able to acquire a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick for a young, ascendent cover corner. They could have -- and should have -- gotten at least a first-round pick by playing this differently and dealing Porter in the spring or earlier in the summer.  -- Solak 

 
 

 Vikings trade QB McCarthy to Giants 
 Giants get: QB J.J. McCarthy 
 Vikings get: 2027 fifth-round pick

 Giants grade: C 
 Vikings grade: B+

 A mere 22 days after the Giants signed Jameis Winston to a two-year, $13 million extension , New York decided it needed to trade a fifth-round pick for an alternative at quarterback. Of course, a lot has happened in three weeks.

 Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury in Week 2 that is expected to keep him out for at least the regular season. And Winston has delivered two poor performances in Dart's stead, with a 19.0 QBR in relief in Week 2 against the Rams and a 27.9 in Sunday's 12-7 win over the Titans. So in comes McCarthy, the No. 10 pick in the 2024 draft.

 McCarthy's pro career has gone poorly so far, which is putting it mildly. He suffered a season-ending knee injury in August 2024, which helped Sam Darnold become Minnesota's starting quarterback. McCarthy was named the starter last season after Darnold departed in free agency but started only 10 games after a series of injuries cost him time. And when he was on the field, the results were not good.

 McCarthy posted a 36.1 QBR in 2025 (which ranked 38th out of 45 quarterbacks with at least 100 pass attempts) and recorded a minus-5% pass rate over expected, per NFL Next Gen Stats (43rd out of 45). He threw interceptions at a 4.2% clip (44th), took sacks on 9.4% of dropbacks (40th) and had a 1.8% fumble rate (41st). More alarming is that he did all that while playing for Kevin O'Connell, who has seemingly elevated most of the non-McCarthy quarterbacks he has called plays for.

 

 During training camp, not only did McCarthy lose the Vikings' starting quarterback competition to Kyler Murray , but he then lost the backup competition to Carson Wentz , too. That is a telling red flag.

 So why would the Giants trade for him? McCarthy presumably still has some upside based on his draft pedigree, and the Giants are hoping they can profit from him realizing it. But it's hard not to notice the fact that this is John Harbaugh trading for the quarterback his brother, Jim Harbaugh, coached in college at Michigan.

 It is difficult to know from the outside which other backup quarterbacks would have been available, but McCarthy still does not seem like an ideal choice. Mac Jones and Spencer Rattler ought to have been the team's first calls (maybe they were). Kirk Cousins probably is off the board with the Raiders sitting at 3-0. Mitchell Trubisky might have been available, considering this already looks like a lost season for Tennessee. And I'm assuming  Gardner Minshew II  surely must be available, considering he sits in veteran no-man's land between Jacoby Brissett and rookie  Carson Beck  in Arizona. Stetson Bennett IV could have been an option, too, after the Rams selected Ty Simpson in the first round of this year's draft. I'll grant that some of those options have less upside than McCarthy.

 But the Giants' front office should look in the mirror over its bungling of the Winston situation. It's not unreasonable for the Giants to be aggressive in finding a better replacement given how much time is left in the season. But they clearly shouldn't have signed Winston to an extension right before the season if this…

title: Christian Izien stars in strong defensive week for NFL stars with Africa ties
summary: Detroit Lions safety Christian Izien - who is from Far Rockaway, Queens, but has always proudly represented Nigeria too - was a standout among many NFL stars with ties to Africa who shone in Week 3.
full_text:
Detroit Lions safety Christian Izien - who is from Far Rockaway, Queens, but has always proudly represented Nigeria too - was a standout among many NFL stars with ties to Africa who shone in Week 3.

 There were some highlights on offense too - notably from Jaxon Smith-Njigba and John Metchie III - but generally, this was a week where defense shone brightest for the continent's stars.

 Africa Player of the Week: Christian Izien (Detroit Lions) 
 

 Izien was immensely influential for the Detroit Lions in their 31-24 win over the New York Jets, making a total of 11 tackles - nine of which were solo tackles - and defending one pass.

 Izien - who has family ties to Nigeria - made three tackles for loss in addition to a vital intervention to prevent a touchdown right on the stroke of half-time. Geno Smith went for a Hail Mary with the Jets 10-7 down, but amid a sea of bodies from both teams, it was Izien who got to the ball first to tip it away.

 His performance played a key role in the game ending in favour of the Lions - who are 2-1 for the season, with the Jets 1-2.

 Africa Moment of the Week: Thomas Incoom and Maema Njongmeta (Carolina Panthers) 

 There were plenty of big hits to choose from among Africa's NFL stars. However, Incoom (born in Ghana) and Njongmeta (born in Cameroon) get the nod for collaborating in a moment which demonstrated what Africa has to offer the NFL.

 

 As their Carolina Panthers faced the Cleveland Browns, Njongmeta forced a fumble with a huge hit on Malachi Corley and then Incoom - who had earlier set the tone with a massive hit himself - was on hand for the fumble recovery.

 Although the Browns ultimately emerged victorious 21-18, it was not for any want of trying from the West African duo.

 Honorable mentions 

 Jaxon Smith-Njigba - who proudly represents Sierra Leone, with which he has ties through his grandparents - scored two touchdowns among a total of 10 receptions for 128 yards. His Seattle Seahawks lost 33-31 to the Washington Commanders despite his contribution on offense and Uchenna Nwosu (ties to Nigeria) defending a pass.

 John Metchie III - who is of Nigerian and Taiwanese descent and lived in Ghana as a young child - scored a touchdown for the Panthers in their defeat to the Browns. Nigerian-American outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen also made a notable contribution even in defeat for the Panthers, picking up a sack.

 Adetomiwa Adebawore deserves special mention for his 1.5 sacks for the Indianapolis Colts in their 19-17 win over the Houston Texans.

 Ruke Orhorhoro (Jacksonville Jaguars), Ogbo Okoronkwo (San Francisco 49ers), Eyioma Uwazurike (Denver Broncos), and Dayo Odeyingbo (Chicago Bears) - all of Nigerian descent - all picked up sacks in Week 3 wins.

 Osa Odighizuwa, who contributed to the Niners' 36-30 win over the Arizona Cardinals with a pass defended, also has ties to Nigeria.

 So, too, do players who had impressive moments on both sides of the Buffalo Bills' 24-16 win over the LA Chargers - Davison Igbinosun defended a pass for the winning side and Justin Eboigbe forced a fumble for the Chargers.

 Africa-born player watch 

 Ghana's Incoom and Cameroon's Njongmeta did the continent proud with their performances for the Panthers in the Browns loss. It is worth noting that Ruke Orhorhoro, who picked up a sack for the Jacksonville Jaguars in their 35-6 thrashing of the New England Patriots, was born in Lagos - one of many players who flew the Nigerian flag high in Week 3.

title: Packers' O-line leaves Jordan Love under constant pressure
summary: The Packers have allowed more "quick pressures" against Love than any team in the NFL -- and it's not close.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- When Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love said after last week's  35-14 loss to the Atlanta Falcons that he needs to make quicker decisions, the next question should have been: How much quicker can he possibly make them given the light speed with which opposing pass rushers have been in his face?

 According to Next Gen Stats, the Packers have allowed the most "quick pressures" -- defined as pressure on the quarterback in less than 2.5 seconds -- in the NFL, and it's not close. Love has been quick pressured 37 times in three games. No other team has allowed more than 28.

 In last Thursday's loss, the Falcons recorded 15 quick pressures, second most in a game this season. The most was the 17 the Packers allowed to the Vikings in Week 1.

 "Obviously you always need time," Love said Wednesday. "The more time you have, the better you're able to pick apart the defense and find those completions. That's with anything, you always want time. Obviously there's times you might not have time, you've got to find those answers.

 "That's an area that we've got to improve on, in pass [protection], making sure we're going to the right people and sustaining blocks for as long as we can, give me some time to pick the defense apart and obviously something that we need to improve on."

 

 At some point, the concern is the impact it will have on Love -- both from a fundamental standpoint and when it comes to his health -- if it hasn't already. The concern is that a quarterback who has been hit so many times can start to feel pressure even when it's not there, or as coaches and scouts call it, "seeing ghosts."

 "There's definitely some plays, especially later in the [Falcons] game, where we talked about my feet are just getting a little bit off and that definitely is some of the pressure being a factor in that," Love said. "In that scenario, I've just got to be better right there.

 "I can improve my game to make sure I'm staying on schedule, trusting my feet, reading with my feet, and it's going to help me be as accurate as possible. But I think it's a natural reaction sometimes as a quarterback, you might feel sped up. I've got to fight that urge and trust my feet and still be great in the pocket."

 

 While Love has thrown for the fourth-most yards (844) through three games and has six touchdown passes against two interceptions, the problem is that he has a 1.7 QBR when pressured. That's the second lowest in the NFL ahead of Denver's Bo Nix (1.1). Love has a 31% completion rate, no touchdowns and both of his interceptions when pressured.

 Teams might even try to send more rushers after Love. He ranks only 10th in pressure percentage this season, according to ESPN tracking, taking pressure on 38% of his dropbacks. However, that could be in part because he's averaging 2.49 seconds per pass, the quickest in the league according to Next Gen Stats. He averaged 2.84 seconds in his first three seasons as a starter.

 "I would say there's certain situations, yes," LaFleur said when asked if Love could get the ball out quicker. "But then there's a lot of times where the rush has been hitting home quick.

 "You've got to look at what you're asking your guys to do and what we're doing schematically, and we've got to do a better job of mixing it up, I would say, so it's not just all these longer developing plays."

 The Packers have a team pass block win rate of 16%, the worst by far since ESPN first began tracking it in 2017. That said, pass rushers have been winning at a higher clip this season, which has caused the league wide pass block win rate to drop to 49% this season from the league average of 59% over the past 10 seasons.

 

 The individual results look just as bad, if not worse.

 Of the 66 qualified tackles, left tackle Jordan Morgan   ranks 65th and right tackle Anthony Belton  is 66th. Belton took over early in Week 2, when Zach Bako-Bewele sustained a season-ending knee injury.

 Of the 67 guards that are ranked,  Donovan Jennings  sits at 63rd, Jacob Monk  66th and Jager Burton  67th.

 At center, Sean Rhyan ranks 32nd out of 33.

 Enough about the numbers. If Love thinks he needs to process things quicker, then it's up to the coaches to help him figure out how.

 "We've had a lot of hard conversations, some really productive conversations, I'll just leave it at that," offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said this week. "But we just need to run our offense."

 It's not just about pass protection, either considering the run game might be a bigger problem. How much of that is because they're without running back Josh Jacobs , who remains on the commissioner exempt list, is debatable. But through three games, the Packers have rushed for a league-low 146 yard -- the fewest by a Packers team through three games since at least 1933. Of course, it's hard to run for much more when they had only nine rushes against the Falcons.

 And then there's the personnel department's responsibility in this.

 Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst was so confident about his offensive line, a group whose only major addition this offseason was Burton, a fifth-round pick, that he kept 10 on the roster because he was "really worried about people poaching our guys."

 Less than a month later, Gutekunst had to revamp the position. In a span of five days in the past week, he signed three former first-round picks: Kevin Zeitler and Laken Tomlinson to the 53-man roster plus Mekhi Becton  to the practice squad.

 They made their practice debuts Wednesday, and it's not out of the question one or more could play Sunday  when the 1-2 Packers are at the 0-3  Tampa Bay Buccaneers  ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ).

 

 Zeitler is the most accomplished of the three, but he had no training camp and before Wednesday had not been on a field since last season's regular-season finale with the Titans. Zeitler has played almost all of his 214 career games at right guard, where Monk has struggled and now is on the injury report with a quadriceps issue.

 Tomlinson has played most of his career at left guard, where the Packers have started three different players. Preferred starter Aaron Banks remains on the injury report with knee and toe injuries.

 "Obviously 1-2, it is what it is," Zeitler said. "A million things have happened, but there's a lot of talent on this team, lot of great guys and things can flip just like that."

title: Can the 0-3 Texans defy history again to make playoffs?
summary: Houston became the first team in the common playoff format to make the postseason after starting 0-3 in 2025.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Is it déjà vu for the Houston Texans ?

 The preseason Super Bowl contenders find themselves at 0-3 for the second straight year -- and the losses have come in similar fashion.

 Last year, the Texans' first three games were lost on the last drive, and this season, the same happened in two of the three weeks.

 Quarterback C.J. Stroud was sacked and fumbled inside the red zone on Houston's last drive against the Buffalo Bills in Week 1, and in Week 3, the Texans' defense allowed a game-winning field goal against the Indianapolis Colts  with 16 seconds remaining.  

 

 But Houston remains confident despite the frustration.

 "We've been here before," Stroud said after the latest loss. "We can get these fixed, and we will." 

 Like last season, Houston's offense hasn't been great. The unit is averaging 18 points (tied for 23rd) and 326 yards (14th in total offense). Stroud also has been sacked 10 times, tied for second most in the NFL.

 They might have been able to circumvent history last year, but even that was a tall task. Entering this season, 25 teams had started 0-3 under the current playoff format (since 2020), and last year's Texans are the only one to reach the postseason, according to ESPN Research. Houston also became the seventh team in the Super Bowl era (1966) to reach the playoffs after 0-3, and the last team to do it before that was ... the 2018 Texans.

 "In this league, no one cares about what happened," Stroud said. "They just want to see if you won or lost. So at the end of the day, we know who we are in our locker room. We know we will hear noise all week.

 "But at the end of the day, it's us in the locker room."

 The Texans started 3-5 last season before winning their final nine games, but slow starts have become a trend for Houston under coach DeMeco Ryans. In Ryans and Stroud's debut season in 2023, the Texans started 0-2. The only anomaly under Ryans is 2024, when they started 2-0. 

 

 Still, the Texans have found a way to climb out of those holes -- reaching the divisional round of the playoffs during the past three years. But Ryans won't lean on past experiences because he believes each year is different.

 "For me, if we're 0-3, obviously I haven't coached good enough," Ryans said. "So, haven't coached good enough. I've got to coach better. If I coach better, we'll find ourselves on the winning side."

 The offense has sorely missed Pro Bowl wideout Nico Collins , who had seven catches for 75 yards and a TD in the opener. After compiling 381 yards in the opener, Houston has averaged 298.5 yards (23rd) and scored 11.5 points (tied for 30th) without Collins (hamstring). 

 Last year through three weeks, Houston's offense averaged 12.7 points (last), but its defense allowed 17 points (tied for fifth best). And while the defense gave up 36 points in Week 1 to the Bills, it has allowed 19.5 points (tied for 11th) and 283 yards per game (eighth fewest). The defense also has the fourth-best success rate (33%), the second-most sacks (nine), ranks third in tackle for loss rate (11.5%), sixth in yards per play (4.4) and fifth in quarterback pressure rate (22.1).

 But an alarming issue for the Texans has been their run game. The offensive line has allowed running backs David Montgomery and Woody Marks to be hit at the line of scrimmage 66.7% (the highest by eight points) on carries, according to Next Gen Stats. The unit has missed right guard Ed Ingram , who has missed the past two weeks with a groin injury, but a 33% stuff rate (the highest against) isn't sustainable for an effective run offense.

 Montgomery and Marks average minus-.3 yards a carry before contact, the lowest in the league -- which might be a telling story as to why Houston has the lowest rushing yards from running backs (33 per game).

 

 Stroud said there's "no excuses" for how they've performed, and Ryans believes they are working to improve things despite the alarming statistics. 

 "We're looking at everything from an offensive standpoint of the running game," Ryans said. "What can we do differently for us to make sure we can turn out some yards in a run game. The guys have to keep working. Have to keep trying to do some different things as well schematically with our run game. We just keep pressing forward. But we're headed in the right direction. We just have to clean up a few things."

 Despite the rough start, ESPN's Football Power Index still gives Houston a 22.4% chance to make the playoffs (the highest of the five remaining winless teams), but to avoid trying to have to defy history -- since 1990, only the 1992 Seattle Seahawks have made the playoffs after starting 0-4 -- a win over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, CBS) would be a good starting point.

 All-Pro defensive end  Will Anderson Jr ., drafted one spot after Stroud, believes the Texans are trending toward a turnaround.

 "We're heading in the right direction," said Anderson, who had 2.5 sacks Sunday. "What would the NFL be without adversity, and it sucks that we had to start this way again. But we're built for it. We have to keep chopping wood."
