title: Why Geno Smith's hot start has been a bright spot for the Jets
summary: Despite being 1-2, the 35-year-old QB is completing over 75% of his passes.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- When the New York Jets traded for Geno Smith in March, bringing him back to where he started his career in 2013, it prompted a loud groan from their quarterback-scarred fanbase.

 Smith 1.0 doesn't evoke fond memories for Jets fans, and his performance last season for the Las Vegas Raiders was so uneven that the franchise was willing to eat $16 million of his 2026 salary to have him play elsewhere.

 Desperate for a bridge starter, the Jets took on the reclamation project, hoping he could recapture his Seattle Seahawks form -- circa 2022 when he led passers with over 100 attempts in completion percentage (69.8) -- and provide stability at their most unstable position.

 Through three games, Smith, 35, has exceeded expectations in New York, giving off early comeback-season vibes.

 

 "He's a warrior, man," tight end Jeremy Ruckert said. "He's a field general. We have the utmost confidence in him."

 Smith's completion rating (75.5%) ranks first in the NFL among qualified passers, and he's giving credence to the slogan, "What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas" -- which is to say, he's not throwing interceptions like he did as a member of the Raiders.

 After a league-high 17 interceptions last season, Smith has yet to throw one in 102 pass attempts. The last time he went three straight games without a pick was the final three games of the 2023 season, his second year as the Seahawks' starter.

 There's a lot of season left, but it's worth noting that Smith is putting up numbers that would rank among the best passing seasons in franchise history.

 Disclaimer: It's not a glittering history. Beyond franchise icon Joe Namath, there's only a sprinkling of above-average to excellent seasons over the last half-century.

 Only two players passed for 3,000 yards, 20 touchdowns and a 65% completion rate in the same season -- Chad Pennington (2002) and Brett Favre (2008). Mind you, these aren't extraordinary benchmarks. In today's NFL, they represent a solid season. In Favre's case, he had as many touchdown passes (22) as interceptions, which blemishes his season.

 With 783 yards and four touchdowns, Smith is on pace to blow away those marks. Of course, perspective is important.

 Smith has battled inconsistency at times in his career, and his current supporting cast is banged up. The status of running back Breece Hall (quad), wide receiver Adonai Mitchell (finger) and tight end Mason Taylor (thumb) are uncertain as they prepare to face the Chicago Bears on Sunday at Soldier Field. Chances are, he won't have Hall, a blow to an already sputtering rushing attack.

 That said, Smith has emerged as one of the early bright spots in the Jets' 1-2 start. On Sunday, he passed for 321 yards and three touchdowns in the 31-24 loss to the Detroit Lions , the first Jets' quarterback since Mike White in 2022 to have 300 yards and three touchdowns in a game.

 

 Coach Aaron Glenn praised Smith for "delivering the ball with confidence," staying in the flow of the offensive scheme and handling pass rushers in his face. Without Mitchell and Taylor, he still connected with eight different receivers, with 14 of his 31 completions going to tight ends. He also found Garrett Wilson on a consistent basis (10 receptions for 107 yards), something he didn't do in the first two games.

 "Are there some things that he has to improve on? Absolutely, absolutely he does, and he would tell you that himself," Glenn said of Smith. "But I think, overall, I was really pleased on how he operated."

 Smith's one mistake was a sack-fumble on the Jets' last possession, from the Lions' 28-yard line. He took the blame for the turnover, his first of the season. Glenn said, "He has to be able to hold on to the ball in that situation, so we can have another opportunity."

 Otherwise, he was almost perfect in the fourth quarter, completing 15 of 17 passes for 156 yards. Smith had more passing yards in that one quarter than Justin Fields produced in five of his nine starts last season.

 "He makes it easy to play receiver," said rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq , who had his first NFL touchdown reception Sunday.

 Smith will be a free agent after the season, and he knows that his chances of remaining a starter in the league will hinge on how he performs with the Jets. Maybe they will ask him back as a transition quarterback, holding the spot while they groom a highly drafted rookie.

 He hasn't talked about his future, though he acknowledged in spring that a triumphant comeback with the Jets, the team that drafted him 13 years ago, "would be like a story in a movie, right? Kind of like one of those superhero movies."

 It's still early in production, but the first few scenes look promising.

title: Why Darnell Washington has become the Steelers' X factor
summary: At 6-foot-7 and nearly 300 pounds, the Pittsburgh tight end is more than a viral hurdle highlight reel.
full_text:
PITTSBURGH --  Darnell Washington vividly remembers the youth football practice where he hurdled his first defender.

 A perpetual outlier among his peers since a third-grade growth spurt, Washington towered over the defender opposite him in the Oklahoma drill. As he strategized his approach before the whistle, Washington got an idea.

 "I'm going to just hurdle him," he thought.

 And that's just what he did.

 "It felt amazing just passing somebody without getting touched because I never juke, so I can't say, 'Oh, I juked somebody clean and just kept running,"' Washington said. "I know I don't do that. So even back then, it's a similar game plan, at least for me. Stiff arm, lower the shoulder or hurdle."

 Nearly two decades later, Washington's size advantage and moves are the same, but the stage is not. Now checking in at 6-foot-7 and officially listed at 264 pounds, but realistically closer to 300 pounds, the Pittsburgh Steelers tight end is making a name for himself with highlight-reel hurdles and stiff arms against the unlucky defensive backs tasked with slowing him down.

 

 Thursday night, the 25-year-old will have an opportunity to add another chapter to his legendary lore in the Steelers' first primetime matchup of the season against the Cleveland Browns ( 8:15 ET, Amazon Prime ).

 Washington, though, is more than a viral clip. He's the X factor of the Steelers offense as a sure-handed pass catcher, practically untackleable runner and selfless blocker.

 The stats support Washington's impact, too. The Steelers are 13-2 when Washington plays at least 40 offensive snaps. When he plays fewer than 40 snaps on offense, the team's record drops to 18-22. Perhaps it's not a coincidence that Washington played 47 snaps in the Steelers' 30-27 Week 3 win against the Cincinnati Bengals .

 And as coach Mike McCarthy watched Washington turn one of those snaps into a 47-yard path of destruction with Bengals defenders trailing helplessly behind him, the Steelers coach had one thought: "Why don't you give him the ball more?" McCarthy said Monday afternoon, laughing as he thought back to that moment. "I think that's probably what everybody else is saying. He's unique. You can see it, and it seems like it's always on the sideline. He's a hard guy to tackle. I mean, he's a tough matchup."

 That has been the case since former Desert Pines (Las Vegas) High School coach Tico Rodriguez first noticed Washington playing wide receiver for a different school in a 7-on-7 tournament in the summer of 2017, just after Washington's freshman year.

 "He was very coordinated for his size," Rodriguez said. "And I was just like, 'Wow, this coach is very lucky to have him.'"

 Three weeks later, Washington unexpectedly walked into the weight room at Desert Pines.

 "He had just moved into our area, and my prayers had been answered," Rodriguez said. "He just walked in, 6-6, 220 and I was like, 'Wow.' It was a perfect fit for him to be here with us."

 

 Each week, Rodriguez said, players from opposing schools looked forward to giving Washington their best shot. More often than not, they failed.

 "They would try," said Rodriguez, who coached Washington from his sophomore to senior year. "And a lot of times Darnell would let them know, 'Yeah, I'm built like an NFL guy. I'm not just a high school guy.' And they would learn really quick that the big man had a lot of power and balance.

 "Pretty much the best thing they could do was take his legs out, but then he's steamrolling over them. He would win a hundred percent of the time."

 In Nevada high school football, hurdling is illegal and penalized with a 15-yard flag. Washington, though, did it out of necessity, and Rodriguez couldn't even be upset.

 "He does it to protect himself, because he's so tall and a lot of guys want to cut tackle him," the coach said. "I could see why he did it and it was just like, we'll take the penalty and we'll just keep moving. We'll get it in the next play."

 Washington did a little bit of everything for Desert Pines: wide receiver, running back, tight end, defensive end and even punter.

 "I was one of those kids who just wanted to be on the field at all times," Washington said. "If I wasn't on punt pro, I wanted to become a punter."

 By his senior season, Washington was a five-star recruit with a bouquet of offers from powerhouse college programs. He chose Georgia, moving across the country to play for coach Kirby Smart and offensive coordinator Todd Monken -- who is coincidentally now the Browns' head coach.

 

 Despite the sure hands and natural bend that made him a formidable pass catcher, the Bulldogs primarily used Washington as a blocking tight end and a complementary player to receiving tight end Brock Bowers , who became the Las Vegas Raiders ' 2024 first-round pick. While Bowers had 175 receptions, 26 touchdowns and more than 2,500 receiving yards from 2021 to 2023, Washington finished his three-year stint in Georgia with 45 career receptions for 774 yards and three touchdowns.

 "You get the ball in his hands, he's hard to bring down," Monken said of Washington. "We probably didn't do it enough even in Georgia. Having him on the edge helps you block the C-gap, helps you be able to run the ball. And he's got such great range and power. He is hard to get. ... You won't bring a big man like that down with his size if you don't gang tackle him and get him well."

 Since he was underutilized in college, Washington slipped to the third round of the 2023 NFL draft , where the Steelers landed him with the No. 93 pick. Though he appeared in every game in each of his first two seasons, Washington's role as a pass catcher was limited. He added more bulk to his frame, prompting some on social media to debate the viability of moving Washington to the offensive line.

 Following the discourse from a distance, Rodriguez could only shake his head at the speculation. While Washington did a little of everything at Desert Pines, Rodriguez never considered that kind of position change.

 "The way he moved and how coordinated he was, we didn't need him at offensive line," Rodriguez said, adding that Washington was a lean 260 pounds playing football and basketball. "We saw him as a vital threat on offense as a weapon. We never thought about him as an O-lineman.

 "Seeing him from high school and how athletic he was and when he caught the ball, how violent he runs with it. I was just hoping he would get opportunities to touch the ball. When he touches the ball, he's very special. When he touches it, he makes things happen."

 Washington's opportunities to do just that -- and on the biggest stage -- increased once quarterback Aaron Rodgers joined the Steelers in 2025. In his first season playing with Rodgers -- the quarterback once compared him to a young Marcedes Lewis  -- Washington had career highs in targets (43), receptions (31), yards (364) and first downs (16). This offseason, the Steelers showed more belief in Washington by committing to him on  a four-year, $42 million extension -- the most for a player primarily labeled as a blocking tight end.

 

 "He's just such a big body," Rodgers said after a win against the Indianapolis Colts last season in which Washington hurdled a defender. "I want to throw it up to him. ... He's a damn good player, and he needs the ball. When he gets the ball, good things happen. He's got good hands and he's good after the catch."

 Through three games this season, Washington has 92 receiving yards and three first downs. He's also averaging a career-best 15.3 yards per reception.

 But it's not the number of yards that makes Washington a uniquely lethal offensive player. It's how he gets them. Nearly 62% of Washington's receiving yards this season have been gained after first contact, and he leads the league in that category with a whopping average of 9.5 yards. The next closest player is Browns wide receiver Denzel Boston with an average of just 5.89 yards.

title: Aaron Rodgers' 2026 NFL season: Tracking records, milestones
summary: The Steelers QB is chasing records in his 22nd NFL season, and ESPN is chronicling his "last rodeo."
full_text:
Entering his 22nd NFL season -- or as Aaron Rodgers says, "his last rodeo" -- the 42-year-old Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback is on the cusp of joining several exclusive clubs as he moves up the ranks in the league record books.

 In 2025, he passed former teammate Brett Favre to take sole possession of fourth place in career touchdown passes thrown with his 509th TD pass in the Week 3 win against the New England Patriots .

 "Every now and then I made some special throws that led to touchdowns, but I've been playing a long time, and it's a longevity thing," Rodgers said before passing Favre's mark last season. "I'm proud of it, but not a big deal."

 Rodgers also went on to supplant Ben Roethlisberger for fifth in all-time passing yards in the second quarter of the Thursday night loss to the Cincinnati Bengals on Oct. 16, 2025.

 But now, Rodgers is closing in on his final opportunities to add to that growing list of historic accomplishments.

 Among the milestones in reach for Rodgers are becoming the fourth quarterback in NFL history to appear in 300 games (as of Week 3 he has appeared in 290), joining Tom Brady (383), Favre (326) and Drew Brees (305), throwing the fourth-most touchdown passes in NFL history (as of Week 3, he has 531) and having the second-most regular-season games with multiple touchdown passes. And after Week 3, he needs 3,026 yards to become the fifth player to reach 70,000 passing yards . 

 This season, we're chronicling Rodgers' individual milestones week by week as he rides his last rodeo. Follow along here for the weekly installments.

 

 
 Preseason: 0-for-0, 0 yards, 0 INTs, 0 sacks, 0 rushes 
 Despite early hints that Rodgers would take the field during the Steelers' first preseason under McCarthy, the veteran quarterback instead spent two games on the sideline and one on his couch at home. With Rodgers' top two receivers in DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr . sidelined with preseason injuries, McCarthy opted to also keep his quarterback under wraps.

 Rodgers isn't a stranger to sitting out the preseason in recent years. He didn't play in any preseason games for the Steelers in 2025, nor for the New York Jets in 2024 following his season-ending left Achilles tear in Week 1 of the 2023 season.

 
 

 Week 1:  Steelers 20, Falcons 13 
 Rodgers' stat line: 221 yards, 1 TD, 0 INTs, 2 sacks, 3 rushes for -1 yard 
 Rodgers didn't break any records this week, but he pulled within one touchdown pass of Peyton Manning for fourth most in NFL history with his second-quarter throw to tight end Pat Freiermuth  for 6 yards. The touchdown toss was Rodgers' 232nd of the regular season. Rodgers had 26 pass attempts in the first half, his most attempts in the first half of a game since 2020 at Minnesota as a member of the  Green Bay Packers , per ESPN Research.

 After Sunday's game, coach Mike McCarthy said he wanted to find more balance in his offense, which ran the ball just 21 times to Rodgers' 40 pass attempts. Rodgers, though, didn't mind all the throwing.

 "No, keep doing it," Rodgers said, urging his coach to keep calling passes. "Keep doing it."

 And although Rodgers and the Steelers got the win, the quarterback struggled under the pressure from the Falcons' front. He completed 3 of 12 attempts under pressure and was sacked twice. And continuing the trend from last season, Rodgers was also 3-of-12 on throws of 15 or more air yards. Some of those incompletions, though, were the result of drops by his receivers.

 "I liked the plan from Mike," Rodgers said. "I liked the playcalling. We took some shots. I felt like we had really close to having one of those really good games. If we come down with a couple of those, it obviously looks a little different on the scoreboard and stat sheet and stuff, but love my guys, love  DK [Metcalf] .

 

 

 Week 2: Patriots 20, Steelers 3 
 Rodgers' stat line: 187 yards, 0 TDs, 1 INT, 4 sacks, 1 rush for 5 yards 
 Rodgers set two personal Steelers milestones in the team's Week 2 loss -- and not in a good way. Rodgers was off target on 26% of his throws (nine attempts) in the loss, his worst as a Steeler. The Patriots frustrated Rodgers with heavy pressures and blitzed on 19 of 44 dropbacks (43%), the second-highest rate he has faced with Pittsburgh. Against the blitz, he was 8-of-17 for 42 yards with two sacks and an interception. And he had his first interception against the blitz as a member of the Steelers.

 "It's frustrating, for sure," Rodgers said of not getting into the end zone at New England on Sunday. "The defense has been playing great. They've been holding [opponents to] 13 points a game in two games, and offensively I think we're averaging like eight points a game. That's not winning football."

 

 

 Week 3: Steelers 30, Bengals 27 
 Rodgers' stat line: 292 yards, 3 TDs, 1 INT, 2 sacks, 3 rushes for 10 yards 
 It turns out Rodgers still has plenty left in the tank. A week after one of his worst performances as a Steeler, Rodgers bounced back with three passing touchdowns to help the offense put up a season-best 30 points and 411 yards in the win against the Cincinnati Bengals . Rodgers aired it out in the first quarter with two touchdown throws and 143 passing yards -- the most he has thrown in the first quarter since Week 6 of 2018 against the 49ers (170). Each of his touchdown passes traveled at least 20 air yards, marking his first time with multiple touchdowns of 20-plus air yards since he joined the Steelers. Entering Sunday's game, Rodgers was 0-of-9 on pass attempts of 20-plus air yards.

 "We definitely needed it because it was just uncharacteristic of us," Steelers wide receiver Ben Skowronek said of the offense's bounce-back performance. "Throughout camp, we felt really confident in what we were doing, moving the ball. And the first two weeks we just weren't us. So credit to the coaching staff, the guys in the building, we locked in this week and we knew we had to have it. We knew we could do it."

 After two weeks without much movement in the record books, Rodgers is starting to make some headway. Sunday's win marked the 165th of his career, tying him with Ben Roethlisberger for fifth most by a starting quarterback since positions were first tracked in 1950. With his first-quarter 38-yard touchdown throw to Roman Wilson , Rodgers also recorded his 233rd career game with at least one passing touchdown, tying Peyton Manning for the fourth most such games in NFL history.

 

 

 Week 4: at Cleveland Browns ( 8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video ) 
 With a 13-6 record in Thursday games, Rodgers enters the Week 4 matchup tied with  Dallas Cowboys  quarterback Dak Prescott for the second-most wins on Thursday in the Super Bowl era. The only person in front of him? Tom Brady with 14, meaning Rodgers can move into a tie for first place with a win in Cleveland.

 Rodgers last played a memorable Thursday night game a season ago in Cincinnati when he and Bengals quarterback Joe Flacco dueled it out in the "Unc Bowl." Though the Steelers lost, Rodgers had one of his best games of the season. His 71.4 QBR was his second highest of the 2025 season -- trailing only the 72.8 he posted against the Browns a week earlier -- as he threw for 249 yards and tied a season best with four touchdown throws.

 

 For his career, Rodgers averages 256 passing yards and completes 68% of his pass attempts in Thursday games. He also has a 69 total QBR on Thursdays.

 So why is Rodgers so good on Thursdays? He said this week: "Probably because I'm so excited about the weekend off. I just suck it up for those three hours and then know you get a reward on the back end.

 "I mean, it's not like I'm feeling excellent today. It's a Tuesday. Normally that's the recovery day. But yeah, I mean, I think it's part of the game now because of the money that's in it. We played a lot of games over the years on Thanksgiving or Thursday night games, so we expect to win a lot of those. We have, but it's nothing special. I…

title: London game reminds Marcus Mariota of the connection between football and soccer
summary: For Mariota, who grew up playing soccer, Sunday's game against the Indianapolis Colts at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium is a chance to combine his love of both sports.
full_text:
HERTFORDSHIRE, England -- The first sport Washington Commanders quarterback Marcus Mariota played as a kid -- soccer -- continues to help him in the one he plays as an adult. But the combination of the two is why Mariota is ecstatic about another opportunity to play in a famed soccer stadium.

 

 There's a strong chance Mariota starts Sunday in place of Jayden Daniels , who was limited in practice Wednesday with a dislocated left elbow. If that happens, then Mariota will have performed a meaningful trifecta for himself: starting football games in three iconic soccer stadiums.

 The Commanders (1-2) play the Indianapolis Colts  on Sunday at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, home of the team of the same name. Mariota started at the Bernabeu Stadium last season ( Real Madrid ) and at Wembley, where the England national team plays, in 2019.

 In those two games, Mariota lost to the Los Angeles Chargers on a failed two-point conversion at Wembley while playing for the Tennessee Titans ; and to the Miami Dolphins in overtime last season. He has a chance to prove that the third time is, indeed, a charm Sunday.

 "I grew up being around the game," Mariota said. "So, to play at Wembley and then last year play in Madrid and then now play at Tottenham that's really cool for me. It's kind of a cool moment. So, I'm looking forward to it."

 When asked who his favorite Spurs player was, Mariota said former star Harry Kane , the club's all-time leading scorer who left to play with Bayern Munich in 2023.

 "I know that might be a little bit rough right now," he said, laughing.

 Mariota has been known for his elusive runs, sometimes spinning out of and emerging from harrowing situations in the pocket. And to be a quarterback in the NFL requires having adept footwork.

 That's why he said there's a definite connection between the sports.

 "Spatial awareness," he said about how soccer helped him. "As you play soccer -- fútbol -- like, you had to know the next move before the ball came to you. And being able to see the field, where people were at, kind of diagnose where to put the ball, I feel like that helped my spatial awareness as a quarterback."

 In the pocket, it's also about taking drops.

 "All the footwork stuff, definitely," he said. "Whether it's taking five, seven step drops, being out of gun, out of pistol. All those things are little things, but things that I felt like fundamentally soccer brought to me. So, I love the game."

 Mariota said he doesn't have a favorite team, but added his brother, Matt, is "religious" about following the English Premier League . Matt Mariota, a former walk-on at Oregon, also played some college football in England at Leeds Carnegie. His team? Liverpool .

 The nice thing for Mariota and Washington is that he's coming off a strong performance in a 33-31 win over Seattle, throwing for 176 yards and three touchdown passes.

 "I've always had a belief in myself. So that 'prove it' has never really crossed my mind," he said. "I'm not here to prove anything."

 Besides, Sunday isn't just about proving what he can do, it's also about enjoying where he's doing it.

 And he wants to hand that love of soccer and its fundamentals to his two children.

 "It was the first game I played, and as my kids are growing up," he said, "I definitely push them into that direction because I think it's just a, it's such a good fundamental sport for everything."
